hard.q: What is the difference between a mammal and a reptile?
hard.a: Mammals have fur/hair and feed young on milk; reptiles have scales and are cold-blooded
hard.hint: Think about how a cat and a lizard are different.

hard.q: Why do some animals migrate?
hard.a: To find food, warmth or better breeding conditions
hard.hint: Think about why birds fly to warmer countries in winter.

hard.q: What is the life cycle of a frog?
hard.a: Egg, tadpole, froglet, frog
hard.hint: Think about the stages from spawn in a pond to an adult frog.

hard.q: What do we call the process when a caterpillar changes into a butterfly?
hard.a: Metamorphosis
hard.hint: This is the big change from one form to another.

hard.q: Why do plants have roots?
hard.a: To absorb water and minerals from soil and to anchor the plant
hard.hint: Think about what roots do underground.

hard.q: What is the difference between a herbivore and a carnivore?
hard.a: Herbivores eat only plants; carnivores eat only meat
hard.hint: Think about the diet of a rabbit compared to a lion.

hard.q: What is a food chain?
hard.a: The order in which animals eat each other, starting with a plant
hard.hint: Think about: grass β†’ rabbit β†’ fox. What does this show?

hard.q: Why do leaves change colour in autumn?
hard.a: The green chlorophyll breaks down as days get shorter and colder
hard.hint: Think about what the green colour in leaves does, and why it disappears.

hard.q: What is an invertebrate?
hard.a: An animal without a backbone
hard.hint: Think about animals like worms, snails and insects.

hard.q: Why is the sun important for life on Earth?
hard.a: It provides light and heat needed for plants to grow and animals to survive
hard.hint: Think about what would happen to all life if the sun disappeared.

hard.q: What is the difference between a solid and a liquid?
hard.a: A solid has a fixed shape; a liquid flows and takes the shape of its container
hard.hint: Think about ice (solid) and water (liquid).

hard.q: What is pollination?
hard.a: When pollen is carried from one flower to another, allowing seeds to form
hard.hint: Think about the role bees play when they visit flowers.

hard.q: Why do animals in cold climates have thick fur?
hard.a: To keep warm by trapping heat
hard.hint: Think about what fur does to help an animal survive cold temperatures.

hard.q: What is the difference between a predator and prey?
hard.a: A predator hunts other animals; prey is the animal that is hunted
hard.hint: In the relationship between a fox and a rabbit, which is which?

hard.q: What are the main parts of a flowering plant?
hard.a: Roots, stem, leaves, flowers
hard.hint: Think from the bottom of the plant to the top.

hard.q: What does nocturnal mean?
hard.a: Active at night and sleeping during the day
hard.hint: Think about owls β€” when do they hunt?

hard.q: Why do fish have gills?
hard.a: To breathe underwater by taking oxygen from water
hard.hint: Think about how fish breathe without coming to the surface.

hard.q: What is a habitat?
hard.a: The natural environment where an animal or plant lives
hard.hint: Think about a fish in a pond or a mole underground.

hard.q: Why do we need sleep?
hard.a: To allow our body and brain to rest and repair
hard.hint: Think about how you feel when you haven't slept enough.

hard.q: What is the difference between weather and climate?
hard.a: Weather is what it is like outside today; climate is the usual weather pattern over many years
hard.hint: Think about today's rain (weather) versus 'England is usually cold and wet' (climate).

hard.q: Why do flowers produce nectar?
hard.a: To attract insects that carry pollen to other flowers
hard.hint: What does the flower get in return for offering nectar to bees?

hard.q: What happens in the water cycle?
hard.a: Water evaporates, forms clouds, falls as rain and flows back to sea
hard.hint: Think about how water moves from the ground, to the sky, and back again.

hard.q: Why do some animals have sharp teeth?
hard.a: To catch, kill and tear meat
hard.hint: Think about what lions and wolves eat and how their teeth help.

hard.q: What is the difference between a deciduous and an evergreen tree?
hard.a: Deciduous trees lose their leaves in autumn; evergreen trees keep their leaves all year
hard.hint: Think about an oak tree in winter compared to a pine tree.

hard.q: What do decomposers do in nature?
hard.a: They break down dead plants and animals and return nutrients to the soil
hard.hint: Think about what happens to a fallen leaf over time.

hard.q: Why do some insects look like flowers or leaves?
hard.a: Camouflage β€” to hide from predators or to ambush prey
hard.hint: If a stick insect looks like a twig, what advantage does it have?

hard.q: What is the role of a flower in a plant's life cycle?
hard.a: To produce seeds for reproduction
hard.hint: Think about why a plant needs to make seeds.

hard.q: What do we call animals that hatch from eggs and have scales?
hard.a: Reptiles
hard.hint: Think about snakes, lizards and crocodiles.

hard.q: Why is it important for plants and animals to live in the right habitat?
hard.a: They need specific conditions (food, shelter, temperature) to survive
hard.hint: Think about why a polar bear could not survive in a desert.

hard.q: What is the difference between a vertebrate and an invertebrate?
hard.a: Vertebrates have a backbone; invertebrates do not
hard.hint: Think about what a fish and a worm have (or don't have) inside them.

hard.q: Why do plants need water?
hard.a: For photosynthesis, to carry nutrients and to keep cells firm
hard.hint: Think about what happens to a plant that is not watered.

hard.q: What is an ecosystem?
hard.a: A community of living things and their environment working together
hard.hint: Think about all the animals, plants and conditions in a pond.

hard.q: Why do some animals live in groups?
hard.a: For protection, hunting and raising young
hard.hint: Think about why lions live in prides or fish swim in schools.

hard.q: What is the purpose of seeds?
hard.a: To grow into new plants
hard.hint: Think about what happens when you plant a seed.

hard.q: What is the difference between evaporation and condensation?
hard.a: Evaporation is water turning to vapour; condensation is vapour turning back to water
hard.hint: Think about a steamy bathroom mirror.

hard.q: Why do carnivores have forward-facing eyes?
hard.a: To judge distance accurately when hunting prey
hard.hint: Think about how a cat watches a mouse β€” why do eyes face forward?

hard.q: What do we mean when we say an animal is endangered?
hard.a: Its numbers are very low and it is at risk of dying out
hard.hint: Think about a species that could disappear from Earth forever.

hard.q: Why is biodiversity important?
hard.a: Different species depend on each other; losing one can affect many others
hard.hint: Think about what would happen if all bees disappeared.

hard.q: What is the difference between instinct and learned behaviour?
hard.a: Instinct is built-in behaviour an animal is born with; learned behaviour is taught or discovered
hard.hint: A spider spinning a web vs a dog learning to sit β€” which is instinct?

hard.q: Why do trees have thick bark?
hard.a: To protect the wood inside from pests, disease and harsh weather
hard.hint: Think about what bark does like a coat around the tree.

hard.q: What is a producer in a food chain?
hard.a: A plant that makes its own food using sunlight
hard.hint: Food chains always start with something green β€” why?

hard.q: Why do some plants have thorns?
hard.a: To stop animals eating them
hard.hint: Think about why a rose bush has sharp thorns.

hard.q: What is the role of oxygen in the human body?
hard.a: It is used by cells to release energy from food
hard.hint: Think about what your body needs air for beyond just breathing.

hard.q: Why do animals have different types of teeth?
hard.a: Different shaped teeth are suited to different diets (cutting, grinding, tearing)
hard.hint: Compare the flat teeth of a horse to the sharp teeth of a dog.

hard.q: What is the difference between a parasite and a predator?
hard.a: A parasite lives on/in a host and feeds without immediately killing it; a predator kills its prey
hard.hint: Think about a flea on a dog versus a fox catching a rabbit.

hard.q: Why do plants grow towards light?
hard.a: They need light for photosynthesis to make food
hard.hint: Think about plants on a windowsill β€” which way do they lean?

hard.q: What does the term 'life cycle' mean?
hard.a: The series of stages a living thing goes through from birth to death and reproduction
hard.hint: Think about an egg becoming a butterfly β€” what is the whole process called?

hard.q: Why is soil important?
hard.a: It provides nutrients, water and support for plant roots
hard.hint: Think about what plants need from the ground.

hard.q: What is the difference between a cold-blooded and warm-blooded animal?
hard.a: Cold-blooded animals rely on the environment for body heat; warm-blooded animals generate their own heat
hard.hint: Why does a lizard sit in the sun but a dog doesn't need to?

hard.q: What does the word 'curious' mean?

hard.q: What is the purpose of a title in a book?
hard.a: To tell the reader what the book or chapter is about

hard.q: What is a sentence that gives an order called?

hard.q: What does the word 'mischievous' mean?

hard.q: What is onomatopoeia?
hard.a: A word that sounds like the noise it describes

easy.a: No

easy.q: What do old and new mean?
easy.a: Old = made or happened long ago; new = made or happened recently

easy.q: What do we call a very important person who ruled a country?
easy.a: A king or queen (or ruler/monarch)

easy.q: Did people in the Stone Age have supermarkets?

easy.q: What do we call a story passed down through generations by word of mouth?
easy.a: An oral tradition or folk tale

easy.q: Did people travel by train in the Stone Age?
easy.a: No
easy.hint: Think about when trains were invented.

easy.q: What do old buildings tell us?

easy.a: Open fires or wood-burning stoves
easy.hint: Think about cooking without modern appliances.

easy.q: What do we call a very large, important story about heroes and gods from the ancient world?

medium.q: What do we mean by 'past', 'present' and 'future'?
medium.a: Past = before now; present = now; future = yet to come
medium.hint: Think about yesterday, today and tomorrow.

medium.q: Why do we study history?
medium.a: To learn from the past and understand how the present came to be
medium.hint: Think about what we can learn from past events and mistakes.

medium.q: What is the difference between a primary source and a secondary source?
medium.a: Primary = made at the time (diary, artefact); secondary = written about the past later
medium.hint: Which is more direct β€” a soldier's diary from WW1 or a textbook written in 2020?

medium.q: Who was Guy Fawkes?
medium.a: He tried to blow up Parliament in 1605 in the Gunpowder Plot
medium.hint: We remember him every 5th November.

medium.q: What is Bonfire Night and when is it?
medium.a: 5th November β€” we remember the Gunpowder Plot with fireworks and bonfires
medium.hint: Think about the plot to blow up Parliament.

medium.q: What was the Great Fire of London?
medium.a: A fire that destroyed much of London in 1666

medium.q: Where did the Great Fire of London start?
medium.a: In a bakery on Pudding Lane
medium.hint: Think about the type of shop and the street name.

medium.q: What year did the Great Fire of London happen?
medium.hint: Think about the number pattern: 1-6-6-6.

medium.q: Who was Florence Nightingale?
medium.a: A famous nurse who improved hospital care in the 1800s
medium.hint: She worked during the Crimean War and is known as the Lady with the Lamp.

medium.q: What is the Gunpowder Plot?
medium.a: The failed attempt by Guy Fawkes to blow up Parliament in 1605

medium.q: What did Samuel Pepys write?
medium.a: A famous diary about life in 17th century London (including the Great Fire)
medium.hint: Think about a famous diary from the 1600s.

medium.q: What is Remembrance Day and when is it?
medium.a: 11th November β€” we remember soldiers who died in wars
medium.hint: Think about poppies and the end of World War One.

medium.q: Who was Mary Seacole?
medium.a: A British-Jamaican nurse who cared for soldiers in the Crimean War
medium.hint: She worked alongside Florence Nightingale's era and built the 'British Hotel'.

medium.q: What do we use poppies to remember?
medium.a: Soldiers who died in World War One and other wars
medium.hint: Think about what poppies symbolise on 11th November.

medium.q: What was a Victorian?
medium.a: Someone who lived during the reign of Queen Victoria (1837-1901)
medium.hint: Think about the era named after Queen Victoria.

medium.q: When did Queen Victoria reign?
medium.hint: She was one of Britain's longest-reigning monarchs.

medium.q: What is a census?
medium.a: An official count of all the people in a country
medium.hint: Think about a survey where every household is counted.

medium.q: What is the difference between a king and a president?
medium.a: A king inherits the title by birth; a president is elected by the people
medium.hint: Think about how each leader gets their position.

medium.q: What is Stonehenge?
medium.a: A prehistoric monument in Wiltshire made of large standing stones
medium.hint: It was built thousands of years ago and its purpose is still a mystery.

medium.q: What were Stone Age people called?
medium.a: Hunter-gatherers
medium.hint: Think about how they found food β€” they hunted animals and gathered plants.

medium.q: What is the difference between BC and AD?
medium.a: BC = Before Christ; AD = Anno Domini (after Christ's birth)
medium.hint: Think about dates before and after the year 0.

medium.q: Who was Queen Victoria?
medium.a: The Queen of the United Kingdom from 1837-1901, one of the longest-reigning British monarchs
medium.hint: The Victorian era is named after her.

medium.q: What was the Great Plague?
medium.a: A deadly disease (bubonic plague) that killed many people in 1665 London
medium.hint: It happened just before the Great Fire of London.

medium.q: What did the Ancient Egyptians use to write?
medium.a: Hieroglyphics (picture writing)
medium.hint: Think about the picture-based writing system of ancient Egypt.

medium.q: What is a pyramid?
medium.a: A large triangular stone monument built by the Ancient Egyptians as a tomb
medium.hint: Think about the giant triangular structures in the desert.

medium.q: What is an empire?
medium.a: A large group of countries ruled by one powerful country or leader
medium.hint: Think about the British Empire or the Roman Empire.

medium.q: Who was Alfred the Great?
medium.a: A Saxon king who defended England against Viking invasions in the 800s
medium.hint: He is one of the most famous Anglo-Saxon kings.

medium.q: What is a charter?
medium.a: An official document granting rights or permissions
medium.hint: Think about Magna Carta β€” what was it?

medium.q: What did Viking longships look like?
medium.a: Long, narrow wooden boats with a dragon head at the front
medium.hint: Think about the shape of a Viking ship.

medium.q: What is a chronicle?
medium.a: A detailed historical account of events in order of time
medium.hint: Think about a written record of what happened year by year.

medium.q: What is the significance of 1066?
medium.a: The year of the Norman Conquest and the Battle of Hastings
medium.hint: William the Conqueror defeated King Harold in this year.

medium.q: What is an invasion?
medium.a: When one country's army enters another country by force
medium.hint: Think about the Vikings or the Romans coming to Britain.

medium.q: What is the Magna Carta?
medium.a: A document signed in 1215 that limited the power of the king and gave rights to people
medium.hint: Think about a charter that made the king follow rules.

medium.q: What was the Silk Road?
medium.a: An ancient trade route connecting Europe to Asia
medium.hint: Think about merchants travelling long distances to trade silk and spices.

medium.q: Who built the Tower of London?
medium.a: William the Conqueror (after 1066)
medium.hint: Think about who came to power after the Norman Conquest.

medium.q: What were Viking warriors called?
medium.a: Vikings or Norsemen
medium.hint: They came from Scandinavia β€” Norway, Sweden and Denmark.

medium.q: What is an oral history?
medium.a: History passed down by speaking and storytelling rather than writing
medium.hint: Think about stories told by elders before books were common.

medium.q: What is Parliament?
medium.a: The place where laws are made and debated in the UK
medium.hint: Think about the Houses of Parliament in London.

medium.q: What happened on D-Day?
medium.a: Allied troops landed in Normandy on 6th June 1944 to free Europe from Nazi control
medium.hint: This was a major turning point in World War Two.

medium.q: What is the Commonwealth?
medium.a: An association of countries mostly formerly part of the British Empire
medium.hint: Think about countries like Australia, Canada and India and their connection to Britain.

medium.q: Who was William the Conqueror?
medium.a: The Norman king who conquered England in 1066
medium.hint: He defeated King Harold at the Battle of Hastings.

medium.q: What were the Crusades?
medium.a: A series of religious wars in which Europeans tried to take control of the Holy Land
medium.hint: Think about medieval Christian soldiers travelling to the Middle East.

medium.q: What is a peasant?
medium.a: A poor farmer who worked land owned by a lord in the Middle Ages
medium.hint: Think about the lowest level of the feudal system.

medium.q: What is the feudal system?
medium.a: A medieval system where the king owned all land and gave it to lords, who gave it to knights and peasants
medium.hint: Think about a pyramid of power with the king at the top.

medium.q: Who was Queen Elizabeth I?
medium.a: Queen of England from 1558-1603, daughter of Henry VIII and Anne Boleyn
medium.hint: She was the last Tudor monarch.

medium.q: What is a pilgrim?
medium.a: Someone who travels to a holy place for religious reasons
medium.hint: Think about people walking to Canterbury Cathedral in medieval times.

medium.q: What is the significance of 1815?
medium.a: The Battle of Waterloo, where Napoleon was defeated
medium.hint: Think about Napoleon's final defeat.

medium.q: What was the industrial revolution?
medium.a: A period in the 1700s-1800s when Britain changed from farming to factory-based industry
medium.hint: Think about the invention of steam engines and factories.

medium.q: What did the Domesday Book record?
medium.a: A survey of all land and property in England ordered by William the Conqueror in 1086
medium.hint: Think about why a conquering king would want to know what he owned.

medium.q: Who was Martin Luther King Jr?
medium.a: An American civil rights leader who fought for equality for Black Americans in the 1950s-60s
medium.hint: He gave the famous 'I Have a Dream' speech.

hard.q: What was the significance of the Magna Carta in 1215?
hard.a: It established that the king must follow the law, laying foundations for democracy and rights
hard.hint: Think about what it meant for an ordinary person that the king could no longer do whatever he wished.

hard.q: How did the Great Fire of London change the city?
hard.a: It destroyed 13,000 homes but led to better building codes and a redesigned city with St Paul's Cathedral rebuilt by Wren
hard.hint: Think about what was rebuilt after the fire and how it improved London.

hard.q: Why did the Romans invade Britain?
hard.a: For land, resources, trade and to expand the empire
hard.hint: Think about what Britain had that Rome wanted.

hard.q: How did the Norman Conquest change England?
hard.a: It changed the language, law, architecture and feudal system β€” French became the language of power
hard.hint: Think about what William brought from Normandy that changed English culture.

hard.q: What was the significance of the Battle of Hastings?
hard.a: It decided who ruled England β€” Harold was killed and William became king, changing England forever
hard.hint: Think about what would have been different if Harold had won.

hard.q: Why were the pyramids built?
hard.a: As tombs for pharaohs and to help their souls reach the afterlife
hard.hint: Think about Ancient Egyptian beliefs about life after death.

hard.q: How did the printing press change history?
hard.a: It allowed books to be made quickly and cheaply, spreading knowledge and ideas to more people
hard.hint: Think about what happened to information when more people could read books.

hard.q: What were the causes of World War One?
hard.a: Alliance system, assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand, nationalism, imperialism and militarism
hard.hint: Think about the spark (assassination) and the deeper causes (alliances and nationalism).

hard.q: Why was the abolition of slavery significant?
hard.a: It recognised the equal humanity of enslaved people and ended a deeply cruel system
hard.hint: Think about what slavery meant for millions of people and why ending it mattered.

hard.q: How did the Industrial Revolution change life for ordinary people?
hard.a: It moved people from farms to factories, created cities, but also caused poor working conditions initially
hard.hint: Think about both the positive and negative effects on workers.

hard.q: What was significant about Boudicca?
hard.a: She was a British queen who led a major revolt against the Roman occupation around 60 AD
hard.hint: Think about a woman warrior who stood up to Roman power.

hard.q: Why is 1066 considered the most important date in English history?
hard.a: The Norman Conquest fundamentally changed England's language, culture, law and government
hard.hint: Think about how much changed after William the Conqueror took control.

hard.q: What was the significance of the moon landing in 1969?
hard.a: It showed that humans could travel to space and marked a triumph in the Space Race between the USA and USSR
hard.hint: Think about what it meant for humanity to step beyond Earth.

hard.q: Why did the British Empire grow so large?
hard.a: Through trade, military power and colonisation, Britain controlled territories across the world
hard.hint: Think about what advantages trade, ships and an army gave Britain.

hard.q: What was the significance of the Great Fire of London for architecture?
hard.a: The city was rebuilt in brick and stone instead of wood, and Christopher Wren designed St Paul's Cathedral
hard.hint: Think about what change was made to prevent future fires.

hard.q: Why did the Vikings raid Britain?
hard.a: For wealth, land and resources β€” monasteries and towns had valuable goods
hard.hint: Think about what the Vikings were looking for and what Britain had.

hard.q: What was the significance of World War Two for Britain?
hard.a: Britain survived but was weakened; the Empire began to break up and the welfare state was created
hard.hint: Think about the changes to Britain after 1945.

hard.q: How did Florence Nightingale change nursing?
hard.a: She introduced hygiene and record-keeping, dramatically reducing death rates in hospitals
hard.hint: Think about what conditions were like before her and what she changed.

hard.q: Why was democracy important in Ancient Athens?
hard.a: It gave citizens a say in decisions for the first time, laying the foundation for modern democracy
hard.hint: Think about the difference between a king deciding everything and citizens voting.

hard.q: What was the significance of the invention of the steam engine?
hard.a: It powered factories, trains and ships, driving the Industrial Revolution and transforming travel and industry
hard.hint: Think about all the things powered by steam engines.

hard.q: Why is it important to question historical sources?
hard.a: Sources may be biased, incomplete or only show one perspective
hard.hint: Think about whose point of view a diary or government document represents.

hard.q: What was the significance of the Domesday Book?
hard.a: It gave William the Conqueror complete knowledge of his kingdom's wealth, enabling efficient taxation
hard.hint: Think about why a ruler would need to know exactly what land and resources existed.

hard.q: How did World War One change the role of women?
hard.a: Women worked in factories and services, proving their ability and leading to the vote in 1918
hard.hint: Think about what women did during the war and what they demanded afterwards.

hard.q: What was the feudal system and why did it eventually break down?
hard.a: A system of loyalty and land in exchange for service; it broke down due to the Black Death reducing the workforce
hard.hint: Think about what happened when so many peasants died from plague.

hard.q: Why was the Renaissance important?
hard.a: It was a rebirth of art, science and learning that challenged old ideas and led to new discoveries
hard.hint: Think about what changed in art, science and thinking during this period.

hard.q: What was the significance of the Suez Crisis for Britain?
hard.a: It showed that Britain was no longer a world superpower, as American pressure forced Britain to withdraw
hard.hint: Think about what it meant when a smaller crisis exposed Britain's reduced global power.

hard.q: How did the Black Death change medieval society?
hard.a: It killed up to half of Europe's population, giving surviving peasants more bargaining power and weakening the feudal system
hard.hint: Think about what happens when there are fewer workers β€” do they have more or less power?

hard.q: What was the significance of the Elizabethan era?
hard.a: It was a golden age of exploration, theatre (Shakespeare), trade and relative stability
hard.hint: Think about what flourished during Elizabeth I's reign.

hard.q: Why is historical bias important to understand?
hard.a: All sources reflect the views of the time or the writer; understanding bias helps us get closer to the truth
hard.hint: Think about why a Roman soldier and a British tribe member would describe the same event differently.

hard.q: What was the significance of Nelson Mandela's release from prison?
hard.a: It marked the end of apartheid in South Africa and the beginning of equality for Black South Africans
hard.hint: Think about what apartheid was and what changed when Mandela became president.

hard.q: How did the invention of the printing press affect the Reformation?
hard.a: Luther's ideas spread rapidly across Europe because books could be printed quickly and cheaply
hard.hint: Think about how Martin Luther's ideas could reach so many people so fast.

hard.q: What was the significance of women getting the vote in Britain (1918, 1928)?
hard.a: It recognised women as equal citizens with a political voice, transforming British democracy
hard.hint: Think about what it meant that half the population had no say in government before this.

hard.q: Why was the Battle of Britain significant in WW2?
hard.a: The RAF defeated the Luftwaffe, preventing a German invasion and keeping Britain in the war
hard.hint: Think about what would have happened if Germany had won control of British skies.

hard.q: What was the significance of the Civil Rights Movement in the USA?
hard.a: It ended legal segregation and secured voting rights for Black Americans, advancing equality
hard.hint: Think about the laws that changed and what life was like for Black Americans before and after.

hard.q: How did the dissolution of the monasteries affect England?
hard.a: Henry VIII seized church wealth and land, redistributing it and breaking the Pope's power in England
hard.hint: Think about why Henry VIII wanted to break away from the Catholic Church.

hard.q: What was the significance of the Battle of Waterloo in 1815?
hard.a: Napoleon's final defeat ended French domination of Europe and reshuffled the European political map
hard.hint: Think about what Napoleon had been doing in Europe before 1815.

hard.q: Why did the British Empire decline after World War Two?
hard.a: Britain was economically weakened; colonies demanded independence inspired by self-determination ideals
hard.hint: Think about the ideas of freedom that WW2 was fought for and how those applied to colonies.

hard.q: What was the Reformation?
hard.a: A 16th-century movement that challenged Catholic Church authority and led to Protestantism
hard.hint: Think about Martin Luther and why people wanted to reform the Church.

hard.q: What was significant about the abolition of the slave trade in Britain (1807)?
hard.a: Britain banned the trading of enslaved people, a step towards total abolition, and used its navy to enforce it
hard.hint: Think about the difference between banning the trade and banning slavery itself.

hard.q: How did the Treaty of Versailles affect Germany after WW1?
hard.a: It imposed harsh reparations and blamed Germany, causing economic hardship that helped Hitler rise to power
hard.hint: Think about what happens when a country is humiliated and impoverished.

hard.q: What was the significance of the first aeroplane flight by the Wright Brothers in 1903?
hard.a: It proved powered flight was possible, transforming transport, warfare and global connection
hard.hint: Think about how the world changed once humans could fly.

hard.q: Why was the Roman invasion of Britain significant?
hard.a: It brought roads, written language, towns, Roman law and new crops to Britain, fundamentally changing it
hard.hint: Think about what the Romans left behind in Britain that still exists today.

hard.q: What was the impact of the Black Death on the power of the Church?
hard.a: People questioned why God allowed such suffering, weakening faith and Church authority
hard.hint: Think about how a devastating plague might make people doubt religious institutions.

hard.q: What was the significance of the United Nations (UN)?
hard.a: Created after WW2 to maintain world peace and prevent future conflicts between nations
hard.hint: Think about why nations agreed to create an international organisation after two world wars.

hard.q: How did colonialism affect the countries that were colonised?
hard.a: It often exploited resources and people, disrupted cultures, but also introduced infrastructure; long-term effects are debated
hard.hint: Think about both what colonisers took and what they built.

hard.q: What was the significance of the Russian Revolution in 1917?
hard.a: It overthrew the Tsar, ended Imperial Russia and created the world's first communist state
hard.hint: Think about what happened to the monarchy and what replaced it.

hard.q: Why is it important to study history from multiple perspectives?
hard.a: To understand the full truth β€” events affect different people differently and a single view is incomplete
hard.hint: Think about how a Viking, a monk and a king would each describe a Viking raid differently.

hard.q: What was the significance of the founding of the NHS in 1948?
hard.a: It gave every British person access to free healthcare regardless of wealth, transforming public health
hard.hint: Think about what happened to poor people who couldn't afford doctors before the NHS.

easy.q: What is the capital city of England?
easy.a: London
easy.hint: Think about the biggest and most important city in England.

easy.q: What country do we live in?
easy.a: England (or UK/United Kingdom)
easy.hint: Think about the name of our country.

easy.q: What are the four countries of the United Kingdom?
easy.a: England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland
easy.hint: Think about the four parts that make up the UK.

easy.q: Is the sea hot or cold in the UK?
easy.a: Cold
easy.hint: Think about what it feels like to swim in the sea in Britain.

easy.q: What do we call the water that surrounds an island?
easy.a: Sea or ocean

medium.q: What are the seven continents?
medium.a: Africa, Asia, Europe, North America, South America, Australia (Oceania), Antarctica
medium.hint: Think of the large landmasses on a world map.

medium.q: What are the five oceans?
medium.a: Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern (Antarctic), Arctic
medium.hint: Think about the large bodies of water between continents.

medium.q: What is a compass used for?
medium.a: To find direction (North, South, East, West)
medium.hint: Think about how explorers find their way.

medium.q: Why does it get colder as you go further from the equator?
medium.a: Because sunlight hits the earth at a more indirect angle near the poles
medium.hint: Think about the angle of the sun's rays β€” are they more direct at the equator or poles?

medium.q: What is the difference between a town and a city?
medium.a: A city is larger and usually has a cathedral or city status
medium.hint: Think about size and any other special features.

medium.q: What is the difference between a lake and a sea?
medium.a: A lake is surrounded by land; a sea is a large body of saltwater connected to the ocean
medium.hint: Think about what is around each body of water.

medium.q: What is the UK's longest river?
medium.a: The River Severn
medium.hint: It starts in Wales and flows through England.

medium.q: Name the four compass points in order clockwise from North.
medium.a: North, East, South, West
medium.hint: Use the saying: Never Eat Shredded Wheat.

medium.q: What is deforestation?
medium.a: The cutting down of large numbers of trees, often destroying forests
medium.hint: Think about what happens when forests are cleared for farming or buildings.

medium.q: What is a settlement?
medium.a: A place where people live β€” from a hamlet to a city
medium.hint: Think about any community where people have built homes.

medium.q: What is erosion?
medium.a: When wind or water wears away land over time
medium.hint: Think about how cliffs get smaller when waves hit them.

medium.q: What makes the UK's climate mild and wet?
medium.a: Its position next to the Atlantic Ocean and warm ocean currents
medium.hint: Think about why Britain is not as cold as Russia even though they are at similar latitudes.

medium.q: What is the difference between a map and a globe?
medium.a: A map is flat; a globe is a 3D sphere β€” a map has more distortion
medium.hint: Think about the difficulty of making a round Earth flat.

medium.q: What is a key (legend) on a map?
medium.a: A guide explaining what the symbols and colours on the map mean
medium.hint: Think about the box on a map that tells you what the symbols mean.

medium.q: What are the British Isles?
medium.a: A group of islands including Great Britain, Ireland and many smaller islands
medium.hint: Think about all the islands that make up the northwest corner of Europe.

medium.q: Why is the climate different in Scotland and London?
medium.a: Scotland is further north so it is colder and wetter on average
medium.hint: Think about how latitude (distance from equator) affects temperature.

medium.q: What is a grid reference on a map?
medium.a: A pair of numbers/letters that pinpoint a location on a map
medium.hint: Think about the numbered lines on an Ordnance Survey map.

medium.q: What is the difference between a physical and a political map?
medium.a: Physical maps show natural features (mountains, rivers); political maps show countries and borders
medium.hint: Think about whether a map shows nature or human boundaries.

medium.q: What is urban and what is rural?
medium.a: Urban = built-up areas like cities; rural = countryside
medium.hint: Think about whether you are in a city or the countryside.

medium.q: What causes the seasons?
medium.a: The tilt of the Earth's axis as it orbits the sun
medium.hint: Think about why summer is warm β€” is the Earth closer to the sun, or tilted towards it?

medium.q: What is a tributary?
medium.a: A smaller river that flows into a larger river
medium.hint: Think about smaller streams joining the main river.

medium.q: What is the source of a river?
medium.a: Where a river begins β€” usually in hills or mountains
medium.hint: Think about where the water starts its journey.

medium.q: What is a mountain range?
medium.a: A series of connected mountains
medium.hint: Think about the Alps or the Himalayas as examples.

medium.q: Name one mountain range in the UK.
medium.a: Pennines, Snowdonia, Grampians, Brecon Beacons (any correct)
medium.hint: Think about major upland areas in England, Wales or Scotland.

medium.q: What is a delta?
medium.a: A fan-shaped area at the mouth of a river where it splits before reaching the sea
medium.hint: Think about a river spreading out as it meets the sea.

medium.q: What is the difference between weather and climate?
medium.a: Weather is day-to-day conditions; climate is the long-term average weather of a region
medium.hint: Think about today's rain (weather) versus 'Britain is generally mild and wet' (climate).

medium.q: What is the Greenwich Meridian (Prime Meridian)?
medium.a: The line of 0Β° longitude that passes through Greenwich, London
medium.hint: Think about the line that divides East and West on a globe.

medium.q: Why is the Amazon rainforest important?
medium.a: It produces oxygen, absorbs CO2, and contains enormous biodiversity
medium.hint: Think about what the rainforest does for the planet's air and wildlife.

medium.q: What is latitude?
medium.a: The distance north or south of the equator, measured in degrees
medium.hint: Think about horizontal lines on a globe β€” what do they measure?

medium.q: What is longitude?
medium.a: The distance east or west of the Prime Meridian, measured in degrees
medium.hint: Think about vertical lines on a globe β€” what do they measure?

medium.q: What is overpopulation?
medium.a: When too many people live in an area for its resources to support
medium.hint: Think about what happens when more people live somewhere than can be fed or housed.

medium.q: What is the difference between the UK and Great Britain?
medium.a: Great Britain = England, Scotland and Wales; UK = Great Britain + Northern Ireland
medium.hint: Northern Ireland is the key difference between the two terms.

medium.q: What is a flood plain?
medium.a: Flat land next to a river that floods regularly
medium.hint: Think about the land that gets covered in water when a river overflows.

medium.q: What is the mouth of a river?
medium.a: Where the river meets the sea or a lake
medium.hint: Think about the end of the river's journey.

medium.q: Name the countries that border the UK.
medium.a: None β€” the UK is an island (but shares a land border with Ireland in Northern Ireland)
medium.hint: Think about whether you need a boat or plane to reach any of the UK's neighbours.

medium.q: What is a tidal wave (tsunami)?
medium.a: A massive ocean wave caused by an underwater earthquake or volcanic eruption
medium.hint: Think about what causes the sea to surge onto land.

medium.q: What is migration?
medium.a: When people or animals move from one place to another
medium.hint: Think about birds flying south in winter or people moving to a new country.

medium.q: What are natural resources?
medium.a: Materials found in nature that people use β€” water, wood, oil, minerals
medium.hint: Think about what exists in the environment that humans depend on.

medium.q: What is a national park?
medium.a: A protected area of countryside preserved for its natural beauty
medium.hint: Think about the Lake District or Snowdonia β€” why are they protected?

medium.q: What is the difference between immigration and emigration?
medium.a: Immigration = coming into a country; emigration = leaving a country
medium.hint: Think about the difference between 'in' and 'out'.

medium.q: Why is the equator warmer than the poles?
medium.a: The sun's rays hit the equator most directly, concentrating heat there
medium.hint: Think about the angle of the sun's rays at different parts of the Earth.

medium.q: What is a county?
medium.a: A region within a country used for local government
medium.hint: Think about areas like Yorkshire, Kent or Cornwall.

medium.q: What is recycling?
medium.a: Converting waste materials into new products to reduce landfill and save resources
medium.hint: Think about what happens to a plastic bottle when you put it in the recycling bin.

medium.q: Name two major rivers in England.
medium.a: Thames, Severn, Trent, Mersey, Great Ouse (any two)
medium.hint: Think about rivers that flow through major English cities.

medium.q: What is population density?
medium.a: The number of people living in a given area β€” how crowded a place is
medium.hint: Think about the difference between a busy city and an empty moorland.

medium.q: What is renewable energy?
medium.a: Energy from sources that naturally replenish β€” wind, solar, tidal, hydroelectric
medium.hint: Think about energy sources that will not run out.

medium.q: What is non-renewable energy?
medium.a: Energy from sources that will eventually run out β€” coal, oil, gas
medium.hint: Think about fossil fuels β€” once burned, they cannot be replaced quickly.

medium.q: What is the difference between a hill and a mountain in the UK?
medium.a: In the UK, a mountain is generally over 600m (some say 2,000 feet); a hill is lower
medium.hint: Think about the height difference between a gentle hill and Ben Nevis.

medium.q: What is the Antarctic?
medium.a: The continent at the South Pole, covered in ice
medium.hint: Think about the continent at the very bottom of the world.

hard.q: How does the water cycle work?
hard.a: Water evaporates from seas/lakes, forms clouds, falls as precipitation, runs into rivers and back to sea
hard.hint: Think about how water moves from the sea to the sky and back to the land.

hard.q: Why is the UK not as cold as Canada despite being at the same latitude?
hard.a: The Gulf Stream (North Atlantic Drift) brings warm water from the Gulf of Mexico
hard.hint: Think about ocean currents and how they carry heat.

hard.q: What is the difference between a renewable and non-renewable energy source? Give examples.
hard.a: Renewable (wind, solar) replenish naturally; non-renewable (coal, oil) will eventually run out
hard.hint: Think about whether the source refills itself or will one day be gone.

hard.q: How does human activity contribute to climate change?
hard.a: Burning fossil fuels releases CO2, which traps heat in the atmosphere
hard.hint: Think about the greenhouse effect and what gases cause it.

hard.q: What is the difference between a hurricane and a tornado?
hard.a: Hurricanes are large ocean storms; tornadoes are narrow, violent spinning columns over land
hard.hint: Think about where each forms and how big it is.

hard.q: Why are coastal areas often densely populated?
hard.a: Access to trade, fishing, transport and milder climates makes coasts attractive for settlement
hard.hint: Think about what advantages living by the sea gives people.

hard.q: How is a river formed and how does it change from source to mouth?
hard.a: Rain collects on hills, forms streams that join into a river; it deepens and widens as it flows downhill
hard.hint: Think about the journey from a tiny stream on a hillside to a wide river at the sea.

hard.q: What is the greenhouse effect?
hard.a: Gases like CO2 trap heat from the sun in the Earth's atmosphere, warming the planet
hard.hint: Think about how a greenhouse keeps plants warm β€” the atmosphere works similarly.

hard.q: Why is the Amazon rainforest called the 'lungs of the Earth'?
hard.a: It produces vast amounts of oxygen and absorbs large amounts of CO2
hard.hint: Think about what lungs do for a body and what the rainforest does for the planet.

hard.q: What is the difference between weather and climate change?
hard.a: Weather is short-term conditions; climate change is a long-term shift in global weather patterns
hard.hint: One bad storm is weather; thirty years of increasing temperatures is climate change.

hard.q: Why do mountain areas have different weather from lowland areas?
hard.a: Higher altitude means cooler temperatures, more cloud and often more precipitation
hard.hint: Think about what happens to temperature as you go up a mountain.

hard.q: What is a biome?
hard.a: A large natural area with a distinctive climate, plants and animals
hard.hint: Think about the differences between a rainforest, a desert and a tundra.

hard.q: How do rivers cause erosion and deposition?
hard.a: Fast-flowing water carries rocks and sediment (erosion); when it slows it drops the material (deposition)
hard.hint: Think about a fast river cutting through rock versus a slow river dropping silt.

hard.q: Why does the UK have a temperate maritime climate?
hard.a: It is surrounded by sea and affected by the warm Gulf Stream, keeping it mild and wet
hard.hint: Think about what the ocean and warm currents do to the temperature of nearby land.

hard.q: What is sustainable development?
hard.a: Development that meets current needs without damaging resources for future generations
hard.hint: Think about how we can use the planet's resources without running out.

hard.q: What are the causes of flooding?
hard.a: Heavy rainfall, deforestation, impermeable surfaces and rivers overflowing their banks
hard.hint: Think about what happens to rainwater when trees are removed and cities are built.

hard.q: How does latitude affect climate?
hard.a: Places nearer the equator receive more direct sunlight and are warmer; poles are colder
hard.hint: Think about the angle of the sun's rays at the equator versus the poles.

hard.q: What is the difference between a stalactite and a stalagmite?
hard.a: Stalactites hang from the ceiling; stalagmites grow from the ground
hard.hint: Stalactites hang 'tight' to the ceiling. Stalagmites 'might' reach the ceiling one day.

hard.q: Why do some rivers flood more than others?
hard.a: Factors include rainfall, steepness, soil type, vegetation cover and urbanisation
hard.hint: Think about what changes how quickly water reaches a river.

hard.q: What is urbanisation?
hard.a: The growth of cities as more people move from rural to urban areas
hard.hint: Think about why people move from the countryside to cities.

hard.q: How does deforestation contribute to climate change?
hard.a: Trees absorb CO2; when they are cut and burned, CO2 is released and fewer trees remain to absorb it
hard.hint: Think about what trees do with carbon dioxide.

hard.q: What is the difference between a coral reef and a mangrove?
hard.a: Coral reefs are underwater structures built by coral polyps; mangroves are coastal trees with roots in saltwater
hard.hint: Think about where each is found and what it looks like.

hard.q: Why are some parts of the world more prone to earthquakes?
hard.a: They lie on tectonic plate boundaries where plates collide, separate or slide past each other
hard.hint: Think about where the Earth's plates meet β€” why is it unstable there?

hard.q: What is globalisation?
hard.a: The process by which the world's economies, cultures and populations become increasingly interconnected
hard.hint: Think about why your trainers might be made in Asia and your food comes from many countries.

hard.q: How do volcanoes form?
hard.a: Magma from inside the Earth pushes up through weak points in the crust, often at plate boundaries
hard.hint: Think about what happens when molten rock finds a way through the Earth's surface.

hard.q: What is the difference between a primary and a secondary industry?
hard.a: Primary = extracting raw materials (farming, mining); secondary = making products (manufacturing)
hard.hint: Think about the stages from raw material to finished product.

hard.q: Why does London have a much larger population than rural Wales?
hard.a: London has more jobs, services, transport links and historical significance
hard.hint: Think about what attracts people to cities rather than the countryside.

hard.q: What is the significance of the Greenwich Meridian?
hard.a: It is the starting point for measuring longitude and the basis for world time zones
hard.hint: Think about how time zones and navigation are organised around this line.

hard.q: What is a microclimate?
hard.a: A local climate that differs from the surrounding area β€” e.g. a sheltered valley being warmer
hard.hint: Think about how a city can be warmer than the countryside around it.

hard.q: How do ocean currents affect climate?
hard.a: Warm currents raise temperatures of nearby coasts; cold currents lower them
hard.hint: Think about why the Gulf Stream makes western Europe warmer than it would otherwise be.

hard.q: What is a meander?
hard.a: A curve or bend in a river
hard.hint: Think about a river snaking across a flat plain.

hard.q: Why do some countries have greater food security than others?
hard.a: Differences in climate, land quality, wealth, political stability and trade access
hard.hint: Think about all the factors that allow a country to feed its people.

hard.q: What is the difference between weathering and erosion?
hard.a: Weathering breaks rock down in place; erosion carries the material away
hard.hint: Think about a cliff face crumbling (weathering) and the sea carrying pieces away (erosion).

hard.q: How does altitude affect vegetation?
hard.a: Higher altitude means colder temperatures and thinner air, supporting only hardy plants
hard.hint: Think about why forests grow on mountain slopes but only grass and rock exist near the top.

hard.q: What is the difference between an ocean trench and a mountain ridge?
hard.a: A trench is the deepest part of the ocean floor; a ridge is an underwater mountain chain
hard.hint: Think about the extremes of the ocean floor topography.

hard.q: Why is fresh water a limited resource?
hard.a: Only 3% of Earth's water is fresh and most is frozen; accessible fresh water is scarce
hard.hint: Think about the proportion of the Earth's water that is actually usable.

hard.q: What is the Ring of Fire?
hard.a: A zone around the Pacific Ocean with many volcanoes and earthquakes due to tectonic activity
hard.hint: Think about where most of the world's volcanoes and earthquakes are found.

hard.q: Why do cities often develop near rivers?
hard.a: Rivers provide fresh water, food, transport routes and fertile soil for farming
hard.hint: Think about what early settlers needed and where rivers could supply that.

hard.q: What is acid rain and what causes it?
hard.a: Rain made acidic by dissolved pollutants (sulphur dioxide, nitrogen oxide) from burning fossil fuels
hard.hint: Think about what happens when factory emissions mix with rain clouds.

hard.q: What is the difference between a savanna and a steppe?
hard.a: Both are grasslands; savanna is tropical with scattered trees; steppe is temperate with few or no trees
hard.hint: Think about where each is found β€” Africa versus Central Asia.

hard.q: What are the consequences of sea level rise?
hard.a: Coastal flooding, loss of land, displacement of people and damage to infrastructure
hard.hint: Think about what happens to low-lying islands and coastal cities as the sea rises.

hard.q: How does relief (shape of the land) affect rainfall in the UK?
hard.a: Wet westerly winds rise over mountains, cool and drop rain; eastern side is drier (rain shadow)
hard.hint: Think about why Wales and the Lake District are wetter than East Anglia.

hard.q: What is the difference between the tropics and the polar regions?
hard.a: Tropics are near equator β€” hot, high rainfall; polar regions are near poles β€” cold, dry and icy
hard.hint: Think about the extreme differences in climate between the middle of the Earth and the top/bottom.

hard.q: What is a trade wind?
hard.a: A steady wind blowing towards the equator from the northeast or southeast
hard.hint: Think about why sailing ships used certain routes across the Atlantic.

hard.q: Why is the Sahara desert so dry?
hard.a: It is in a high-pressure belt where air descends and warms, preventing clouds from forming
hard.hint: Think about the atmospheric conditions that prevent rain from falling.

hard.q: What is a geographer?
hard.a: A scientist who studies the Earth's surface, climates, populations, and how humans interact with their environment
hard.hint: Think about someone who uses maps, data and fieldwork to understand our world.

hard.q: What is tectonic plate movement and why does it matter?
hard.a: The Earth's crust is divided into plates that move slowly; where they meet, earthquakes and volcanoes occur
hard.hint: Think about what happens when two huge pieces of rock push together or pull apart.

medium.q: What is the difference between a living and non-living thing?
medium.a: Living things grow, breathe, reproduce and need food; non-living things do not
medium.hint: Think about what a plant can do that a stone cannot.

medium.q: Name the four seasons in order.
medium.a: Spring, summer, autumn, winter
medium.hint: Start with the season when flowers bloom.

medium.q: What is the life cycle of a butterfly?
medium.a: Egg, caterpillar (larva), chrysalis (pupa), butterfly
medium.hint: Think about the four stages from egg to winged insect.

medium.q: What properties make metal useful for building?
medium.a: It is strong, hard, durable and can be shaped
medium.hint: Think about the properties needed to build a bridge or skyscraper.

medium.q: Why do we wear different clothes in summer and winter?
medium.a: To keep us at the right temperature β€” cool in summer, warm in winter
medium.hint: Think about how our clothes help us adapt to different weather.

medium.q: What is the life cycle of a frog?
medium.a: Egg (frogspawn), tadpole, froglet, adult frog
medium.hint: Think about the stages from the pond spawn to an adult.

medium.q: Why is glass used for windows?
medium.a: It is transparent, letting light in, and is weather-resistant
medium.hint: Think about what properties make glass ideal for windows.

medium.q: What do plants make using sunlight?
medium.a: Food (through photosynthesis)
medium.hint: Think about how plants feed themselves without eating.

medium.q: How do animals change as they grow?
medium.a: They get bigger, develop new features and become able to reproduce
medium.hint: Think about how a kitten is different from an adult cat.

medium.q: Why is plastic used to make bottles?
medium.a: It is waterproof, light, durable and can be moulded into shapes
medium.hint: Think about what properties are useful for a container holding liquid.

medium.q: What happens to the UK in winter compared to summer?
medium.a: Days are shorter, nights longer, and it is colder
medium.hint: Think about daylight hours and temperature in December versus July.

medium.q: What is the difference between a mammal and a bird?
medium.a: Mammals have fur and feed young on milk; birds have feathers and lay eggs
medium.hint: Think about how a cat and a robin are different.

medium.q: Why do some animals hibernate?
medium.a: To save energy during cold months when food is scarce
medium.hint: Think about what happens to food supplies in winter.

medium.q: What properties make wood useful for making furniture?
medium.a: It is strong, rigid, can be shaped, and is a natural material
medium.hint: Think about why wood has been used for making tables and chairs for thousands of years.

medium.q: How does a chick develop from an egg?
medium.a: The egg is laid, kept warm, the chick grows inside, then hatches
medium.hint: Think about what happens from when the egg is laid to hatching.

medium.q: What is the difference between opaque and transparent?
medium.a: Opaque blocks all light; transparent lets all light through
medium.hint: Think about a brick wall versus a glass window.

medium.q: Why do leaves change colour in autumn?
medium.a: The green chlorophyll breaks down as daylight reduces
medium.hint: Think about what the green in leaves does and why it disappears.

medium.q: Name two properties of rubber.
medium.a: Flexible, waterproof, stretchy (any two)
medium.hint: Think about what a rubber band or Wellington boot can do.

medium.q: What is a carnivore?
medium.a: An animal that eats only meat
medium.hint: Think about lions and wolves β€” what do they eat?

medium.q: What is a herbivore?
medium.a: An animal that eats only plants
medium.hint: Think about rabbits and cows β€” what do they eat?

medium.q: Why is metal used to make cooking pots?
medium.a: Metal conducts heat well and is durable at high temperatures
medium.hint: Think about what happens when you put a metal pan on a hob.

medium.q: How does the length of day change through the year?
medium.a: Days are longer in summer and shorter in winter
medium.hint: Think about when it gets dark in December versus July.

medium.q: What does an omnivore eat?
medium.a: Both plants and animals
medium.hint: Humans eat both vegetables and meat β€” what does that make us?

medium.q: Why are feathers useful to birds?
medium.a: They keep birds warm, help them fly and can provide camouflage
medium.hint: Think about all the things feathers do for a bird.

medium.q: What is the difference between a solid and a liquid?
medium.a: A solid has a fixed shape; a liquid flows and takes the container's shape
medium.hint: Think about ice (solid) and water (liquid).

medium.q: Why do animals need food?
medium.a: For energy to move, grow and carry out life processes
medium.hint: Think about what happens when you are very hungry.

medium.q: How do fish breathe underwater?
medium.a: Through gills, which extract oxygen from water
medium.hint: Think about what gills do that lungs cannot.

medium.q: What is camouflage?
medium.a: When an animal blends in with its surroundings to hide
medium.hint: Think about a stick insect β€” why does it look like a twig?

medium.q: Why are windows made from glass and not plastic?
medium.a: Glass is more scratch-resistant, clearer and lasts longer
medium.hint: Think about the advantages of glass over plastic for windows.

medium.q: What happens to water when it gets very cold?
medium.a: It freezes and becomes ice
medium.hint: Think about water in a freezer.

medium.q: What is a food chain?
medium.a: The order in which living things eat each other, starting with a plant
medium.hint: Grass β†’ rabbit β†’ fox. What does this show?

medium.q: Name two materials that are waterproof.
medium.a: Plastic, rubber, metal, glass (any two)
medium.hint: Think about materials that water cannot pass through.

medium.q: Why do humans need water?
medium.a: Our bodies are mostly water β€” we need it to survive, digest food and regulate temperature
medium.hint: Think about what happens if you go a day without drinking.

medium.q: What is the difference between a reptile and an amphibian?
medium.a: Reptiles have dry scaly skin; amphibians have moist skin and can live on land and in water
medium.hint: Think about a snake (reptile) and a frog (amphibian).

medium.q: What properties make stone useful for building?
medium.a: It is very hard, durable, waterproof and abundant
medium.hint: Think about why stone has been used for buildings for thousands of years.

medium.q: How do plants take in water?
medium.a: Through their roots
medium.hint: Think about which part of the plant is underground.

medium.q: Why do some materials bend and others do not?
medium.a: Flexible materials have a looser structure; rigid materials have a tighter, stronger structure
medium.hint: Think about the difference in structure between rubber and metal.

medium.q: What is the role of roots in a plant?
medium.a: To anchor the plant and absorb water and minerals from the soil
medium.hint: Think about what roots do underground.

medium.q: Why is the sky lighter in summer mornings?
medium.a: The sun rises earlier in summer because of the Earth's tilt
medium.hint: Think about how the length of day changes with the seasons.

medium.q: How does a butterfly feed?
medium.a: It uses a long tube called a proboscis to drink nectar from flowers
medium.hint: Think about how a butterfly's mouth works like a drinking straw.

medium.q: What is a predator?
medium.a: An animal that hunts and eats other animals
medium.hint: Think about what a lion or eagle does to find food.

medium.q: What is prey?
medium.a: An animal that is hunted and eaten by another animal
medium.hint: Think about what a mouse is to a cat.

medium.q: Why do materials need to be tested?
medium.a: To make sure they have the right properties for their intended use
medium.hint: Think about why you wouldn't build a house out of tissue paper.

medium.q: What is the difference between summer and winter daylight in the UK?
medium.a: Summer has up to 16+ hours of daylight; winter can have as few as 8 hours
medium.hint: Think about how long it is light outside in June versus December.

medium.q: Name two properties of glass.
medium.a: Transparent, rigid, brittle, smooth, waterproof (any two)
medium.hint: Think about what you can see and feel about glass.

medium.q: What makes feathers waterproof?
medium.a: Birds coat feathers with oil from a gland near the tail
medium.hint: Think about why a duck doesn't get soaked in rain.

medium.q: What is the difference between a fish and a mammal that lives in water?
medium.a: Fish breathe through gills; aquatic mammals breathe air through lungs
medium.hint: Think about how a shark and a dolphin breathe differently.

medium.q: Why do leaves fall off deciduous trees in autumn?
medium.a: To conserve water and energy during cold, dark winter months
medium.hint: Think about why a tree would benefit from losing its leaves in winter.

medium.q: What is an invertebrate?
medium.a: An animal without a backbone
medium.hint: Think about worms, snails and insects.

medium.q: Name two things that all living things need.
medium.a: Water, food, air, warmth (any two)
medium.hint: Think about the basic requirements for life.

hard.q: Explain how a plant makes its own food.
hard.a: Through photosynthesis β€” using sunlight, water and carbon dioxide to make glucose
hard.hint: Think about the ingredients a plant needs and what it produces.

hard.q: Why do different materials have different properties?
hard.a: Because of their internal structure β€” how atoms and molecules are arranged
hard.hint: Think about why metal is strong but cotton is soft.

hard.q: How does the Earth's tilt cause seasons?
hard.a: When tilted towards the sun we have summer (more direct light, longer days); away gives winter
hard.hint: Think about how the angle of sunlight changes as Earth orbits the sun.

hard.q: What is the difference between a vertebrate and an invertebrate? Give an example of each.
hard.a: Vertebrate has a backbone (fish, bird, human); invertebrate has none (worm, spider, crab)
hard.hint: Think about whether the animal has a spine inside its body.

hard.q: Explain the life cycle of a frog.
hard.a: Frogspawn (eggs) hatch into tadpoles, which grow legs and absorb their tail to become froglets, then adult frogs
hard.hint: Think about how the frog changes at each stage.

hard.q: Why is it important to choose the right material for a job?
hard.a: The wrong material could fail, be dangerous or be wasteful
hard.hint: Think about why you wouldn't make a raincoat from paper.

hard.q: How do the seasons affect animals' behaviour?
hard.a: Animals hibernate, migrate or change feeding habits to survive seasonal changes
hard.hint: Think about what hedgehogs, swallows and squirrels do in different seasons.

hard.q: What is the difference between a food chain and a food web?
hard.a: A food chain is one sequence; a food web shows many interconnected food chains
hard.hint: Think about how many different things a fox eats compared to one food chain.

hard.q: Why do plants have different shaped leaves?
hard.a: Different shapes are adapted to maximise light capture, reduce water loss or aid identification
hard.hint: Think about how a cactus needle and a rainforest leaf are shaped for their environments.

hard.q: What would happen if producers (plants) were removed from a food chain?
hard.a: All animals in that chain would eventually die as there would be no food source
hard.hint: Think about what every food chain starts with and what happens if that is removed.

hard.q: What is the difference between physical and chemical changes?
hard.a: Physical changes are reversible (ice melting); chemical changes are not (burning wood)
hard.hint: Can you always get back to what you started with?

hard.q: How do animals in cold climates adapt to survive?
hard.a: Thick fur, fat layers (blubber), hibernation, or white colouring for camouflage
hard.hint: Think about a polar bear and all the ways it copes with Arctic cold.

hard.q: Why do some plants have thorns or poisons?
hard.a: As defence against animals that would eat them
hard.hint: Think about why a plant would benefit from being dangerous to eat.

hard.q: What is pollination and why is it important?
hard.a: Pollen is moved between flowers (by insects or wind) allowing seed production and plant reproduction
hard.hint: Think about what would happen to plants if bees disappeared.

hard.q: Explain the difference between opaque, translucent and transparent materials.
hard.a: Opaque blocks all light; translucent lets some light through; transparent lets all light through clearly
hard.hint: Think about a brick, frosted glass and a clear window.

hard.q: How does food provide energy for animals?
hard.a: Digestion breaks food into nutrients absorbed into the blood, which carry energy to cells
hard.hint: Think about what your body does with the food you eat.

hard.q: Why do nocturnal animals have large eyes?
hard.a: To collect as much light as possible in the dark
hard.hint: Think about what large eyes do in low-light conditions.

hard.q: What is the difference between a habitat and an ecosystem?
hard.a: A habitat is where an organism lives; an ecosystem includes all organisms and their environment together
hard.hint: A pond is a habitat for a frog, but the whole pond community is an ecosystem.

hard.q: How do roots help a plant survive drought?
hard.a: Deep roots reach underground water; some plants store water in roots
hard.hint: Think about cacti and how their roots help in desert conditions.

hard.q: What is natural selection?
hard.a: The process where animals best suited to their environment survive and reproduce
hard.hint: Think about why fast rabbits survive more often than slow ones.

hard.q: Why is biodiversity important?
hard.a: Different species depend on each other; losing one can affect the whole ecosystem
hard.hint: Think about what would happen to all the plants if all the bees died.

hard.q: How does an insect's life cycle differ from a mammal's?
hard.a: Insects undergo metamorphosis (complete change of body form); mammals grow gradually
hard.hint: Think about how a caterpillar changes compared to how a puppy grows into a dog.

hard.q: What is the water cycle?
hard.a: Evaporation from oceans β†’ water vapour rises β†’ clouds form β†’ rain falls β†’ rivers run to sea
hard.hint: Think about how water moves from sea to sky and back to land.

hard.q: Why do some animals have good camouflage and others have bright colours?
hard.a: Camouflage hides from predators; bright colours warn predators the animal is toxic
hard.hint: Think about a stick insect (hidden) versus a poison dart frog (bright warning).

hard.q: What is the difference between a deciduous and an evergreen plant?
hard.a: Deciduous loses leaves in autumn; evergreen keeps leaves year round
hard.hint: Compare an oak tree in winter to a pine tree.

hard.q: How do humans affect biodiversity?
hard.a: Deforestation, pollution and hunting reduce habitats and drive species to extinction
hard.hint: Think about all the ways human activity removes places for animals to live.

hard.q: What is symbiosis?
hard.a: When two different species live in close relationship, often benefiting each other
hard.hint: Think about clownfish living among sea anemones β€” both benefit.

hard.q: Why does metal feel colder to touch than wood in a cold room?
hard.a: Metal conducts heat away from your hand faster than wood does
hard.hint: Think about which material moves heat more quickly.

hard.q: What is the function of a flower in a plant's life cycle?
hard.a: To attract pollinators and enable fertilisation so that seeds can form
hard.hint: Think about why flowers are colourful and produce nectar.

hard.q: How does deforestation affect local climate?
hard.a: Trees release moisture into the air; removing them reduces rainfall and increases temperature
hard.hint: Think about what happens to the water cycle when forests are removed.

hard.q: What is the difference between a parasite and a predator?
hard.a: A parasite feeds off a host without immediately killing it; a predator kills and eats its prey
hard.hint: A flea on a dog versus a lion killing a wildebeest β€” which is which?

hard.q: Why are some habitats more biodiverse than others?
hard.a: Warm, wet environments like rainforests support more life than cold, dry deserts
hard.hint: Think about how temperature and moisture affect how many different species can survive.

hard.q: What is the role of decomposers in an ecosystem?
hard.a: They break down dead organisms and return nutrients to the soil for plants to use
hard.hint: Think about what happens to a dead leaf on the forest floor.

hard.q: How does a seed germinate?
hard.a: Given warmth, water and air, a seed splits open, a root grows down and a shoot grows up
hard.hint: Think about what conditions a seed needs to start growing.

hard.q: Why do animals in hot climates have large ears?
hard.a: Large ears radiate body heat, helping the animal cool down
hard.hint: Think about an elephant's ears and what they do in hot weather.

hard.q: What is an adaptation?
hard.a: A feature or behaviour that helps an organism survive in its environment
hard.hint: Think about how a polar bear's white fur and thick fat help it survive in the Arctic.

hard.q: Why is the sun essential for all life on Earth?
hard.a: It provides light and heat for plant growth (photosynthesis), which forms the base of all food chains
hard.hint: Think about what would happen if the sun disappeared β€” what would plants do?

hard.q: How does pollution affect living things?
hard.a: It contaminates air, water and soil, harming or killing plants and animals
hard.hint: Think about what happens to fish when a river is polluted.

hard.q: What is the difference between a herbivore's and a carnivore's teeth?
hard.a: Herbivores have flat grinding teeth; carnivores have sharp pointed teeth for tearing meat
hard.hint: Compare the teeth of a horse and a wolf.

hard.q: Why do some birds migrate and others do not?
hard.a: Migratory birds need warmer climates or specific food sources that are not available in winter
hard.hint: Think about why a swallow leaves the UK in autumn but a robin stays.

hard.q: What is a keystone species?
hard.a: A species that has a disproportionately large effect on its ecosystem; removing it causes major change
hard.hint: Think about how removing wolves from Yellowstone affected the whole ecosystem.

hard.q: How does a Venus flytrap get its nutrients?
hard.a: It traps and digests insects, supplementing nutrients from poor soil
hard.hint: Think about why a plant that lives in nutrient-poor soil might need an alternative food source.

hard.q: What is the difference between a virus and a bacterium?
hard.a: Bacteria are living cells that can reproduce on their own; viruses need a host cell to reproduce
hard.hint: Think about whether each one can grow and divide by itself.

hard.q: Why do some trees lose their leaves in winter?
hard.a: To reduce water loss and conserve energy when there is not enough light for photosynthesis
hard.hint: Think about what a leaf needs to function and whether those conditions exist in winter.

hard.q: What is meant by a balanced diet?
hard.a: Eating the right amounts of different food groups to provide all nutrients the body needs
hard.hint: Think about eating a variety of fruit, vegetables, protein, carbohydrates and dairy.

hard.q: How does exercise benefit the human body?
hard.a: It strengthens muscles and bones, improves heart and lung function, and boosts mental health
hard.hint: Think about all the body systems that benefit from regular physical activity.

hard.q: Why is the ocean important for life on Earth?
hard.a: It regulates climate, produces oxygen, provides food and supports enormous biodiversity
hard.hint: Think about all the things the ocean does for the planet.

hard.q: What is the difference between asexual and sexual reproduction?
hard.a: Asexual uses one parent (e.g. plant cuttings); sexual requires two parents combining genetic material
hard.hint: Think about how a plant growing a new shoot compares to a bird laying fertilised eggs.

hard.q: Why do plants grow towards light?
hard.a: They need light for photosynthesis; growing towards it maximises their food production
hard.hint: Watch a plant on a windowsill β€” which way does it lean?
