medium.q: What is a capital letter used for? Give two examples.
medium.a: Start of a sentence; names of people, places, days, months; the word 'I'
medium.hint: Think about the rules for when we must use a big letter.

medium.q: What does the prefix 'un-' mean? Give an example.
medium.a: Not or opposite of β€” e.g. unhappy, undo, unfair
medium.hint: Think about what 'un' does to the meaning of a word.

medium.q: What is a compound word? Give an example.
medium.a: Two words joined to make a new one β€” e.g. sunshine, football, bedroom
medium.hint: Think about two smaller words you can see inside a bigger word.

medium.q: What is the past tense of 'run'?
medium.a: Ran
medium.hint: What do you say if you did this yesterday? 'I ___ in the race.'

medium.q: What is a proper noun?
medium.a: The specific name of a person, place or organisation β€” always capitalised
medium.hint: Think about names like 'Emma', 'London' or 'Monday'.

medium.q: What is the plural of 'mouse'?
medium.a: Mice
medium.hint: This is an irregular plural β€” it doesn't just add -s.

medium.q: What does an exclamation mark mean?
medium.a: Strong feeling, surprise or a command
medium.hint: Think about when you'd say 'Watch out!' or 'What a goal!'

medium.q: What is the past tense of 'go'?
medium.a: Went
medium.hint: 'I ___ to school yesterday.' The word changes completely.

medium.q: What is the plural of 'child'?
medium.a: Children
medium.hint: This is an irregular plural.

medium.q: What does the suffix '-ful' mean? Give an example.
medium.a: Full of β€” e.g. helpful, careful, wonderful
medium.hint: Think about what 'ful' adds to the meaning of a word.

medium.q: What is a synonym? Give an example.
medium.a: A word with the same or similar meaning β€” e.g. happy/joyful, big/large
medium.hint: Think about two words that mean nearly the same thing.

medium.q: What is the past tense of 'see'?
medium.a: Saw
medium.hint: 'I ___ a rainbow yesterday.'

medium.q: What is the plural of 'tooth'?
medium.a: Teeth
medium.hint: This is an irregular plural.

medium.q: What does the suffix '-less' mean? Give an example.
medium.a: Without β€” e.g. helpless, careless, hopeless
medium.hint: Think about what '-less' removes from the meaning.

medium.q: What is an antonym? Give an example.
medium.a: A word with the opposite meaning β€” e.g. hot/cold, tall/short
medium.hint: Think about words that are complete opposites.

medium.q: What is the past tense of 'come'?
medium.a: Came
medium.hint: 'She ___ to my party last week.'

medium.q: What is the plural of 'foot'?
medium.a: Feet
medium.hint: This is an irregular plural.

medium.q: What does the prefix 're-' mean? Give an example.
medium.a: Again β€” e.g. redo, rewrite, replay
medium.hint: Think about doing something a second time.

medium.q: What is a question? How do you write one?
medium.a: A sentence that asks something; ends with a question mark
medium.hint: Think about the features of a question sentence.

medium.q: What is the past tense of 'write'?
medium.a: Wrote
medium.hint: 'She ___ a story yesterday.'

medium.q: What is the plural of 'man'?
medium.a: Men
medium.hint: This is an irregular plural.

medium.q: What does the suffix '-er' mean when added to a verb?
medium.a: A person who does that action β€” e.g. teacher, runner, swimmer
medium.hint: Think about what 'teacher' means β€” someone who...

medium.q: What is a statement? Give an example.
medium.a: A sentence that tells us something β€” e.g. 'The dog is brown.'
medium.hint: Think about a sentence that just gives information.

medium.q: What is the past tense of 'eat'?
medium.a: Ate
medium.hint: 'We ___ dinner at six o'clock.'

medium.q: What is an apostrophe used for in 'can't'?
medium.a: To show letters are missing (can + not = can't)
medium.hint: Think about what letters the apostrophe replaces.

medium.q: What is a command? Give an example.
medium.a: A sentence that gives an order β€” e.g. 'Sit down.' or 'Open the door.'
medium.hint: Think about sentences that tell someone what to do.

medium.q: What is the past tense of 'have'?
medium.a: Had
medium.hint: 'I ___ a cold last week.'

medium.q: What does an apostrophe show in 'the dog's bone'?
medium.a: The bone belongs to the dog (possession)
medium.hint: Think about apostrophe + s showing ownership.

medium.q: What is a rhyme? Give an example.
medium.a: Words that end with the same sound β€” e.g. cat/hat, moon/spoon
medium.hint: Think about words that sound the same at the end.

medium.q: What is the past tense of 'say'?
medium.a: Said
medium.hint: 'She ___ hello to me.'

medium.q: What is alliteration?
medium.a: When nearby words start with the same sound β€” e.g. 'Peter Piper picked'
medium.hint: Think about tongue twisters β€” what do you notice about the sounds?

medium.q: What is a conjunction?
medium.a: A joining word β€” e.g. and, but, because, so
medium.hint: Think about words that join two parts of a sentence together.

medium.q: What does 'fiction' mean?
medium.a: A made-up story, not real
medium.hint: Think about fairy tales and adventure stories β€” are they real?

medium.q: What does 'non-fiction' mean?
medium.a: Writing about real facts and true information
medium.hint: Think about books about animals or history β€” are those made up?

medium.q: What is the past tense of 'make'?
medium.a: Made
medium.hint: 'She ___ a cake yesterday.'

medium.q: What is a simile?
medium.a: A comparison using 'like' or 'as' β€” e.g. 'as fast as a cheetah'
medium.hint: Think about sentences that compare using the words 'like' or 'as'.

medium.q: What does the suffix '-ly' do to an adjective?
medium.a: Turns it into an adverb β€” e.g. quick β†’ quickly
medium.hint: Think about how 'quickly' describes a verb whereas 'quick' describes a noun.

medium.q: What is an adverb?
medium.a: A word that describes how, when or where something is done
medium.hint: Think about words like 'quickly', 'yesterday', 'outside'.

medium.q: What is the difference between 'there', 'their' and 'they're'?
medium.a: there = place; their = belonging to them; they're = they are
medium.hint: Think about what each version means separately.

medium.q: What does the word 'enormous' mean?
medium.a: Very large
medium.hint: Think of a word that means bigger than big.

medium.q: What is onomatopoeia? Give an example.
medium.a: A word that sounds like what it describes β€” e.g. buzz, crash, sizzle
medium.hint: Say the word β€” does it sound like the thing it names?

medium.q: What is the past tense of 'give'?
medium.a: Gave
medium.hint: 'She ___ me a present.'

medium.q: What is the difference between 'to', 'too' and 'two'?
medium.a: to = direction; too = also/very; two = number 2
medium.hint: They sound the same but mean very different things.

medium.q: What is a paragraph?
medium.a: A group of sentences about the same idea, shown by indentation or a line break
medium.hint: Think about how a page of writing is organised into sections.

medium.q: What does the word 'ancient' mean?
medium.a: Very old
medium.hint: Think about something from thousands of years ago.

medium.q: What is a subordinate clause?
medium.a: A part of a sentence that cannot stand alone β€” e.g. 'because I was tired'
medium.hint: Think about whether the clause makes sense on its own.

medium.q: What does the word 'exhausted' mean?
medium.a: Extremely tired
medium.hint: Think of a word that means more than just 'tired'.

medium.q: What is the purpose of an index in a non-fiction book?
medium.a: To help the reader find specific topics by listing them with page numbers
medium.hint: Think about what you look at when searching for a topic in a reference book.

medium.q: What is the past tense of 'begin'?
medium.a: Began
medium.hint: 'The lesson ___ at nine o'clock.'

medium.q: What is a metaphor?
medium.a: A comparison that says one thing IS another β€” e.g. 'The classroom was a zoo'
medium.hint: Unlike a simile, a metaphor doesn't use 'like' or 'as'.

hard.q: Explain the difference between a simile and a metaphor.
hard.a: A simile compares using 'like' or 'as'; a metaphor says something IS something else directly
hard.hint: 'Fast as a cheetah' (simile) vs 'He was a cheetah on the track' (metaphor).

hard.q: What is the subjunctive mood? Give an example.
hard.a: A verb form used for hypothetical or wished-for situations β€” e.g. 'If I were you...'
hard.hint: Think about sentences that talk about things that are not real or certain.

hard.q: What is a relative clause?
hard.a: A clause that gives extra information about a noun, introduced by who, which, that, where or whose
hard.hint: Think about the underlined part: 'The dog, which was brown, ran away.'

hard.q: What is the difference between active and passive voice?
hard.a: Active: the subject does the action ('The dog bit the man'); passive: subject receives it ('The man was bitten')
hard.hint: Think about who is doing the action and who is having it done to them.

hard.q: What are fronted adverbials?
hard.a: Adverbial phrases placed at the start of a sentence, followed by a comma
hard.hint: Think about sentences that start with 'Slowly, she opened the door.'

hard.q: What is the difference between direct and reported speech?
hard.a: Direct uses exact words in speech marks; reported rephrases without speech marks
hard.hint: 'She said, "I am tired"' (direct) vs 'She said she was tired' (reported).

hard.q: What is the Oxford comma?
hard.a: A comma placed before 'and' in a list of three or more items to avoid ambiguity
hard.hint: Compare: 'I love my parents, Tom and Jerry.' versus 'I love my parents, Tom, and Jerry.'

hard.q: Explain the difference between a phrase and a clause.
hard.a: A clause has a subject and verb and can sometimes stand alone; a phrase does not have both
hard.hint: 'Running fast' is a phrase; 'She ran fast' is a clause.

hard.q: What is personification?
hard.a: Giving human characteristics to non-human things
hard.hint: Think about phrases like 'the wind howled angrily' β€” can wind be angry?

hard.q: What is the difference between a colon and a semicolon?
hard.a: Colon introduces a list or explanation; semicolon joins two related independent clauses
hard.hint: Think about their different jobs in a sentence.

hard.q: What is an embedded clause?
hard.a: A clause in the middle of a sentence, usually separated by commas
hard.hint: The cat, which was very old, sat on the mat β€” what is the embedded part?

hard.q: What is the difference between 'affect' and 'effect'?
hard.a: Affect is usually a verb (to influence); effect is usually a noun (a result)
hard.hint: 'The rain affected the game' (verb) vs 'The rain had an effect' (noun).

hard.q: What is a rhetorical question?
hard.a: A question asked for effect, not expecting an answer
hard.hint: Think about 'Isn't it obvious?' β€” do you expect a genuine answer?

hard.q: What is hyperbole?
hard.a: Extreme exaggeration for effect β€” e.g. 'I've told you a million times'
hard.hint: Think about phrases that are clearly not literally true but make a point strongly.

hard.q: What is the rule for adding '-ing' to a word ending in a single vowel + consonant?
hard.a: Double the final consonant before adding '-ing' β€” e.g. run β†’ running, sit β†’ sitting
hard.hint: Think about why 'runing' looks wrong but 'running' looks right.

hard.q: What is a determiner?
hard.a: A word that introduces a noun β€” e.g. a, the, this, those, my, some
hard.hint: Think about words that come before nouns to tell us which one or how many.

hard.q: What is the difference between a common noun and an abstract noun?
hard.a: Common nouns name physical things; abstract nouns name ideas, feelings or concepts
hard.hint: 'Chair' (common) vs 'happiness' (abstract) β€” which can you touch?

hard.q: What is a modal verb?
hard.a: A verb that expresses possibility, necessity or permission β€” e.g. can, could, might, should, must
hard.hint: Think about words like 'could', 'might' and 'must' β€” what do they add to a verb?

hard.q: Explain the 'i before e except after c' spelling rule and an exception.
hard.a: 'ie' in most words (believe, field) but 'ei' after c (receive, ceiling); exceptions: weird, seize
hard.hint: Think about the words 'believe' and 'receive' β€” how does the rule work?

hard.q: What is a parenthesis?
hard.a: Extra information added to a sentence in brackets, dashes or commas that can be removed
hard.hint: The word (or phrase), like this, adds information that isn't essential.

hard.q: What is pathetic fallacy?
hard.a: When the weather or nature reflects the mood of a character or story
hard.hint: Think about a storm in a story β€” is it ever just about weather?

hard.q: What is an iambic pentameter?
hard.a: A line of poetry with 10 syllables, alternating unstressed and stressed β€” used by Shakespeare
hard.hint: Think about the rhythm: da-DUM da-DUM da-DUM da-DUM da-DUM.

hard.q: What is the difference between a simile, metaphor and analogy?
hard.a: Simile uses like/as; metaphor says X is Y; analogy explains a complex idea by comparing it to a familiar one
hard.hint: Each is a comparison, but they serve different purposes and have different structures.

hard.q: What is narrative voice?
hard.a: The perspective from which a story is told β€” e.g. first person (I), third person (he/she)
hard.hint: Think about who is telling the story and how that affects how we experience it.

hard.q: What is dramatic irony?
hard.a: When the audience knows something characters do not
hard.hint: Think about a horror film where you can see the monster but the character cannot.

hard.q: What is the difference between denotation and connotation?
hard.a: Denotation is the literal meaning; connotation is the implied or emotional meaning
hard.hint: 'Snake' literally means a reptile, but it connotes dishonesty.

hard.q: What is an oxymoron?
hard.a: Two opposite or contradictory terms used together β€” e.g. 'bittersweet', 'deafening silence'
hard.hint: Think about how two opposing ideas can create a striking effect together.

hard.q: What is the difference between syntax and semantics?
hard.a: Syntax is the rules of grammar; semantics is about meaning
hard.hint: A sentence can be grammatically correct but meaningless ('Colourless green ideas sleep furiously').

hard.q: What is a homophone?
hard.a: Words that sound the same but have different meanings and spellings
hard.hint: Think about 'their', 'there', 'they're' β€” they all sound the same.

hard.q: What is the difference between persuasive and argumentative writing?
hard.a: Persuasive writing tries to change opinion; argumentative writing presents a balanced case with evidence
hard.hint: Think about a one-sided advert versus a balanced debate essay.

hard.q: What is a Shakespearean sonnet?
hard.a: A 14-line poem with three quatrains and a rhyming couplet, usually in iambic pentameter
hard.hint: Think about the structure: ABAB CDCD EFEF GG.

hard.q: What is the difference between a prologue and an epilogue?
hard.a: A prologue comes at the beginning to introduce; an epilogue comes at the end to conclude
hard.hint: Think about their positions in a book or play.

hard.q: What is foreshadowing?
hard.a: Clues or hints in a story that hint at future events
hard.hint: Think about an author planting seeds early that grow later in the story.

hard.q: What is the difference between first, second and third person narrative?
hard.a: First: I/we; second: you; third: he/she/they β€” each creates a different relationship with the reader
hard.hint: Think about how the reader feels differently depending on who is telling the story.

hard.q: What is assonance?
hard.a: The repetition of vowel sounds in nearby words
hard.hint: Think about 'the rain in Spain stays mainly in the plain' β€” what vowel sound repeats?

hard.q: What is the difference between a static and dynamic character?
hard.a: A static character doesn't change; a dynamic character changes through the story
hard.hint: Think about characters who learn and grow versus those who stay the same.

hard.q: What is an unreliable narrator?
hard.a: A narrator whose account is questionable β€” due to bias, limited knowledge or dishonesty
hard.hint: Think about a story told by a character who might not be telling the truth.

hard.q: What is the difference between connotation and denotation? Give an example.
hard.a: Denotation is the dictionary definition; connotation is the cultural or emotional associations
hard.hint: The word 'home' means a place to live (denotation) but connotes warmth and safety (connotation).

hard.q: What is a Bildungsroman?
hard.a: A coming-of-age story following a character's moral and psychological development
hard.hint: Think about stories like 'David Copperfield' or 'Harry Potter' where we watch a character grow up.

hard.q: What is deus ex machina?
hard.a: When an unsolvable problem is suddenly resolved by an unexpected event or character
hard.hint: Think about a story where someone is magically rescued at the last moment with no prior hints.

hard.q: What is the difference between allegory and symbolism?
hard.a: An allegory is an extended metaphor where characters represent ideas; symbolism uses individual objects to represent ideas
hard.hint: Animal Farm is an allegory; a dove symbolising peace is symbolism.

hard.q: What is a soliloquy?
hard.a: A speech in drama where a character speaks their thoughts aloud, alone on stage
hard.hint: Think about Hamlet saying 'To be or not to be' β€” who is he talking to?

hard.q: What is the difference between a tragic hero and an anti-hero?
hard.a: A tragic hero is noble but has a fatal flaw leading to downfall; an anti-hero lacks traditional heroic qualities
hard.hint: Macbeth (tragic hero) vs Walter White (anti-hero).

hard.q: What is a motif in literature?
hard.a: A recurring element β€” image, idea or symbol β€” that has significance throughout the text
hard.hint: Think about how blood keeps appearing in Macbeth and what it represents each time.

hard.q: What is catharsis in drama?
hard.a: The emotional release felt by an audience at the end of a tragedy
hard.hint: Think about feeling cleansed or relieved after watching a sad but meaningful play.

hard.q: What is the difference between comedy and tragedy in classical terms?
hard.a: Comedy ends happily with social harmony (often marriage); tragedy ends with death and downfall
hard.hint: Think about how the story ends β€” does the hero triumph or fall?

hard.q: What is stream of consciousness writing?
hard.a: A narrative technique that represents a character's continuous, unfiltered thought process
hard.hint: Think about writing that tries to mimic how a mind actually thinks β€” messy, non-linear.

hard.q: What is intertextuality?
hard.a: When a text references or is influenced by other texts
hard.hint: Think about how knowing another story changes how you read a new one.

easy.hint: Think about Samuel Pepys or Anne Frank's famous diaries.

easy.q: What did Stone Age people use for weapons?

easy.q: What is a tower used for in a castle?

easy.q: What was a Viking longship used for?

easy.q: What do we call a person who digs up historical remains?

easy.q: Was the steam train invented before or after the horse and cart?

easy.a: To shape and repair metal tools and horseshoes

easy.q: What was a monk's job in the Middle Ages?

easy.a: Any object, document or account that gives us information about the past
easy.hint: Think about what historians use to find out about history.

medium.q: What was the Great Fire of London and what caused it?
medium.a: A huge fire in 1666 that destroyed most of London; it started in a bakery on Pudding Lane
medium.hint: Think about the year, the location and what started the fire.

medium.q: How did the Great Fire of London change the city?
medium.a: London was rebuilt in brick and stone, and St Paul's Cathedral was redesigned by Christopher Wren
medium.hint: Think about what improvements were made after the fire.

medium.q: What was the significance of Florence Nightingale?
medium.a: She improved hospital hygiene and nursing standards, dramatically reducing soldier death rates
medium.hint: Think about what conditions were like before and after her work.

medium.q: What was the significance of the Stone Age?
medium.a: It was the earliest period of human history when people made tools from stone
medium.hint: Think about why this long period is called the Stone Age.

medium.q: What is the difference between BC and AD in dates?
medium.a: BC = Before Christ; AD = Anno Domini (after Christ's birth). BC counts backwards, AD forwards
medium.hint: The dividing point is the approximate birth of Jesus.

medium.q: What did the Romans contribute to British life?
medium.a: Roads, towns, baths, written records, Latin language, underfloor heating (hypocaust)
medium.hint: Think about lasting Roman influences still visible in Britain.

medium.q: What was life like for a child in Victorian times?
medium.a: Many worked in mines or factories; school gradually became compulsory; discipline was strict
medium.hint: Think about the difference between rich and poor children in Victorian Britain.

medium.q: What was the Gunpowder Plot of 1605?
medium.a: A failed attempt by Guy Fawkes and others to blow up Parliament and kill King James I
medium.hint: Think about why people still celebrate Bonfire Night on 5th November.

medium.q: Who was Mary Seacole and why is she significant?
medium.a: A British-Jamaican nurse who cared for soldiers in the Crimean War; significant as a black woman pioneering nursing
medium.hint: Think about the barriers she overcame and what she achieved.

medium.q: Why was the Great Wall of China built?
medium.a: To protect China from invasions from the north
medium.hint: Think about why you would build a very long wall.

medium.q: What was significant about Queen Victoria's reign?
medium.a: It was the longest of any British monarch at the time; Britain became a global superpower with a huge empire
medium.hint: Think about the length of her reign and what Britain was like during it.

medium.q: What is the difference between a primary and secondary historical source?
medium.a: Primary sources are from the time (diaries, artefacts); secondary sources are written about the time later
medium.hint: Which is more direct β€” a soldier's letter or a modern history textbook?

medium.q: What did the Vikings do when they came to Britain?
medium.a: They raided monasteries and towns, then later settled and traded
medium.hint: Think about why the Vikings first came to Britain and what they eventually did.

medium.q: What were the main achievements of the Ancient Egyptians?
medium.a: Pyramids, hieroglyphics, mummification, complex government, irrigation
medium.hint: Think about what the Egyptians are most famous for.

medium.q: What is significant about Stonehenge?
medium.a: It is a prehistoric monument whose purpose is still debated β€” possibly for ceremonies or astronomy
medium.hint: Think about why people thousands of years ago would build such an enormous stone structure.

medium.q: What was the role of a monk in the Middle Ages?
medium.a: Prayer, copying manuscripts, educating children and providing medical care
medium.hint: Think about all the things that happened inside a medieval monastery.

medium.q: What was the difference between rich and poor people in Victorian Britain?
medium.a: Rich had servants, fine houses and education; poor often lived in overcrowded slums and worked in dangerous conditions
medium.hint: Think about the inequality between social classes in the 1800s.

medium.q: Why did the Romans build straight roads?
medium.a: For efficient troop movement and communication across the empire
medium.hint: Think about why an army would need to travel quickly.

medium.q: What was the significance of the Battle of Hastings in 1066?
medium.a: William the Conqueror defeated King Harold, changing England's ruling class, language and culture forever
medium.hint: Think about what changed in England after William won.

medium.q: What was life like for a Viking?
medium.a: Farmers, traders and warriors; they lived in longhouses, farmed and sailed
medium.hint: Think about the everyday life of a Viking β€” not just the raiding.

medium.q: What were pyramids used for?
medium.a: As tombs for pharaohs, to help their souls reach the afterlife
medium.hint: Think about what ancient Egyptians believed about death.

medium.q: What was the impact of the Black Death in medieval Britain?
medium.a: It killed up to half the population, weakening the feudal system as surviving peasants gained more power
medium.hint: Think about what happens when so many workers die suddenly.

medium.q: Why were castles built with moats?
medium.a: The moat of water acted as a barrier making it very difficult for enemies to attack the castle walls
medium.hint: Think about what an attacker would have to do to get past a moat.

medium.q: What was the significance of Samuel Pepys' diary?
medium.a: It gives us a detailed, first-hand account of events like the Great Plague and Great Fire of London
medium.hint: Think about the value of a primary source written at the time.

medium.q: What was the feudal system?
medium.a: A medieval system where the king owned all land; lords gave land to knights in exchange for military service; peasants worked the land
medium.hint: Think about a pyramid of power with the king at the top.

medium.q: Why did ancient people build Stonehenge?
medium.a: Its exact purpose is unknown β€” possibly for religious ceremonies or as a calendar using the sun
medium.hint: Think about why people would spend decades moving enormous stones.

medium.q: What changes did William the Conqueror make after 1066?
medium.a: He replaced English nobles with Normans, ordered the Domesday Book, built castles and changed the language of government to French
medium.hint: Think about how a conqueror would want to control everything he won.

medium.q: What was the significance of the invention of the printing press?
medium.a: It allowed books to be produced quickly and cheaply, spreading knowledge and ideas rapidly
medium.hint: Think about what changed when books could be made by machine instead of by hand.

medium.q: How did the Roman Empire affect Britain after the Romans left?
medium.a: Roads, towns, Christianity and Latin words remained as legacies
medium.hint: Think about what the Romans built and left behind.

medium.q: What were the Crusades?
medium.a: A series of religious military campaigns (11th-13th centuries) by European Christians to reclaim the Holy Land
medium.hint: Think about the conflict between Christian and Muslim powers over Jerusalem.

medium.q: Why is the Domesday Book historically significant?
medium.a: It recorded everything William the Conqueror owned in England, making it the earliest national census
medium.hint: Think about why a king would need to know exactly what was in his kingdom.

medium.q: What were the main causes of World War One?
medium.a: Alliances, militarism, imperialism, nationalism, and the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand
medium.hint: Think about the MAIN acronym and the spark that set it off.

medium.q: How did life change for women in Britain during World War One?
medium.a: Women took on men's factory and transport jobs, proving capability and leading to gaining the vote in 1918
medium.hint: Think about what women did while men were fighting, and what they demanded afterwards.

medium.q: What was the significance of Rosa Parks?
medium.a: Her refusal to give up her seat on a bus in 1955 sparked the Montgomery Bus Boycott and the US Civil Rights Movement
medium.hint: Think about the small action that triggered a major change in history.

medium.q: What were the main features of a medieval castle?
medium.a: Keep, moat, drawbridge, battlements, portcullis, towers, great hall
medium.hint: Think about all the defensive and residential parts of a castle.

medium.q: What was the significance of the Battle of Waterloo?
medium.a: Napoleon's final defeat in 1815 ended French domination of Europe
medium.hint: Think about what Napoleon had been doing in Europe before this battle.

medium.q: How did the Industrial Revolution change Britain?
medium.a: It moved the population from farming to factories, created cities, railways and mass production
medium.hint: Think about all the changes that came from new machines and factories.

medium.q: What was the significance of the invention of the steam engine?
medium.a: It powered factories, trains and ships, driving the Industrial Revolution
medium.hint: Think about all the things that ran on steam power.

medium.q: Why was the Magna Carta signed in 1215?
medium.a: Rebellious barons forced King John to sign it, limiting royal power and establishing that even the king must follow the law
medium.hint: Think about what was new about the idea that a king had to obey rules.

medium.q: Who was Boudicca?
medium.a: A British queen of the Iceni tribe who led a major uprising against Roman rule around 60 AD
medium.hint: Think about a powerful British woman who fought against the Romans.

medium.q: What was the significance of the Apollo 11 moon landing?
medium.a: In 1969, it proved humans could travel to and walk on the moon, marking a triumph in the Space Race
medium.hint: Think about what it meant for humanity to step on another world.

medium.q: How did the Norman Conquest change the English language?
medium.a: French became the language of government and the elite; many French words entered English
medium.hint: Think about words like 'beef', 'pork', 'justice' β€” they came from French after 1066.

medium.q: What was the significance of the discovery of penicillin?
medium.a: Alexander Fleming discovered it in 1928, leading to antibiotics that save millions of lives
medium.hint: Think about what doctors could do for infected wounds before antibiotics.

medium.q: Who was William Wilberforce?
medium.a: A British politician who campaigned to abolish the slave trade, succeeding in 1807
medium.hint: Think about the man who spent decades fighting for the end of the British slave trade.

medium.q: What was the significance of the English Civil War?
medium.a: It resulted in the execution of King Charles I and temporarily replaced monarchy with a republic under Cromwell
medium.hint: Think about what it meant when Parliament defeated and executed a king.

medium.q: How did World War Two affect daily life in Britain?
medium.a: Rationing, evacuation of children, air raids, women in the workforce, blackouts
medium.hint: Think about the many ways the war changed how ordinary people lived.

medium.q: What was the significance of the founding of the NHS in 1948?
medium.a: It gave every British person free healthcare regardless of wealth, transforming public health
medium.hint: Think about what happened to poor people who couldn't afford doctors before the NHS.

medium.q: Why is 1066 often called the most important date in English history?
medium.a: The Norman Conquest changed England's language, culture, ruling class and legal system permanently
medium.hint: Think about how much changed in England because William the Conqueror won.

medium.q: What was the significance of Charles Darwin's theory of evolution?
medium.a: It provided a scientific explanation for the diversity of life, challenging religious explanations of creation
medium.hint: Think about how the idea that species change over time challenged existing beliefs.

hard.q: Analyse why the Norman Conquest of 1066 was a turning point in English history.
hard.a: It changed language, culture, law, architecture, and the ruling class; England became more connected to continental Europe
hard.hint: Think about multiple areas of life that changed β€” not just who was king.

hard.q: Why did the Roman Empire fall?
hard.a: Overexpansion, military pressures from barbarian tribes, economic troubles, political instability and corruption
hard.hint: Think about multiple factors rather than a single cause.

hard.q: How did the Black Death transform medieval European society?
hard.a: It killed up to half the population, weakening the feudal system, empowering peasants, and causing people to question the Church
hard.hint: Think about all the ways such enormous death would change society.

hard.q: Evaluate the importance of the Magna Carta for modern democracy.
hard.a: It established that rulers must obey the law, laying the foundation for constitutional government and human rights
hard.hint: Think about what ideas from 1215 are still important today.

hard.q: Why was the printing press (c.1440) one of the most significant inventions in history?
hard.a: It democratised knowledge, enabled the Reformation, spread scientific ideas and transformed literacy rates
hard.hint: Think about how the ability to mass-produce books changed power structures in society.

hard.q: Compare the lives of a rich Victorian and a poor Victorian child.
hard.a: Rich: education, servants, leisure, good food; poor: child labour, malnutrition, overcrowded slums, no schooling initially
hard.hint: Think about every aspect of life β€” home, work, education, health, food.

hard.q: Why did Britain become the first industrial nation?
hard.a: Coal and iron resources, colonial wealth, stable government, inventive culture and access to global trade
hard.hint: Think about all the advantages Britain had compared to other countries.

hard.q: How did World War One change the political map of Europe?
hard.a: It ended four empires (Ottoman, Austro-Hungarian, Russian, German) and created many new nations
hard.hint: Think about what happened to the old empires and what replaced them.

hard.q: Why is historical bias important to consider?
hard.a: All sources reflect the perspective of their creator; understanding bias helps us get a more accurate picture
hard.hint: Think about how a Roman soldier and a British tribesperson would describe the same battle differently.

hard.q: How did the abolition of slavery in Britain (1833) and the USA (1865) come about?
hard.a: Decades of campaigning by abolitionists, economic arguments, slave rebellions and changing moral attitudes
hard.hint: Think about the combination of moral, economic and political factors involved.

hard.q: Why was the Cold War significant even though it never became a 'hot' war?
hard.a: It shaped global politics for 45 years, caused proxy wars, the nuclear arms race and the Space Race
hard.hint: Think about the indirect effects of two superpowers in constant tension.

hard.q: Assess the impact of the British Empire on the countries it colonised.
hard.a: Mixed: infrastructure and education were introduced, but exploitation, cultural suppression and economic extraction caused lasting harm
hard.hint: Think about both what the Empire built and what it took.

hard.q: Why did the United States develop differently from Britain after the American Revolution?
hard.a: Democratic republic vs constitutional monarchy, frontier expansion, immigration, slavery as a defining issue
hard.hint: Think about the different political and social paths the two countries took.

hard.q: How did World War Two lead to the creation of the welfare state in Britain?
hard.a: Wartime solidarity, the Beveridge Report (1942), and Labour's 1945 landslide led to NHS, social security and education reform
hard.hint: Think about what people expected after sacrificing so much during the war.

hard.q: Evaluate the significance of the Renaissance for European history.
hard.a: It reawakened classical learning, produced artistic masterpieces, challenged Church authority and laid groundwork for scientific revolution
hard.hint: Think about multiple areas β€” art, science, religion, politics β€” that the Renaissance affected.

hard.q: Why is it difficult to be objective about recent historical events?
hard.a: We lack distance, living witnesses are present, sources are plentiful but often partial, and political implications remain live
hard.hint: Think about why historians disagree more about recent events than ancient ones.

hard.q: How did colonialism shape the modern world?
hard.a: It created current borders, languages, economic inequalities, and racial ideologies that still affect nations today
hard.hint: Think about Africa, Asia and the Americas β€” how did colonial borders affect them?

hard.q: Why did the League of Nations fail to prevent World War Two?
hard.a: US non-membership, no army, nations ignored it, appeasement of aggression, Great Depression weakened cooperation
hard.hint: Think about all the structural weaknesses and political failures of the League.

hard.q: Compare the methods used by Nelson Mandela and Martin Luther King Jr to fight racial injustice.
hard.a: Both used peaceful protest and rhetoric; King used marches and civil disobedience; Mandela initially also used armed resistance before choosing reconciliation
hard.hint: Think about the similarities and differences in their contexts and methods.

hard.q: How significant was the role of propaganda in both World Wars?
hard.a: Essential for recruitment, maintaining morale, demonising enemies and shaping public opinion β€” governments controlled information tightly
hard.hint: Think about the power of government-controlled messaging during total war.

hard.q: Why is it important to study history from multiple perspectives?
hard.a: A single perspective gives an incomplete picture; understanding different experiences leads to more accurate and just historical understanding
hard.hint: Think about how the same event looks completely different from different sides.

hard.q: Evaluate the causes of the French Revolution.
hard.a: Absolute monarchy, inequality between estates, financial crisis, Enlightenment ideas and food shortages combined to cause revolution
hard.hint: Think about social, economic and intellectual causes together.

hard.q: How did the development of writing change human civilisations?
hard.a: It enabled record-keeping, law codes, literature, complex administration and the transmission of knowledge across generations
hard.hint: Think about all the things that become possible once information can be written down.

hard.q: Why did Hitler come to power in Germany in 1933?
hard.a: Humiliation of Versailles Treaty, Great Depression, fear of communism, weak Weimar democracy, effective Nazi propaganda
hard.hint: Think about the economic, political and emotional conditions in Germany.

hard.q: How did the discovery of the Americas change the Old World?
hard.a: New foods, diseases, trade routes, silver and gold, slavery, and population exchange transformed European economies and societies
hard.hint: Think about the Colombian Exchange β€” what flowed in both directions?

hard.q: Assess the impact of the Scientific Revolution on Western thought.
hard.a: It replaced religious and classical authority with empirical observation and reason, laying foundations for modern science
hard.hint: Think about what changed when people started testing ideas rather than accepting ancient authority.

hard.q: Why was decolonisation significant in the 20th century?
hard.a: It ended European empires, created over 50 new nations, shifted global power and raised questions of development and identity
hard.hint: Think about the scale of change when empires dissolved.

hard.q: How did the Treaty of Versailles contribute to the rise of Nazism?
hard.a: Harsh reparations, loss of territory, war guilt clause and economic devastation created conditions for extremist politics
hard.hint: Think about how humiliation and poverty made people desperate for a strong leader.

hard.q: Evaluate the significance of the Industrial Revolution for global inequality.
hard.a: Britain and Western powers industrialised first, gaining economic and military dominance over the rest of the world
hard.hint: Think about who benefited from industrialisation and who was exploited.

hard.q: Why is the study of prehistory challenging?
hard.a: There are no written records; historians rely on archaeology, which gives incomplete physical evidence only
hard.hint: Think about the difference between history (written records) and prehistory.

hard.q: How did nationalism contribute to both World Wars?
hard.a: It drove empires to compete, created ethnic tensions, fuelled arms races and made compromise very difficult
hard.hint: Think about how the idea that nations should serve their own interests above all else causes conflict.

hard.q: Assess the long-term significance of the civil rights movement in the USA.
hard.a: It ended legal segregation, secured voting rights, but structural inequality persisted β€” the movement continues today
hard.hint: Think about what changed legally, what changed socially, and what has not yet fully changed.

hard.q: Why did the Soviet Union collapse in 1991?
hard.a: Economic stagnation, failed arms race, Gorbachev's reforms, nationalist movements and loss of Eastern European satellite states
hard.hint: Think about internal economic and political weaknesses rather than external pressure alone.

hard.q: How has the role of women in British society changed since the Victorian era?
hard.a: From legal non-entities with no vote to equal legal rights, workplace participation, political representation β€” a gradual, contested process
hard.hint: Think about changes in law, work, family, politics and culture over 150 years.

hard.q: Evaluate how geography shaped the development of ancient civilisations.
hard.a: River valleys (Nile, Tigris-Euphrates) provided water and fertile soil; trade routes determined which cultures thrived
hard.hint: Think about how where you live β€” coast, river, fertile plain β€” affects what you can build.

hard.q: How did the Holocaust happen?
hard.a: Years of antisemitic legislation, propaganda, dehumanisation, complicity of ordinary people and a totalitarian state enabled systematic genocide
hard.hint: Think about the gradual escalation from discrimination to genocide and the conditions that allowed it.

hard.q: Why did democracy spread after World War Two?
hard.a: Allied victory, decolonisation, US influence, discrediting of fascism and a desire for stable governance all promoted democracy
hard.hint: Think about who won the war and what political model they promoted.

hard.q: How significant was the role of technology in changing warfare from 1914 to 1945?
hard.a: Tanks, aircraft, chemical weapons, radar, nuclear weapons and industrialised production transformed the nature and scale of war
hard.hint: Think about how each new technology changed what war looked like.

hard.q: Assess the causes and consequences of the partition of India in 1947.
hard.a: Caused by communal tension, British policy, Congress-Muslim League conflict; consequences included massive displacement and violence
hard.hint: Think about the human cost of dividing a subcontinent along religious lines.

hard.q: Why is the United Nations significant in world history?
hard.a: Created after WW2 to maintain peace, set human rights standards and coordinate international action on global problems
hard.hint: Think about what the UN was created to prevent and what it has achieved.

hard.q: How did the Cold War shape the world we live in today?
hard.a: It created current nuclear arsenals, shaped borders in Asia/Europe/Americas, and established US global dominance after Soviet collapse
hard.hint: Think about the long-term effects of 45 years of superpower rivalry.

hard.q: Why is it important that history is taught in schools?
hard.a: It develops critical thinking, teaches from past mistakes, builds national and global identity and helps us understand the present
hard.hint: Think about all the ways understanding the past helps us live in the present.

hard.q: Evaluate the role of individuals versus structural forces in history.
hard.a: Both matter: individuals like Churchill or Hitler made crucial decisions, but they acted within structural conditions they did not create
hard.hint: Think about whether history is driven by great leaders or by economic/social forces beyond anyone's control.

easy.q: What are the four countries of the United Kingdom?
easy.a: England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland
easy.hint: Think about the four parts that make up the UK.

easy.q: What is the capital of England?
easy.a: London
easy.hint: The most famous and largest city in England.

easy.q: What is the capital of Scotland?
easy.a: Edinburgh
easy.hint: Home of the Scottish Parliament and Edinburgh Castle.

easy.q: What is the capital of Wales?
easy.a: Cardiff
easy.hint: The largest city in Wales.

easy.q: What is the capital of Northern Ireland?
easy.a: Belfast
easy.hint: The main city in Northern Ireland.

easy.q: What ocean is to the west of the UK?
easy.a: The Atlantic Ocean
easy.hint: The ocean you cross to get to America.

easy.q: What sea is between England and France?
easy.a: The English Channel
easy.hint: Think about the stretch of water you cross on a ferry from Dover to Calais.

easy.q: What are the four compass directions?
easy.a: North, South, East, West
easy.hint: Remember: Never Eat Shredded Wheat.

easy.a: Russia

easy.a: Africa, Asia, Europe, North America, South America, Australia (Oceania), Antarctica

easy.q: Which continent is the UK in?
easy.a: Europe
easy.hint: Think about the group of countries closest to the UK.

easy.a: A large area of land with its own government and borders

easy.a: The most important city in a country, where the government is based

easy.a: Asia

easy.a: An imaginary line around the middle of the Earth

easy.q: Is the UK closer to the North Pole or the equator?
easy.a: The North Pole β€” the UK is in the northern hemisphere
easy.hint: Think about whether the UK is near the top or middle of a globe.

easy.q: What is the name of the river that flows through London?
easy.a: The River Thames
easy.hint: The most famous river in England.

easy.q: What do we call the line where land meets the sea?
easy.a: The coast (or coastline)
easy.hint: Think about cliffs and beaches.

easy.hint: Think about Ben Nevis or the Alps.

easy.a: A large stream of water flowing to the sea or a lake

easy.q: What do we call very dry, sandy land with little rain?
easy.a: A desert
easy.hint: Think about the Sahara.

easy.a: A dense, hot, wet forest with enormous biodiversity
easy.hint: Think about the Amazon in South America.

easy.q: What do we call the area of land completely surrounded by water?
easy.a: An island
easy.hint: Great Britain is one.

easy.a: A large body of water surrounded by land

easy.a: Scotland

easy.a: A map

easy.q: What language do people speak in France?
easy.a: French
easy.hint: The language named after the country.

easy.q: What language do people speak in Spain?
easy.a: Spanish
easy.hint: The language named after the country.

easy.q: What is the name of the ocean south of the UK?
easy.a: The English Channel (and beyond that the Atlantic)
easy.hint: Think about the water between England and France.

easy.a: Paris

easy.a: France, Netherlands, Belgium, Luxembourg, Switzerland, Austria, Czech Republic, Poland, Denmark (any correct)

easy.q: What do we call the place where a river starts?
easy.a: The source
easy.hint: Think about a stream beginning high up on a hillside.

easy.a: France
easy.hint: It is in the capital city of France.

easy.a: The North Sea
easy.hint: Think about the sea between England and Scandinavia.

easy.hint: Think about the world's most populous continent.

easy.q: What do we call a narrow strip of water between two areas of land?
easy.a: A strait or channel
easy.hint: Think about the English Channel β€” it is narrow enough to see France on clear days.

easy.a: Antarctica
easy.hint: Think about the continent at the very bottom of the globe.

easy.q: What do we call a very large area of saltwater?
easy.a: An ocean or sea
easy.hint: Think about the Pacific or Atlantic.

easy.q: Name a country in South America.
easy.a: Brazil, Argentina, Colombia, Peru, Chile (any correct)
easy.hint: Think about the large continent below North America.

easy.q: What is the capital of Germany?
easy.a: Berlin
easy.hint: The largest and most important city in Germany.

easy.q: What do we call land that is lower than the surrounding land and often wet?
easy.a: A valley or marsh
easy.hint: Think about low ground between hills.

medium.q: What is the difference between the UK and Great Britain?
medium.a: Great Britain = England, Scotland and Wales; UK = Great Britain + Northern Ireland
medium.hint: Northern Ireland is the key difference between the two terms.

medium.q: Why does the UK have a mild, wet climate?
medium.a: It is surrounded by sea and warmed by the Gulf Stream ocean current
medium.hint: Think about how the ocean and warm currents affect nearby land temperatures.

medium.q: What is the difference between weather and climate?
medium.a: Weather is day-to-day conditions; climate is the long-term average weather pattern
medium.hint: Today's rain is weather; 'Britain is usually mild and wet' is climate.

medium.q: What is a grid reference?
medium.a: Numbers and letters used to pinpoint a location on a map
medium.hint: Think about the numbered lines on an Ordnance Survey map.

medium.q: How does rainfall vary across the UK?
medium.a: The west (Wales, Scotland) is wetter; the east is drier β€” due to prevailing westerly winds and mountains
medium.hint: Think about where rain-bearing winds come from and what stops them.

medium.q: What is a tributary?
medium.a: A smaller river or stream that flows into a larger one
medium.hint: Think about smaller streams joining the main river.

medium.q: What is the difference between a physical and a political map?
medium.a: Physical maps show natural features; political maps show countries and human borders
medium.hint: One shows nature; the other shows what humans have created.

medium.q: Why are cities often built near rivers?
medium.a: Rivers provide fresh water, food, transport and fertile land for farming
medium.hint: Think about what early settlers needed and where rivers could provide it.

medium.q: What is a contour line on a map?
medium.a: A line joining points of equal height, showing the shape of the land
medium.hint: Think about how closely spaced contours show steep hills.

medium.q: Name the countries that share a land border with England.
medium.a: Scotland (north) and Wales (west); the Republic of Ireland shares a border with Northern Ireland
medium.hint: Think about which UK countries touch England directly.

medium.q: What is deforestation?
medium.a: Cutting down large areas of forest, usually for farming or development
medium.hint: Think about what happens when forests are cleared.

medium.q: What is urbanisation?
medium.a: The growth of towns and cities as more people move from rural to urban areas
medium.hint: Think about the trend of people leaving the countryside for cities.

medium.q: What are natural resources?
medium.a: Materials from nature that humans use β€” water, timber, coal, oil, minerals
medium.hint: Think about what exists in the environment that we depend on.

medium.q: What is the difference between a mountain and a hill?
medium.a: In the UK, a mountain is generally over 600m; a hill is lower
medium.hint: Think about the height difference between a gentle hill and Ben Nevis.

medium.q: What is the source of the River Thames?
medium.a: The Cotswolds in Gloucestershire
medium.hint: Think about where England's most famous river begins.

medium.q: What is the mouth of a river?
medium.a: Where the river meets the sea, a lake or another river
medium.hint: Think about the end of the river's journey.

medium.q: Why do some parts of the UK experience more flooding than others?
medium.a: Heavy rainfall, low-lying land, impermeable surfaces and building on flood plains all contribute
medium.hint: Think about the conditions that make flooding more likely.

medium.q: Name the UK's main mountain ranges.
medium.a: Pennines (England), Highlands (Scotland), Cambrian Mountains (Wales), Mourne Mountains (N. Ireland)
medium.hint: Think about the main upland areas in each UK country.

medium.q: What is the difference between a bay and a headland?
medium.a: A bay is where the sea cuts into the land; a headland is a promontory of land jutting into the sea
medium.hint: Think about the shapes of coastlines β€” what curves in and what sticks out?

medium.q: What causes erosion on coastlines?
medium.a: Waves constantly hitting cliffs break them down over time
medium.hint: Think about the force of waves hitting rocks over many years.

medium.q: What is a National Park in the UK?
medium.a: A protected area of outstanding natural beauty β€” e.g. Lake District, Snowdonia, Dartmoor
medium.hint: Think about why certain areas of countryside need official protection.

medium.q: What is the Greenwich Meridian?
medium.a: The line of 0Β° longitude running through Greenwich, London β€” the basis for world time zones
medium.hint: Think about why time zones are measured from London.

medium.q: What is the difference between latitude and longitude?
medium.a: Latitude measures north-south distance from the equator; longitude measures east-west from the Prime Meridian
medium.hint: Latitude lines are horizontal; longitude lines are vertical on a globe.

medium.q: What is the difference between renewable and non-renewable energy?
medium.a: Renewable replenishes naturally (wind, solar); non-renewable will run out (coal, oil)
medium.hint: Think about whether the energy source refills itself.

medium.q: What is a settlement?
medium.a: A place where people live β€” ranging from a hamlet to a large city
medium.hint: Think about the range from a few houses to a million people.

medium.q: What is the difference between immigration and emigration?
medium.a: Immigration = moving into a country; emigration = leaving a country
medium.hint: Think about in and out.

medium.q: Why do rivers flood?
medium.a: Heavy or prolonged rain, snowmelt, deforestation and urban development all increase flood risk
medium.hint: Think about what prevents water from soaking into the ground.

medium.q: What is a delta?
medium.a: Where a river splits into channels before entering the sea, creating a fan shape
medium.hint: Think about the Nile Delta in Egypt.

medium.q: What is the difference between a city, a town and a village?
medium.a: Cities are largest (usually with a cathedral or city status); towns are medium-sized; villages are small and rural
medium.hint: Think about population size and whether it has rural or urban character.

medium.q: Why is the south of England generally warmer than the north?
medium.a: The south is further from the Arctic and receives more direct sunlight due to its lower latitude
medium.hint: Think about how latitude (distance from equator) affects temperature.

medium.q: What is a meander?
medium.a: A bend or curve in a river, formed as it erodes the outer bank and deposits on the inner
medium.hint: Think about a snake-like river crossing flat land.

medium.q: What is the difference between a hill and a cliff?
medium.a: A hill rises gradually from surrounding land; a cliff is a steep vertical or near-vertical rock face
medium.hint: Think about the shape β€” gradual slope versus sheer drop.

medium.q: What are the main uses of rivers?
medium.a: Drinking water, irrigation, transport, fishing, hydroelectric power, recreation
medium.hint: Think about all the ways humans have used rivers throughout history.

medium.q: What is a peninsula?
medium.a: Land almost entirely surrounded by water, connected to the mainland by a narrow strip
medium.hint: Think about Italy or Cornwall β€” surrounded by water on most sides.

medium.q: What is the difference between a sea and an ocean?
medium.a: Oceans are larger bodies of water; seas are smaller, often partly enclosed by land
medium.hint: Think about the Mediterranean Sea versus the Pacific Ocean.

medium.q: What is global warming?
medium.a: The gradual increase in average global temperatures, largely caused by greenhouse gas emissions
medium.hint: Think about the overall warming trend and what is causing it.

medium.q: What is the greenhouse effect?
medium.a: Gases like CO2 trap heat from the sun in the atmosphere, warming the planet
medium.hint: Think about how a greenhouse keeps plants warm and apply that to the atmosphere.

medium.q: What is a biome?
medium.a: A large natural region with a distinctive climate, vegetation and animals
medium.hint: Think about rainforest, desert, tundra β€” what makes each unique?

medium.q: What is sustainable development?
medium.a: Meeting current needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs
medium.hint: Think about using resources in a way that doesn't run them out.

medium.q: What is population density?
medium.a: The number of people living per square kilometre β€” how crowded an area is
medium.hint: Think about London (very crowded) versus the Highlands of Scotland (very empty).

medium.q: What is trade?
medium.a: The buying and selling of goods and services between people, businesses or countries
medium.hint: Think about how countries exchange what they are good at producing.

medium.q: What is a fossil fuel?
medium.a: A fuel formed from ancient organic material β€” coal, oil and natural gas
medium.hint: Think about fuels formed from creatures that lived millions of years ago.

medium.q: Why does it rain more in western Scotland than eastern England?
medium.a: Prevailing winds bring wet air from the Atlantic; mountains force the air up, cooling it and causing rainfall
medium.hint: Think about which direction rain-bearing winds come from and what happens when they hit mountains.

medium.q: What is the water cycle?
medium.a: Water evaporates, forms clouds, falls as precipitation, flows through rivers back to the sea
medium.hint: Think about how water moves continuously from sea to sky and back to land.

medium.q: What is an earthquake?
medium.a: A sudden violent shaking of the ground caused by movement of tectonic plates
medium.hint: Think about what happens when the enormous plates of rock that make up the Earth's surface shift.

medium.q: What is a volcano?
medium.a: An opening in the Earth's crust through which magma, ash and gases erupt
medium.hint: Think about the mountain that can explode with lava and ash.

medium.q: Why is the Amazon rainforest important?
medium.a: It produces oxygen, absorbs CO2, supports enormous biodiversity and regulates regional climate
medium.hint: Think about what the rainforest does for the atmosphere and wildlife.

medium.q: What are tectonic plates?
medium.a: Giant pieces of the Earth's crust that move slowly, causing earthquakes and volcanoes at their edges
medium.hint: Think about the Earth's surface being divided into huge moving pieces.

medium.q: What is acid rain?
medium.a: Rain made acidic by dissolved pollutants (SO2, NOx) from burning fossil fuels
medium.hint: Think about what happens when factory emissions dissolve in water in clouds.

medium.q: What is the difference between a developed and a developing country?
medium.a: Developed countries have higher income, education, health and infrastructure; developing have lower levels of these
medium.hint: Think about the wide range of living standards around the world.

hard.q: Explain how the water cycle links the oceans, atmosphere and land.
hard.a: Evaporation from oceans creates water vapour; condensation forms clouds; precipitation falls as rain/snow; rivers return water to sea
hard.hint: Think about each stage of water's journey and how they connect.

hard.q: Why is the UK's climate described as 'temperate maritime'?
hard.a: Temperate = moderate temperatures; maritime = influenced by the sea, bringing mild winters and cool summers
hard.hint: Think about what both words mean and how the sea affects the UK's weather.

hard.q: How does relief (shape of the land) affect rainfall distribution across the UK?
hard.a: West-facing hills force moist Atlantic air upwards, cooling it and causing orographic rainfall; east is in the rain shadow
hard.hint: Think about what happens when wet air from the Atlantic hits mountains.

hard.q: What is the difference between weather, climate and climate change?
hard.a: Weather = day conditions; climate = long-term average; climate change = long-term shift in global climate patterns
hard.hint: Think about timescales: hours/days, decades, centuries.

hard.q: Explain how urbanisation creates the 'urban heat island' effect.
hard.a: Buildings, roads and human activity absorb and release heat, making cities warmer than surrounding rural areas
hard.hint: Think about all the ways a city generates heat that the countryside does not.

hard.q: What are the human and physical causes of flooding?
hard.a: Physical: heavy rain, impermeable rock, steep slopes; human: deforestation, urban development, building on flood plains
hard.hint: Think separately about what nature contributes and what humans do that makes flooding worse.

hard.q: Explain the process of coastal erosion and the formation of sea stacks.
hard.a: Waves erode cliffs β†’ caves form β†’ caves break through to form arches β†’ arches collapse leaving stacks
hard.hint: Think about the sequence of erosion from a solid cliff to an isolated pillar of rock.

hard.q: How does globalisation affect the UK?
hard.a: Imports/exports, multicultural population, global supply chains, foreign investment and cultural exchange all connect UK to world
hard.hint: Think about where your food, clothes and technology come from.

hard.q: Why does the world's population continue to grow?
hard.a: Birth rates exceed death rates globally; improved medicine and food security have reduced mortality
hard.hint: Think about what has changed to allow more people to survive to adulthood and old age.

hard.q: What are the consequences of deforestation for global climate?
hard.a: Trees absorb CO2; deforestation releases stored carbon, reduces rainfall and destroys habitats
hard.hint: Think about what trees do for the atmosphere and what happens when they are removed.

hard.q: Explain the difference between renewable and non-renewable energy with examples of each.
hard.a: Renewable (wind, solar, tidal, hydro) replenishes naturally; non-renewable (coal, oil, gas) forms over millions of years and will run out
hard.hint: Think about how long each type takes to form and whether it can run out.

hard.q: What is the connection between tectonic plates and the formation of mountains?
hard.a: When plates collide, rock is forced upward, forming fold mountains like the Alps or Himalayas
hard.hint: Think about what happens to rock when two enormous plates push against each other.

hard.q: Why are some countries much wealthier than others?
hard.a: History (colonialism), natural resources, governance, geography, education, trade access and climate all contribute
hard.hint: Think about multiple factors β€” no single cause explains global inequality.

hard.q: How does the formation of a river delta occur?
hard.a: As a river slows at its mouth, it deposits sediment; over time this builds up into a fan of land
hard.hint: Think about what happens to the material a river is carrying when the river slows down.

hard.q: Explain the causes and consequences of desertification.
hard.a: Overgrazing, deforestation and climate change degrade land; desertification leads to food insecurity and migration
hard.hint: Think about how human activity and climate together turn fertile land to desert.

hard.q: What is the relationship between biodiversity and ecosystem stability?
hard.a: Greater biodiversity makes ecosystems more resilient; losing species can cause cascading failures
hard.hint: Think about what happens if you remove a key species β€” how does the rest of the ecosystem respond?

hard.q: Why is the Amazon rainforest being deforested and what are the global consequences?
hard.a: Cattle farming, soy farming and logging drive deforestation; consequences include CO2 release, biodiversity loss and climate disruption
hard.hint: Think about why people clear the forest and what the world loses as a result.

hard.q: Explain why coastal areas are often densely populated.
hard.a: Access to trade, fishing, milder climates, tourism and historical settlement patterns make coasts attractive
hard.hint: Think about all the economic and practical advantages of living by the sea.

hard.q: What is food security and why is it threatened globally?
hard.a: Food security means reliable access to sufficient food; threatened by population growth, climate change and inequality
hard.hint: Think about who has access to food and what might reduce global food supply.

hard.q: How do human activities contribute to climate change?
hard.a: Burning fossil fuels, deforestation and agriculture release greenhouse gases that trap heat in the atmosphere
hard.hint: Think about the different ways humans add CO2 and methane to the atmosphere.

hard.q: What is the significance of the Prime Meridian (Greenwich Meridian)?
hard.a: It is the basis for measuring longitude and the foundation of the international time zone system
hard.hint: Think about how we measure east-west position on Earth and how that relates to time.

hard.q: Why do tectonic plates move?
hard.a: Convection currents in the molten mantle beneath the crust carry the plates
hard.hint: Think about what drives the enormous plates of rock that form the Earth's surface.

hard.q: Explain how a river valley changes from its upper course to its lower course.
hard.a: Upper: narrow, steep, V-shaped valleys; lower: wide, flat flood plains, meanders and wider channels
hard.hint: Think about how erosion and deposition change the landscape as the river descends.

hard.q: What is the difference between primary, secondary and tertiary industries?
hard.a: Primary = extracting resources; secondary = manufacturing; tertiary = services
hard.hint: Think about the chain from raw material to finished product to service.

hard.q: How does overpopulation affect the environment?
hard.a: It increases demand for food, water and energy, causing deforestation, pollution and habitat loss
hard.hint: Think about what more people need and what the environment loses to provide it.

hard.q: What is the impact of tourism on local environments?
hard.a: Tourism brings money but can also damage fragile ecosystems, increase pollution and displace local communities
hard.hint: Think about both the economic benefit and the environmental cost of many visitors.

hard.q: Why is fresh water a scarce resource globally?
hard.a: Only 3% of Earth's water is fresh; most is frozen; population growth and pollution reduce accessible supplies
hard.hint: Think about how little fresh water there is compared to the total.

hard.q: What is the link between poverty and environmental degradation?
hard.a: Poor communities often lack alternatives to overusing land; environmental damage worsens poverty in a cycle
hard.hint: Think about why a poor farmer might cut down trees even knowing the consequences.

hard.q: Explain how geographers use GIS (Geographic Information Systems).
hard.a: GIS layers multiple types of geographic data on digital maps to analyse patterns β€” e.g. disease spread, traffic, climate
hard.hint: Think about how digital mapping can combine many types of data to reveal patterns.

hard.q: Why is the Sahara Desert expanding?
hard.a: Climate change, overgrazing and deforestation at its edges are pushing the desert southward into the Sahel
hard.hint: Think about the combination of climate and human pressure on land at the desert's edge.

hard.q: What is the relationship between global trade and carbon emissions?
hard.a: Shipping and air freight goods around the world produces significant CO2, linking consumption to emissions
hard.hint: Think about the carbon cost of transporting goods from one side of the world to another.

hard.q: What are the social, economic and environmental impacts of urbanisation?
hard.a: Social: better services but overcrowding; economic: growth but inequality; environmental: pollution and habitat loss
hard.hint: Think about the mixed effects of cities growing rapidly.

hard.q: How does the Atlantic Ocean affect the climate of Western Europe?
hard.a: The Gulf Stream brings warm water northward, keeping western Europe much warmer than its latitude would suggest
hard.hint: Think about why London is warmer than Moscow despite being at a similar latitude.

hard.q: What is the significance of the Himalayas for South Asia?
hard.a: They block cold Arctic air, determine monsoon patterns and are the source of Asia's major rivers
hard.hint: Think about the wide range of effects one mountain range can have on an entire region.

hard.q: Why is Antarctica important to global climate science?
hard.a: Its ice cores contain ancient air bubbles giving us records of past atmospheres and climate change
hard.hint: Think about what information might be locked in hundreds of thousands of years of ice.

hard.q: What are the challenges of sustainable fishing?
hard.a: Overfishing depletes stocks; quotas are hard to enforce; illegal fishing persists; ecosystems are disrupted
hard.hint: Think about why fishing sustainably is so difficult given the economic pressures involved.

hard.q: What is the difference between a refugee and an economic migrant?
hard.a: A refugee flees danger (war, persecution); an economic migrant moves voluntarily seeking better opportunities
hard.hint: Think about whether someone is forced to leave or chooses to leave.

hard.q: How does climate change threaten coastal communities?
hard.a: Sea level rise, more intense storms and erosion threaten low-lying settlements and infrastructure
hard.hint: Think about all the ways rising seas and stronger weather affect people who live on coasts.

hard.q: What is the human development index (HDI)?
hard.a: A composite measure of a country's development using income, education and life expectancy
hard.hint: Think about what factors beyond just money tell us how well people in a country are living.

hard.q: What are the causes and effects of soil erosion?
hard.a: Caused by deforestation, overfarming and wind/rain; effects include reduced fertility, flooding and sedimentation of rivers
hard.hint: Think about what protects soil and what happens when that protection is removed.

hard.q: Why do some river valleys have flat flood plains?
hard.a: Over time, rivers deposit sediment when they flood; this builds up flat, fertile land beside the river
hard.hint: Think about what a river does when it overflows its banks and what it leaves behind.

hard.q: What is the relationship between economic development and carbon emissions?
hard.a: More developed countries historically emit more CO2; developing nations are catching up as they industrialise
hard.hint: Think about the link between industry, energy use and greenhouse gas production.

medium.q: Explain the difference between transparent, translucent and opaque.

medium.q: Give two properties of metal that make it useful for making a bridge.
medium.a: Strong (can bear heavy loads) and rigid (holds its shape under stress).
medium.hint: What stresses does a bridge experience?

medium.q: Why are sponges used to clean surfaces?
medium.a: They are absorbent β€” they soak up liquids β€” and soft so they don't scratch.
medium.hint: Think about what properties make a good cleaning material.

medium.a: Evaporation (water heats and rises), condensation (forms clouds), precipitation (falls as rain/snow).
medium.hint: Think of water going up, forming clouds, and coming back down.

medium.q: What is the difference between deciduous and evergreen trees?
medium.a: Deciduous trees lose their leaves in autumn/winter; evergreen trees keep their leaves all year.
medium.hint: Does an oak keep or drop its leaves in winter?

medium.q: Why do animals in cold climates often have thick fur?
medium.a: Thick fur acts as insulation, trapping heat and preventing body heat from escaping.
medium.hint: Think of a polar bear β€” why doesn't it freeze?

medium.q: What is photosynthesis?
medium.a: The process by which plants use sunlight, water and carbon dioxide to make their own food (glucose) and release oxygen.
medium.hint: Think of what plants take in and what they produce.

medium.q: Explain a simple food chain from a meadow habitat.
medium.a: E.g. Grass β†’ rabbit β†’ fox. Grass is the producer; rabbit is the prey; fox is the predator.
medium.hint: Start with what grows and end with the top predator.

medium.q: Why do plants have flowers?
medium.a: Flowers are the reproductive organs of the plant β€” they attract pollinators to carry pollen for reproduction.
medium.hint: Think about bees and what they do when visiting flowers.

medium.q: What is the difference between a herbivore and a carnivore? Give an example of each.
medium.a: Herbivore: eats only plants (e.g. rabbit, deer). Carnivore: eats only animals (e.g. lion, hawk).
medium.hint: Think about what each animal's teeth look like.

medium.q: Name three ways materials can be changed.
medium.a: E.g. bending, twisting, squashing, stretching, cutting, heating, cooling
medium.hint: Think of how you can physically change a piece of clay.

medium.a: No. Melting ice can be reversed (refreeze), but burning wood cannot be reversed.

medium.a: E.g. deforestation (destroys homes), pollution (poisons water/air), farming (removes wild land)
medium.hint: Think about what happens when a forest is cut down.

medium.q: What is the role of the producer in a food chain?
medium.a: Producers (plants) make their own food using sunlight and form the base of all food chains.
medium.hint: Who provides the energy for every other organism?

medium.q: Why is exercise important for the heart?
medium.a: Exercise strengthens the heart muscle, improves circulation, and keeps the cardiovascular system healthy.
medium.hint: The heart is a muscle β€” what happens to muscles that get regular exercise?

medium.q: Name four types of teeth and their functions.
medium.a: Incisors (bite/cut), canines (tear), premolars (crush), molars (grind)
medium.hint: Think about the different jobs teeth do when you eat.

medium.q: What is the difference between a vertebrate and an invertebrate?
medium.a: Vertebrates have a backbone (e.g. fish, birds, mammals); invertebrates do not (e.g. insects, worms, jellyfish).
medium.hint: Do insects have a spine?

medium.q: Name three properties that make plastic a useful material.
medium.a: Waterproof, lightweight, flexible, mouldable, durable β€” any three.
medium.hint: Think of all the plastic objects around you.

medium.a: Wind (e.g. dandelion), animals/fur (e.g. burrs), water (coconuts), eaten then deposited (berries)
medium.hint: Think about how a dandelion clock spreads.

medium.q: Explain why a cactus can survive in a desert.
medium.a: It stores water in its thick stem, has spines instead of leaves to reduce water loss, and has deep/wide roots.
medium.hint: What adaptations help in a hot, dry habitat?

medium.q: What is a predator?
medium.a: An animal that hunts and eats other animals.
medium.hint: Think of the animal at the top of a food chain.

medium.q: What is prey?
medium.a: An animal that is hunted and eaten by a predator.
medium.hint: The rabbit in 'fox eats rabbit' is the prey.

medium.q: Name two animals that are reptiles and two that are amphibians.
medium.a: Reptiles: snake, crocodile, lizard. Amphibians: frog, toad, newt.
medium.hint: Reptiles have scales; amphibians live in both water and land.

medium.q: Why do we classify animals into groups?
medium.a: To organise them by shared characteristics, making it easier to study and understand them.
medium.hint: Think about sorting objects β€” why is sorting useful?

medium.q: What does the stomach do?
medium.a: It breaks down food using acids and muscles, continuing digestion after the mouth.
medium.hint: It's part of the digestive system.

medium.q: Name three parts of the digestive system in order.
medium.a: Mouth β†’ oesophagus β†’ stomach β†’ small intestine β†’ large intestine
medium.hint: Follow the journey of food from start to finish.

medium.q: Why do animals in hot deserts often come out at night?
medium.a: To avoid the extreme heat of the day β€” they are nocturnal to stay cool.
medium.hint: Think about how the desert temperature changes between day and night.

medium.q: What is meant by a 'balanced diet'?
medium.a: Eating the right amounts of different food groups (carbohydrates, protein, fat, vitamins, minerals, water) for good health.
medium.hint: Think of the Eatwell plate showing proportions.

medium.q: What is insulation? Give an example.
medium.a: Insulation prevents heat from transferring β€” e.g. a woolly jumper keeps you warm by trapping air.
