medium.a: When an opaque object blocks light from a light source, it casts a shadow on the surface behind it.
medium.hint: Think about what happens on a sunny day when you stand outside.

medium.q: How do the seasons affect animals' behaviour?
medium.a: Some migrate (birds), some hibernate (hedgehogs/bears), some change colour (arctic fox) for camouflage.
medium.hint: Think about what animals do when winter comes.

medium.q: What is the difference between a mammal and a fish?
medium.a: Mammals breathe air (lungs), feed young on milk, usually have fur. Fish breathe via gills, lay eggs (most), have scales.
medium.hint: How does each breathe underwater vs on land?

medium.q: Name two ways plants reproduce.
medium.a: Seeds (sexual reproduction) and vegetative reproduction (e.g. bulbs, runners, cuttings).
medium.hint: Some plants grow from seeds; others from parts of the parent plant.

medium.q: What is the function of the lungs?
medium.a: To take in oxygen from the air and release carbon dioxide from the body.
medium.hint: They are like bellows β€” breathing in and out.

medium.q: What happens to most materials when they are heated?
medium.a: They expand (get bigger). Solids may melt, liquids may evaporate.
medium.hint: Think of metal on a hot day or ice in sunlight.

medium.q: Why is it important that habitats are protected?
medium.a: If habitats are destroyed, the animals and plants that depend on them lose food and shelter, potentially leading to extinction.
medium.hint: What would happen to fish if all rivers were polluted?

medium.q: Explain the difference between a fossil and a living organism.
medium.a: A fossil is the preserved remains or impression of an organism that died long ago; a living organism is alive now.
medium.hint: Think of dinosaur bones versus a living dog.

medium.q: What is camouflage? Give an example.
medium.a: When an animal's colour or pattern matches its environment, making it hard to see β€” e.g. a stick insect looks like a twig.
medium.hint: Why might a zebra's stripes be useful?

medium.q: Why do plants need nitrogen?
medium.a: To make proteins needed for cell growth.
medium.hint: Plants get nitrogen from the soil or from fertiliser.

medium.q: Name the process by which water turns from liquid to gas.
medium.a: Evaporation
medium.hint: What happens to a puddle on a hot day?

medium.q: Describe one way humans can help protect wildlife.
medium.a: E.g. creating nature reserves, planting wildflowers, reducing pollution, not littering
medium.hint: Think of what humans do to hurt wildlife and the opposite.

medium.q: What are vertebrates grouped into? Name the five main classes.
medium.a: Fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, mammals
medium.hint: Think of animals with backbones from water to land.

medium.q: Name three materials that can conduct heat.
medium.a: Metals such as copper, aluminium, iron
medium.hint: Why are pots and pans made of metal?

medium.q: Name three materials that are good insulators of heat.
medium.a: Wood, plastic, glass, rubber, fabric β€” any three
medium.hint: Pot handles are often made from insulating materials. Why?

medium.q: What is pollination?
medium.a: The transfer of pollen from the male part (anther) to the female part (stigma) of a flower, enabling fertilisation.
medium.hint: Bees carry pollen from flower to flower.

medium.q: Why do animals have adaptations?
medium.a: To improve their chances of survival in their particular habitat.
medium.hint: Why does a fish have gills but a rabbit has lungs?

medium.q: Name the organ that pumps blood in the human body.
medium.a: Heart
medium.hint: You can feel it beating in your chest.

medium.q: Describe one adaptation of a duck for living near water.
medium.a: E.g. webbed feet for swimming, waterproof feathers to keep dry, flat bill to filter food from water.
medium.hint: What physical features help a duck in its habitat?

medium.q: Why do we need a skeleton?
medium.a: Support (holds the body upright), protection (shields organs), movement (muscles pull on bones to move joints).
medium.hint: Think of three different jobs the skeleton does.

medium.q: What is meant by 'irreversible change'? Give an example.
medium.a: A change that cannot be undone β€” e.g. burning paper; once burned it cannot be unburned.
medium.hint: Can you un-bake a cake?

medium.q: Name two things that affect how fast a shadow changes in length during the day.
medium.a: The position of the sun in the sky (which changes with time of day) and the height of the object casting the shadow.
medium.hint: Shadows are long in the morning and evening β€” why?

hard.q: Explain why we can see the Moon even though it doesn't produce its own light.
hard.a: The Moon reflects sunlight. When sunlight hits its surface, it bounces toward Earth, making the Moon visible.
hard.hint: Think about what a mirror does with light.

hard.q: Compare the advantages and disadvantages of using wood versus plastic for making a chair.
hard.a: Wood: natural, strong, renewable, biodegradable but heavy, can rot. Plastic: lightweight, waterproof, cheap, moulded easily but non-biodegradable, can break.
hard.hint: Think about durability, cost, environmental impact and weight.

hard.q: Explain why a food chain always starts with a plant.
hard.a: Plants are the only organisms that can produce their own food (via photosynthesis), providing the initial energy for all other organisms.
hard.hint: Where does the energy in a food chain originally come from?

hard.q: Why do some animals become extinct? Give two reasons.
hard.a: Habitat loss, hunting/over-exploitation, climate change, disease, introduction of new predators β€” any two with explanation.
hard.hint: Think about what animals need to survive.

hard.q: Describe an experiment to test which material is the best insulator. Include what you would change, measure and keep the same.
hard.a: Wrap identical containers of hot water in different materials. Measure temperature drop over 10 minutes. Keep container size and volume of water the same.
hard.hint: Think about a fair test: one variable changes, all others stay the same.

hard.q: Explain the nitrogen cycle briefly.
hard.a: Plants absorb nitrogen from soil; animals eat plants and gain nitrogen; decomposers break down dead matter, returning nitrogen to soil; bacteria also fix nitrogen from the air.
hard.hint: Think about how nitrogen travels from soil β†’ plant β†’ animal β†’ decomposer β†’ soil.

hard.q: How does a plant use the products of photosynthesis?
hard.a: Glucose is used for energy (respiration), growth, and making cellulose for cell walls; oxygen is released as a by-product.
hard.hint: Think about all the things a plant needs glucose for.

hard.q: Explain why materials in Group 1 metals react violently with water, using the concept of reactivity.
hard.a: Group 1 metals (sodium, potassium) have low ionisation energies β€” they readily give up electrons to water molecules, producing hydrogen gas and an alkali. Higher reactivity = more violent reaction.
hard.hint: Think about how easily they lose electrons and what hydrogen does when released rapidly.

hard.q: Describe how Darwin's theory of natural selection explains how animals become adapted over time.
hard.a: Individuals with useful variations survive better (survival of the fittest), reproduce more, passing on favourable traits. Over generations, these traits become more common, leading to adaptation.
hard.hint: Think: random variation β†’ selection pressure β†’ better-adapted individuals reproduce more.

hard.q: Explain the difference between a reversible and an irreversible change at a particle level.
hard.a: Reversible: particles rearrange but no new substances form (e.g. melting). Irreversible: particles bond in new ways creating new substances (e.g. burning β€” carbon dioxide and water form).
hard.hint: Are the original substances still present after the change?

hard.q: Why might two habitats in the same country have completely different animal communities?
hard.a: Different habitats offer different food sources, shelter, temperatures and water availability β€” these conditions select for different species.
hard.hint: Compare a woodland to a coastal rockpool.

hard.q: Explain why plants in rainforests have very large leaves.
hard.a: The forest floor receives little sunlight due to the dense canopy above. Large leaves maximise surface area for capturing the limited light available.
hard.hint: Think about the relationship between leaf size and available light.

hard.q: What is the difference between aerobic and anaerobic respiration?
hard.a: Aerobic: uses oxygen; releases more energy; produces COβ‚‚ and water. Anaerobic: no oxygen; releases less energy; produces lactic acid (animals) or ethanol/COβ‚‚ (yeast).
hard.hint: Think about exercise: when you sprint, can your body always get enough oxygen?

hard.q: Describe how human activities contribute to climate change.
hard.a: Burning fossil fuels releases COβ‚‚; deforestation reduces COβ‚‚ absorption; agriculture releases methane β€” increasing greenhouse gases trap more heat, raising global temperature.
hard.hint: Think about what gases trap heat and where they come from.

hard.q: Explain the concept of a 'microhabitat' and give an example.
hard.a: A microhabitat is a small, localised environment within a larger habitat with distinct conditions β€” e.g. under a rock in a garden (damp, dark) supports woodlice and centipedes.
hard.hint: Think of a small specific spot within a bigger habitat.

hard.q: Why does evaporation cause cooling?
hard.a: When water evaporates, the molecules with the most energy escape, lowering the average kinetic energy of those left behind β€” making the remaining liquid cooler.
hard.hint: Think about sweating: why do you feel cooler as sweat evaporates?

hard.q: Explain what happens in the human body during digestion.
hard.a: Food is mechanically broken down (chewing), enzymes break down carbohydrates, proteins and fats, nutrients are absorbed in the small intestine, water is absorbed in the large intestine, waste exits.
hard.hint: Follow the journey of a sandwich from mouth to exit.

hard.q: What is the difference between an inherited characteristic and an acquired one? Give examples.
hard.a: Inherited: passed from parents via genes (e.g. eye colour, blood type). Acquired: developed through environment/experience (e.g. a scar, speaking French, a tan).
hard.hint: Can you pass your tan to your children?

hard.q: Explain why the same material (e.g. wax) can exist as a solid or liquid.
hard.a: State depends on temperature. Below melting point, particles vibrate but stay in fixed positions (solid). Above melting point, particles have enough energy to move freely (liquid).
hard.hint: Think about particles and how temperature affects their energy.

hard.q: Describe the role of decomposers in an ecosystem.
hard.a: Decomposers (bacteria and fungi) break down dead organisms and waste, releasing nutrients back into the soil, which plants then absorb β€” completing the nutrient cycle.
hard.hint: Think of what would happen if nothing ever decomposed.

hard.q: Explain why the heart has four chambers.
hard.a: The right side receives deoxygenated blood and pumps it to the lungs. The left side receives oxygenated blood and pumps it to the body. Separation prevents mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood, maximising efficiency.
hard.hint: Think about why you need two separate circuits.

hard.q: Why do plants in desert climates have shallow but wide-spreading roots?
hard.a: Shallow roots quickly absorb rain before it evaporates. Wide spread maximises the area covered to catch as much water as possible from rare rainfall.
hard.hint: Think about rainfall patterns and how quickly water disappears in a desert.

hard.q: Explain the concept of a 'keystone species' and why removing one can collapse an ecosystem.
hard.a: A keystone species has a disproportionately large role in its ecosystem. Removing it disrupts food webs β€” prey species explode, vegetation may be destroyed, and other species collapse too.
hard.hint: Think of sea otters controlling sea urchins controlling kelp forests.

hard.q: Why might two closely related species in the same habitat evolve different diets?
hard.a: To avoid competition for the same food resource, one species adapts to a slightly different food source β€” this is called resource partitioning.
hard.hint: Think about different beak shapes in Darwin's finches.

hard.q: Describe one long-term consequence of melting polar ice caps.
hard.a: E.g. rising sea levels (flooding coastal cities), loss of habitat for polar bears and penguins, disruption of ocean currents affecting global climate.
hard.hint: Think about what is stored in ice and what happens when it melts.

hard.q: What is the difference between conduction, convection and radiation as forms of heat transfer?
hard.a: Conduction: through solids (particle vibration). Convection: through fluids (hot fluid rises, cool falls). Radiation: electromagnetic waves, no medium needed.
hard.hint: Think of a metal spoon in hot soup, steam rising, and sun warming skin.

hard.q: Explain why biodiversity is important.
hard.a: Biodiversity ensures ecosystem stability β€” diverse species perform different functions, so if one fails, others compensate. It also provides medicines, food, clean air and water for humans.
hard.hint: Think about what services nature provides and what happens if one species disappears.

hard.q: Describe the process of seed germination and what conditions are needed.
hard.a: A seed absorbs water, activating enzymes that break down stored food for energy. The embryo grows: root (radicle) first, then shoot. Needs water, warmth, and oxygen (not necessarily light initially).
hard.hint: Think about what you provide when planting a seed.

hard.q: Why do mammals maintain a constant body temperature, and how do they achieve it?
hard.a: Constant temperature allows enzymes to work optimally. Mechanisms: shivering (generates heat), sweating (cools down), blood vessel dilation/constriction, fat insulation.
hard.hint: Think about what 37Β°C means for chemical reactions in your body.

hard.q: Explain how pesticide use can unintentionally harm birds of prey at the top of a food chain.
hard.a: Pesticide accumulates in insects, then in small birds that eat insects, then in raptors that eat many small birds β€” concentration increases at each level (bioaccumulation/biomagnification).
hard.hint: Each animal eats many of the animals below β€” what happens to the poison as you go up the chain?

hard.q: What is a fair test? Why is it important in science?
hard.a: A fair test changes only one variable at a time (the independent variable), measures the effect (dependent variable), and keeps everything else the same (controlled variables). This ensures results are valid and reliable.
hard.hint: What would happen if you changed two things at once in an experiment?

hard.q: Describe two adaptations of a fish to its aquatic habitat.
hard.a: Gills (absorb dissolved oxygen from water), streamlined body (reduces water resistance for swimming), scales (protect and reduce drag), lateral line (detects vibrations) β€” any two with explanation.
hard.hint: Think about the challenges of living, breathing and moving in water.

hard.q: Why is sunlight described as the 'ultimate source of energy' for almost all food chains?
hard.a: Plants (producers) convert sunlight into chemical energy via photosynthesis. All other organisms ultimately depend on this stored energy, either by eating plants or eating animals that ate plants.
hard.hint: Trace the energy in a burger back to its origin.

hard.q: Explain why rusting is an irreversible chemical change.
hard.a: When iron reacts with oxygen and water, a new substance (iron oxide/rust) is formed with different properties. The original iron cannot be recovered without a separate chemical process.
hard.hint: Can you turn rust back into shiny iron just by cooling or drying it?

hard.q: How does the structure of the small intestine maximise absorption of nutrients?
hard.a: Finger-like projections called villi (and microvilli) massively increase surface area; thin walls; rich blood supply carries nutrients away quickly.
hard.hint: Think about surface area and why it matters for absorption.

hard.q: Describe the carbon cycle in three stages.
hard.a: 1. Plants absorb COβ‚‚ via photosynthesis. 2. Animals eat plants and release COβ‚‚ via respiration. 3. Dead organisms decompose, releasing COβ‚‚; burning also releases stored carbon.
hard.hint: Carbon moves between atmosphere, plants, animals and soil.

hard.q: Explain why a polar bear would NOT survive in a tropical rainforest.
hard.a: Polar bears are adapted to cold (thick fur, fat insulation, white camouflage). In a rainforest, their insulation would cause overheating, white fur provides no camouflage, and prey animals are different.
hard.hint: List the polar bear's adaptations and ask whether each would help in a rainforest.

hard.q: What evidence would you use to decide if an object is alive?
hard.a: Check the seven life processes: Movement, Respiration, Sensitivity, Growth, Reproduction, Excretion, Nutrition (MRS GREN).
hard.hint: A fire moves, grows and 'feeds' β€” but is it alive? Which MRS GREN criteria does it fail?

hard.q: Compare sexual and asexual reproduction in plants.
hard.a: Sexual: involves male and female gametes (pollen + egg), produces genetically diverse offspring. Asexual: one parent, offspring genetically identical (clones), e.g. runners in strawberries.
hard.hint: Think about whether genetic diversity is an advantage or disadvantage.

hard.q: Explain what scientists mean by a 'model' in science. Give an example.
hard.a: A model is a simplified representation of a complex system used to explain or predict β€” e.g. the particle model of matter (solid/liquid/gas particles) helps explain physical properties.
hard.hint: Is a model an exact copy or a simplification?

hard.q: Why might a new predator introduced to an island devastate the native bird population?
hard.a: Native birds evolved without ground predators, so have no defensive behaviours against them (e.g. they may nest on the ground, not fly away). The predator exploits this vulnerability.
hard.hint: Think about New Zealand's kakapo β€” why is it so vulnerable to cats?

hard.q: What is the difference between a tissue, an organ and an organ system?
hard.a: Tissue: a group of similar cells (e.g. muscle tissue). Organ: made of several tissues working together (e.g. heart). Organ system: several organs working together (e.g. circulatory system).
hard.hint: Think of it as layers of organisation from small to large.

hard.q: Describe an experiment to show that light is needed for photosynthesis.
hard.a: Cover part of a leaf with foil to block light. After 24β€“48 hours, test with iodine β€” the shaded part will not turn black (no starch made), proving light is essential.
hard.hint: Starch is produced by photosynthesis β€” test for starch to see where photosynthesis occurred.

hard.q: Why do metals feel cold to touch, even at room temperature?
hard.a: Metals conduct heat very well. They rapidly draw heat away from your hand, making them feel cold β€” even though they are at the same temperature as wooden surfaces nearby.
hard.hint: The metal isn't colder β€” it just transfers heat away from you faster.

hard.q: Explain the difference between speed and velocity.
hard.a: Speed is how fast an object moves (scalar, distance Γ· time). Velocity is speed in a specific direction (vector β€” includes direction as well as magnitude).
hard.hint: A car going 60 km/h north and one going 60 km/h south have the same speed but different velocities.

hard.q: Why do ice cubes in a drink eventually melt?
hard.a: Heat flows from the warmer drink to the colder ice cube. As the ice absorbs heat, its particles gain energy and eventually overcome the bonds holding them in a solid β€” they become liquid.
hard.hint: Heat always moves from warmer to cooler objects.

hard.q: What is meant by 'natural selection'?
hard.a: The process by which individuals with traits better suited to their environment survive longer, reproduce more, and pass on those traits β€” leading to gradual adaptation of a species over generations.
hard.hint: Think: who survives to breed? And what do they pass on?

hard.q: Describe how fossils are formed.
hard.a: An organism dies and is quickly buried in sediment. Soft tissues decay, but hard parts (bones/shells) are slowly replaced by minerals. Over millions of years, sediment compresses into rock, preserving the fossil.
hard.hint: Think about what conditions are needed to preserve a dead animal.

hard.q: Explain why burning fossil fuels is a much faster way of releasing carbon dioxide than natural processes.
hard.a: Fossil fuels contain carbon stored over millions of years. Burning releases all that carbon in decades β€” far faster than natural decomposition or volcanic activity can reabsorb it.
hard.hint: Think about the time scale of carbon storage versus the time scale of burning.

hard.q: What is the electromagnetic spectrum? Name three types of radiation on it.
hard.a: The range of all electromagnetic radiation ordered by wavelength/frequency: radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays β€” any three.
hard.hint: Visible light is only a tiny portion of the full spectrum.

easy.hint: Cat, table, London are all nouns.

easy.hint: Run, jump, think, is β€” these are all verbs.

easy.hint: Big, red, happy β€” these describe things.

easy.q: Choose the correct homophone: 'She is (their/there) sister.'

easy.q: What punctuation mark goes at the end of a question?

easy.q: What punctuation mark goes at the end of an exclamation?
easy.a: Exclamation mark (!)
easy.hint: It's a straight line with a dot.

easy.q: Which sentence is correct? a) 'the dog ran away.' b) 'The dog ran away.'
easy.a: b) 'The dog ran away.' β€” capital letter at the start.
easy.hint: Every sentence starts with a capital letter.

easy.a: Unhappy

easy.q: Rewrite in the present tense: 'He kicked the ball.'
easy.a: 'He kicks the ball.'

easy.q: Underline the verb: 'The cat sat on the mat.'
easy.a: Sat

easy.q: What is an expanded noun phrase? Give an example.
easy.a: A noun with adjectives and other words added β€” e.g. 'the big, hairy dog'.
easy.hint: Expand the noun with describing words.

easy.q: Which word is a conjunction: and, cat, blue?
easy.a: And
easy.hint: A conjunction joins clauses or sentences.

easy.q: Add a conjunction to join these: 'I was tired. I went to bed.'
easy.a: E.g. 'I was tired so I went to bed.'
easy.hint: Words like so, because, and, but join sentences.

easy.a: When words near each other start with the same sound β€” e.g. 'Peter Piper picked a peck'.
easy.hint: It's about repeating the same starting sound.

easy.a: E.g. 'silly slippery snakes' or 'big brown bear'

easy.a: A comparison using 'like' or 'as' β€” e.g. 'as brave as a lion'.
easy.hint: It always uses the words 'like' or 'as'.

easy.a: Hopeless
easy.hint: Adding -less means 'without' something.

easy.a: Faster

easy.q: What is the root word in 'unhelpful'?
easy.a: Help

easy.q: What does a comma do in a list?
easy.a: It separates items in a list.
easy.hint: E.g. 'I bought apples, bananas, and oranges.'

easy.q: Give one word that means the same as 'big'.
easy.a: E.g. large, huge, enormous, great
easy.hint: Think of other words that describe size.

easy.q: Give one word that means the opposite of 'happy'.
easy.a: Sad (or unhappy, miserable, upset)
easy.hint: These are antonyms.

easy.a: A group of words that makes complete sense, starting with a capital letter and ending with a full stop, question mark or exclamation mark.
easy.hint: It must have a subject and a verb.

easy.q: Identify the adjective: 'The small, red kite flew high.'
easy.a: Small and red
easy.hint: Which words describe the kite?

easy.a: A group of letters added to the end of a word to change its meaning.

easy.q: Add the suffix -est to the word 'tall'.
easy.a: Tallest
easy.hint: -est means the most of something.

easy.a: A sentence that asks something and ends with a question mark.
easy.hint: It often starts with who, what, where, when, why or how.

easy.a: A sentence that expresses strong feeling and ends with an exclamation mark.
easy.hint: E.g. 'What a wonderful day it is!'

easy.q: Identify the noun in: 'The brave knight rode his horse.'
easy.a: Knight and horse (and 'his' refers to the knight)
easy.hint: Nouns name people, places or things.

easy.a: Came
easy.hint: This is an irregular verb.
