easy.hint: It forms a band across Africa from west to east.

easy.q: What is meant by 'land use conflict'?
easy.a: When different groups want to use the same land for different purposes β€” e.g. farmers vs conservationists in the Amazon.
easy.hint: Think about what happens when developers want to build on a nature reserve.

easy.a: A series of large ocean waves caused by a submarine earthquake, volcanic eruption or landslide.
easy.hint: The 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami was one of history's deadliest natural disasters.

easy.q: What is the highest mountain in the world?
easy.a: Mount Everest (8,849 m), in the Himalayas on the Nepal-Tibet border.
easy.hint: Climbers need oxygen masks to reach its summit.

easy.q: What is the Tropic of Cancer?
easy.a: A line of latitude at 23.5Β°N, marking the northern boundary of the tropics.
easy.hint: The sun is directly overhead at the Tropic of Cancer on the summer solstice.

easy.q: What is the Tropic of Capricorn?
easy.a: A line of latitude at 23.5Β°S, marking the southern boundary of the tropics.
easy.hint: The sun is directly overhead here on the winter solstice (in the Northern Hemisphere).

medium.q: Explain why tectonic plates move.
medium.a: Convection currents in the Earth's mantle (driven by heat from the core) create circulation that drags the plates above them. Hot mantle material rises, spreads, cools, and sinks β€” this motion drives plate movement.
medium.hint: Think of convection in a pan of boiling soup β€” hot liquid rises, cool sinks.

medium.q: Describe the three types of tectonic plate boundary.
medium.a: Constructive (divergent): plates move apart, new crust forms (e.g. Mid-Atlantic Ridge). Destructive (convergent): one plate subducts under another, melts (e.g. Andes). Conservative (transform): plates slide past each other (e.g. San Andreas Fault).
medium.hint: Think about what happens to the crust at each type β€” is it created, destroyed or just moved?

medium.q: Explain why LEDCs suffer more casualties from natural hazards than MEDCs.
medium.a: Poorer construction (buildings collapse in earthquakes); less early warning systems; worse emergency services; more people in high-risk areas; less insurance/ability to rebuild; corruption diverts disaster funds; geographic risk factors (tropical cyclone belts).
medium.hint: Compare Haiti 2010 (7.0 magnitude, ~300,000 deaths) with Japan 2011 (9.0 magnitude, ~20,000 deaths).

medium.q: Describe the formation of a V-shaped valley by river erosion.
medium.a: In the upper course, the river has high energy and erodes mainly downwards (vertical erosion). The sides are steepened by weathering (rain, frost). Material falls in, is transported away, leaving a narrow V-shape.
medium.hint: Think about a young mountain stream β€” which direction does it erode most?

medium.q: What is hard engineering in coastal management? Give two examples.
medium.a: Using artificial structures to prevent coastal erosion or flooding. E.g. sea walls (reflect wave energy), groynes (trap beach material), rock armour (absorb wave energy).
medium.hint: Hard = built structures that fight the sea directly.

medium.q: What is soft engineering in coastal management? Give two examples.
medium.a: Working with natural processes rather than against them. E.g. beach nourishment (adding sand), managed retreat (allowing flooding of low-value land), dune restoration.
medium.hint: Soft = letting nature do the work, or working with it rather than against it.

medium.q: Explain the difference between birth rate and death rate.
medium.a: Birth rate: number of live births per 1,000 people per year. Death rate: number of deaths per 1,000 people per year. Natural increase = birth rate minus death rate.
medium.hint: Both are measured per thousand to allow fair comparison between different-sized countries.

medium.q: Describe two factors that cause a country's population to grow rapidly.
medium.a: High birth rate (many children per family β€” often in agricultural societies or without contraception access); falling death rate (medical improvements, better nutrition, clean water); net positive migration.
medium.hint: Think about both biological and social factors.

medium.q: Explain why population growth is slowing in many developed countries.
medium.a: Lower birth rates: women in work (later childbearing), contraception, higher cost of raising children, urbanisation (children less economically useful). Death rates already low. These combine to slow or reverse growth.
medium.hint: Think about what makes people in developed countries choose to have fewer children.

medium.q: Describe the causes and effects of urban sprawl.
medium.a: Causes: population growth, rising car ownership, preference for larger homes, cheaper land at edges. Effects: loss of countryside/greenbelt, traffic congestion, pressure on services, increased commuting, air pollution.
medium.hint: Think about what happens when cities grow outward, consuming surrounding land.

medium.q: Explain the difference between trade and aid in development.
medium.a: Trade: countries exchange goods/services β€” can build self-sustaining economy but developing countries often face unequal terms. Aid: wealthy countries/organisations give money/resources β€” helpful short-term but can create dependency if not carefully managed.
medium.hint: Is it better to teach someone to fish or to give them fish?

medium.q: What is the difference between climate change and global warming?
medium.a: Global warming: the rise in average global surface temperature due to greenhouse gas emissions. Climate change: the broader set of changes driven by global warming β€” including altered rainfall, more extreme weather, sea level rise, ecosystem disruption.
medium.hint: Global warming is one aspect of climate change β€” which is broader.

medium.q: Describe the effects of climate change on the Arctic.
medium.a: Sea ice melting (25% reduction since 1979); permafrost thawing (releasing methane); polar bear habitat loss; new shipping routes opening; indigenous communities' livelihoods threatened; sea level contribution from Greenland ice sheet melting.
medium.hint: Think about how a warmer Arctic affects ice, wildlife, people and the wider climate system.

medium.q: Explain the process of desertification and two human causes.
medium.a: Desertification: the spread of desert-like conditions into semi-arid areas. Human causes: overgrazing (removes vegetation holding soil), deforestation (same), over-extraction of groundwater, unsustainable farming β€” all remove vegetation, expose soil to erosion and drying.
medium.hint: Think about the Sahel β€” what human activities remove vegetation and why does that matter?

medium.q: Describe two ways that tourists can damage fragile natural environments.
medium.a: Physical damage: trampling vegetation, disturbing wildlife nesting sites, coral reef damage from snorkelling/anchoring, littering. Pollution: cruise ships, waste disposal, noise pollution disrupting wildlife.
medium.hint: Think about what millions of tourists do to a fragile ecosystem.

medium.q: Explain what causes the seasons.
medium.a: Earth's axis is tilted at 23.5Β°. As it orbits the sun, different hemispheres tilt toward or away from the sun, causing changes in the sun's angle and day length β€” creating seasons.
medium.hint: If Earth weren't tilted, every place would have the same temperature year-round.

medium.q: Describe the global pattern of tectonic hazards.
medium.a: Most concentrated along plate boundaries: 'Ring of Fire' (Pacific plate margin) has ~75% of world's volcanoes. Earthquake zones along constructive and destructive boundaries. Mid-ocean ridges (constructive). Hotspot volcanoes (Hawaii) β€” away from boundaries.
medium.hint: Almost all tectonic hazards occur at plate boundaries β€” can you describe what happens at each type?

medium.q: What is fair trade and how does it benefit producers?
medium.a: Fair trade guarantees producers in developing countries a minimum price above market rate, stable income, community premiums for schools/clinics, and better working conditions. Reduces exploitation by multinational corporations.
medium.hint: Think about what a coffee farmer in Ethiopia receives for a bean that becomes a Β£3 coffee.

medium.q: Explain how rivers transport material.
medium.a: Solution: dissolved minerals. Suspension: fine particles carried in the flow. Saltation: larger particles bounced along the bed. Traction: heaviest boulders rolled along the bed. All four increase with river speed.
medium.hint: Think about different-sized particles and how each needs different amounts of energy to move.

medium.q: Describe two effects of flooding on people and two on the environment.
medium.a: People: property/livestock damage, displacement, disease outbreaks, crop loss, infrastructure damage. Environment: sediment deposited renews soil fertility, wetlands replenished, habitats created, groundwater recharged.
medium.hint: Flooding can be both destructive and beneficial β€” think about both sides.

medium.q: Explain how human activity has increased the risk of flooding.
medium.a: Deforestation (no interception/transpiration); urban surfaces impermeable (no infiltration); building on floodplains; river straightening (water moves faster); climate change intensifying rainfall events.
medium.hint: Think about each activity that prevents water from being absorbed into the ground or slowed down.

medium.q: What is a cold desert and give an example?
medium.a: A desert characterised by low precipitation (not necessarily heat) β€” e.g. Gobi Desert (Asia), Antarctic Desert. Cold deserts have freezing winters and often very hot summers but critically receive under 250 mm of rain.
medium.hint: Remember: a desert is defined by low rainfall, not high temperature.

medium.q: Describe the ecosystem services provided by forests.
medium.a: Oxygen production, carbon sequestration (absorbing COβ‚‚), water cycle regulation (transpiration), biodiversity habitat, soil stabilisation, medicines, flood prevention, pollination support, climate regulation.
medium.hint: Think about all the things a forest does that benefit humans and nature.

medium.q: Explain the concept of 'push and pull factors' in migration.
medium.a: Push: factors that drive people to leave their home country (war, poverty, drought, persecution). Pull: factors that attract people to a destination (safety, jobs, family, better services). People migrate when pull factors outweigh push factors.
medium.hint: Think about the decision from both ends β€” why leave AND why go there specifically?

medium.q: Why are tropical coasts at risk from sea level rise?
medium.a: Many tropical countries have low-lying coastlines with high population density (Bangladesh, Pacific island nations). Sea level rise from thermal expansion and ice melt threatens flooding, saltwater intrusion into freshwater, and displacement of millions.
medium.hint: Think about countries like Tuvalu or Bangladesh β€” what happens when sea levels rise 1 metre?

medium.q: Describe the impacts of deforestation in the Amazon on the global climate.
medium.a: Reduces carbon sequestration (forest stores ~150 billion tonnes of carbon); burning trees releases COβ‚‚; reduces water cycle regulation (less transpiration reduces rainfall globally); biodiversity loss destroys potential medicines.
medium.hint: Think about the Amazon as a global climate regulator β€” what happens when you remove it?

medium.q: Explain the difference between weather patterns and climate zones.
medium.a: Weather: short-term, specific atmospheric conditions at a location. Climate zone: the long-term characteristic weather conditions of a broad region β€” e.g. tropical (hot/wet), arid (dry), polar (cold), temperate. Climate zones are determined by latitude, ocean currents and altitude.
medium.hint: You can have a wet day in a desert (weather) but the climate there is still arid.

medium.q: What is sustainable development? Give one example in geography.
medium.a: Development meeting present needs without compromising future generations' ability to meet theirs. Geography example: sustainable fishing quotas that allow fish stocks to recover; eco-tourism that funds conservation; renewable energy replacing fossil fuels.
medium.hint: Think about using resources in ways that don't run out or damage the environment permanently.

medium.q: Describe two advantages and two disadvantages of building a large hydroelectric dam.
medium.a: Advantages: renewable electricity, flood control, water supply/irrigation, job creation during construction. Disadvantages: displacement of communities, habitat destruction, altered sediment flow, changed river ecosystem, earthquake risk from weight of reservoir.
medium.hint: Think about who gains power and water, and who loses their home and ecosystem.

medium.q: Explain how the jet stream affects weather in the UK.
medium.a: The jet stream is a fast-moving river of air at high altitude that steers weather systems. When it dips south, it brings cold, stormy weather to the UK. When it moves north, warm, dry weather follows. It is increasingly erratic due to Arctic warming.
medium.hint: Think about the jet stream as a railway track for weather systems.

medium.q: Why is the Mediterranean climate particularly suited to agriculture?
medium.a: Hot, dry summers (good for grapes, olives, citrus); mild, wet winters (winter crops possible); long growing seasons; irrigation from winter rainfall storage. However: drought stress is increasing with climate change.
medium.hint: Think about what specific crops thrive in hot, dry summers with mild, wet winters.

medium.q: Describe the economic and social impacts of migration on the destination country.
medium.a: Positive: fills labour shortages, contributes taxes, cultural diversity, entrepreneurship. Negative: pressure on housing/schools/hospitals, potential cultural tensions, wage competition at lower skill levels.
medium.hint: Think about who benefits and who might feel threatened by large-scale immigration.

medium.q: Why do some countries rely heavily on primary industries while others focus on tertiary industries?
medium.a: Primary (farming, mining): low-income countries rely on this as it requires less capital/technology. Tertiary (services, finance, retail): require education, infrastructure, capital β€” characteristics of developed economies. As countries develop they typically shift from primary β†’ secondary β†’ tertiary.
medium.hint: Think about the stages of economic development.

medium.q: Explain the difference between a fluvial and a coastal landform. Give an example of each.
medium.a: Fluvial: shaped by rivers β€” e.g. meander, V-shaped valley, delta. Coastal: shaped by sea β€” e.g. cliffs, wave-cut platforms, beaches, arches, stacks.
medium.hint: Fluvial = river. Coastal = sea. Think about the agent of erosion and deposition in each case.

medium.q: What is urbanisation and what are its main drivers?
medium.a: The process by which a greater proportion of a population lives in cities. Drivers: rural-urban migration (better jobs, education, healthcare), natural population growth of cities, industrialisation attracting workers.
medium.hint: Over 50% of the world's population now lives in cities. Why have people moved there?

medium.q: Describe the concept of the demographic transition model's relationship to development.
medium.a: As countries develop economically: death rate falls first (medical improvements), then birth rate falls (education, urbanisation, women's rights). Population booms during transition (Stage 2). Wealthy countries reach Stage 4 (stable/falling population). Economic development drives demographic change.
medium.hint: Think about how education, healthcare and women's opportunities all affect family size.

medium.q: What is an ox-bow lake and how does it form?
medium.a: In the lower course, a meander bends acutely. During flooding, the river cuts across the neck of the meander, taking a shorter route. The old bend is cut off and becomes a stagnant crescent-shaped lake β€” an ox-bow (or billabong in Australia).
medium.hint: Think about what happens when a river takes a shortcut across a meander bend.

medium.q: Explain what is meant by 'global interdependence' and give an example.
medium.a: Countries are economically, politically and environmentally connected β€” each depends on others for resources, trade, finance and security. E.g. UK food: sourced from 100+ countries; UK clothing: manufactured in Asia; UK financial system: connected to global markets.
medium.hint: Think about where your food, clothes and technology come from β€” no country produces everything it needs.

medium.q: Describe the causes and consequences of soil erosion in sub-Saharan Africa.
medium.a: Causes: deforestation, overgrazing, unsustainable farming, drought. Consequences: loss of fertile topsoil, falling crop yields, food insecurity, poverty, migration to cities, desertification, river silting (reducing fish).
medium.hint: Follow the chain: no trees β†’ exposed soil β†’ wind/rain removes it β†’ no food β†’ hunger/migration.

medium.q: What is the relationship between altitude and temperature?
medium.a: Temperature decreases with increasing altitude at approximately 6.5Β°C per 1000 m (environmental lapse rate). Higher = colder, because the atmosphere is less dense and absorbs less solar radiation. Mountains may have snow even in tropical latitudes.
medium.hint: Why is it snowy on Mount Kilimanjaro even though it's near the equator?

medium.q: Explain the difference between a conurbation and a megacity.
medium.a: Conurbation: a large urban area formed by merging of several towns/cities (e.g. West Midlands in England). Megacity: any city with over 10 million people (e.g. Tokyo, Mumbai, Lagos). Some megacities are also conurbations.
medium.hint: Scale is key β€” a megacity is defined by population size; a conurbation by the merger of settlements.

hard.q: Evaluate the effectiveness of international agreements in tackling climate change.
hard.a: Kyoto Protocol (1997): binding targets for developed nations but US didn't ratify; developing countries exempt. Paris Agreement (2015): all countries submit targets voluntarily β€” more inclusive but non-binding. Progress: renewable energy growing fast; but actual emissions still rising. Gap between pledges and action remains large.
hard.hint: Think about who is included, whether agreements are binding, and whether actual emissions are falling.

hard.q: Critically assess the view that geography determines a country's development.
hard.a: For (Sachs): landlocked countries have higher transport costs; tropical diseases impede productivity; natural disasters divert resources. Against (Acemoglu/Robinson): institutions (rule of law, democracy, property rights) explain most development differences. Geography is a factor but not destiny β€” Botswana (resources + good governance) vs DRC (resources + bad governance).
hard.hint: Compare two countries with similar geography but very different outcomes β€” what explains the difference?

hard.q: Analyse the environmental, social and economic consequences of rapid urbanisation in a named developing city.
hard.a: E.g. Lagos, Nigeria: Environmental: pollution (air, water, plastic), mangrove destruction, urban heat island. Social: slums (Makoko), poor sanitation, overcrowding. Economic: informal economy (60% of workers), some formal sector growth, infrastructure investment. Conclusion: gains and losses are unevenly distributed β€” wealthy areas benefit, informal settlements remain marginalised.
hard.hint: Think about the unequal geography of a rapidly growing city β€” who gains and who loses?

hard.q: Explain the paradox of the 'resource curse' with a geographical example.
hard.a: Resource-rich countries often have slower growth, more conflict and worse governance than resource-poor ones. Reasons: Dutch Disease (resource exports raise exchange rate, making other exports uncompetitive), rent-seeking (elites fight over resource profits), corruption, under-investment in education. E.g. Nigeria: oil revenues but high poverty and conflict.
hard.hint: Why do countries like oil-rich Nigeria or diamond-rich Sierra Leone remain poor? What's different about oil-poor South Korea?

hard.q: Evaluate the competing theories about how best to reduce global inequality.
hard.a: Modernisation theory (Rostow): poor countries follow same path as rich ones β€” need investment and trade. Dependency theory (Frank): rich countries keep poor ones dependent through unequal trade. Neoliberal: free markets and trade are the solution. Aid: necessary but creates dependency. Most economists: combination β€” institutions, investment, education, fair trade, debt relief.
hard.hint: Think about whether the problem is internal to poor countries or external (imposed by rich ones).

hard.q: Assess the geopolitical significance of the Arctic in the 21st century.
hard.a: Melting ice opens new shipping routes (Northwest Passage), revealing oil/gas reserves; territorial claims by Russia, Canada, US, Norway, Denmark unresolved; military build-up; indigenous community rights threatened; scientific monitoring importance; feedback loops amplifying global warming. A new arena for great power competition.
hard.hint: Think about resources, routes, territorial claims, military strategy and climate science all converging.

hard.q: Explain how the geography of food production creates global food insecurity.
hard.a: Physical: water-stressed regions can't sustain crops (sub-Saharan Africa); climate change shifts growing conditions; extreme weather. Economic: poor farmers lack capital, credit, markets. Political: conflict disrupts agriculture; trade policies disadvantage developing countries; land grabs reduce small farmer access.
hard.hint: Think about all the barriers between food production and food reaching hungry people.

hard.q: Evaluate the sustainability of current global energy systems.
hard.a: Fossil fuels: provide 80% of energy; finite; massive COβ‚‚ emissions. Renewables: growing fast (20% of electricity) but intermittent; storage challenge; land use. Nuclear: low carbon but waste and safety concerns. Overall: current system unsustainable β€” transition needed but faces technical, economic and political obstacles.
hard.hint: Think about whether the current system can last and what barriers prevent change.

hard.q: Analyse the relationship between population growth and resource consumption.
hard.a: Population growth increases demand for food, water, energy and land. But consumption per person matters more: a US citizen uses ~50x more resources than a Malawian. So global inequality in consumption means that reducing Western consumption may matter as much as slowing population growth in poor countries.
hard.hint: If everyone lived like a US citizen, we'd need 5 Earths. If everyone lived like an Indian, we'd need 0.7 Earths.

hard.q: Why is the concept of 'ecological footprint' more useful than GDP for measuring sustainability?
hard.a: GDP measures economic output but not sustainability or wellbeing. Ecological footprint measures how much of the Earth's regenerative capacity a country uses. High GDP countries often have large footprints exceeding Earth's capacity. More useful for sustainability planning than economic growth alone.
hard.hint: Can a country be wealthy AND sustainable? What would that require?

hard.q: Evaluate the effectiveness of protected areas (national parks, nature reserves) in conserving biodiversity.
hard.a: Strengths: reduce direct habitat destruction, provide wildlife corridors, support ecotourism, protect endemic species. Weaknesses: insufficient size, isolated (species can't migrate), illegal poaching, climate change crosses park boundaries, exclusion of indigenous communities. Need to be part of broader landscape conservation strategy.
hard.hint: A fence around 10% of a habitat won't save species that need 100% of the habitat.

hard.q: Explain the concept of 'planetary boundaries' and how human activity is testing them.
hard.a: RockstrΓ¶m's framework identifies nine Earth system processes with boundaries (climate, biodiversity, nitrogen/phosphorus cycles, freshwater, etc.) within which humanity can safely operate. We have already exceeded four (climate change, biodiversity loss, nitrogen cycle, land use change) β€” threatening Earth system stability.
hard.hint: Think about tipping points β€” at what point does human pressure on Earth systems become irreversible?

hard.q: Assess the social and environmental trade-offs involved in large-scale palm oil production.
hard.a: Benefits: cheap vegetable oil, high yield per hectare, employment in Southeast Asia. Costs: deforestation (orangutan/tiger habitat loss), peat bog burning (massive COβ‚‚), indigenous land seizure, monopolisation by corporations. 'Sustainable' palm oil certification contested. Classic development vs environment trade-off.
hard.hint: Think about who benefits (palm oil companies, cheap food consumers) and who pays (orangutans, indigenous communities, global climate).

hard.q: How do ocean currents affect climate, and what might happen if they were disrupted by climate change?
hard.a: Thermohaline circulation (global conveyor belt) transports heat globally β€” Gulf Stream warms NW Europe by ~5Β°C. Climate change (freshwater from melting ice) could slow/stop this, causing dramatic cooling in Europe despite global warming. Evidence: slowing already detected. Multiple tipping point risk.
hard.hint: Why is London so much milder than Labrador at the same latitude? What depends on ocean currents?

hard.q: Critically evaluate strategies used to manage rapid population growth in developing countries.
hard.a: China's One Child Policy: effective demographically but human rights abuses, gender imbalance (female infanticide), ageing population. Education and women's empowerment: most effective long-term (voluntary family planning). Family planning services: effective when available. Aid with contraception: debated. Evidence: educating women most sustainably reduces birth rates.
hard.hint: Compare coercive approaches (China) with rights-based approaches (Kerala, India) β€” which works better and at what cost?

hard.q: Explain why coastal areas face particularly complex management challenges.
hard.a: Multiple competing uses (tourism, fishing, development, conservation); erosion vs accretion dynamics; sea level rise threat; storm surge; multiple stakeholders with conflicting interests; long time scales vs short political cycles; hard engineering in one location displaces erosion elsewhere.
hard.hint: Think about all the people who use coastlines and what each one wants β€” and how those wants conflict.

hard.q: Analyse the relationship between urbanisation and inequality within cities.
hard.a: Rapid urbanisation creates spatial inequality: prime locations (centre, good transport) = expensive; peripheral locations = affordable but worse services. Informal settlements (slums) emerge for those priced out. Gentrification displaces existing communities. Urban geography reflects and reinforces social inequality.
hard.hint: Why do people in the same city have vastly different access to schools, healthcare and jobs based on which neighbourhood they live in?

hard.q: Evaluate the geopolitical consequences of water scarcity.
hard.a: Nile Basin: Ethiopia's dam threatens Egypt's water supply β€” potential conflict. Jordan River: Israel/Palestine/Jordan tensions. Indus: India/Pakistan dispute. Climate change intensifies competition. Virtual water trade (importing water-intensive goods) redistributes scarcity. Water wars increasingly likely; water diplomacy equally important.
hard.hint: When a finite resource crosses international borders, who controls it β€” and what happens when downstream countries run dry?

hard.q: How does the concept of 'just transition' apply to moving away from fossil fuels?
hard.a: 'Just transition' ensures that as fossil fuel industries decline, affected workers and communities are supported β€” through retraining, investment, compensation. Without it: communities suffer economic collapse (e.g. Welsh mining valleys, Appalachian coal). Transition must be both environmentally necessary and socially fair.
hard.hint: Think about what happens to coal miners in Yorkshire or West Virginia when their industry ends β€” and who has a responsibility to help them.

hard.q: Critically assess the argument that technology can solve environmental problems without changing consumption patterns.
hard.a: Techno-optimism: renewable energy, carbon capture, precision agriculture, lab meat. Limitations: rebound effect (efficiency gains consumed by more consumption), some technologies not scaled, carbon capture not commercially viable at scale, biodiversity loss not technological problem. Technology necessary but not sufficient β€” fundamental consumption change required.
hard.hint: If electric cars are twice as efficient, but we drive four times as much, have we solved anything?

hard.q: Explain how geography intersects with social justice in determining vulnerability to natural hazards.
hard.a: Physical vulnerability: location (earthquake zones, flood plains). Social vulnerability: poor communities can't afford earthquake-resistant buildings or insurance; marginalised communities excluded from evacuation plans; women and elderly disproportionately affected. Recovery slower for those without capital. Natural hazards become disasters through inequality.
hard.hint: Two people in the same earthquake: one in a steel-reinforced building, one in a mud house. Geography (same place) but social justice determines who survives.

hard.q: Evaluate the effectiveness of carbon offsetting as a strategy for addressing climate change.
hard.a: Positive: funds reforestation, renewable energy in developing countries, raises awareness. Criticism: often involves land in developing countries (neo-colonial), trees may die or be cut, allows rich individuals/countries to continue emitting without reducing, measured inaccurately. Most effective: reduce emissions first, offset remaining irreducible amount.
hard.hint: Is paying someone to plant a tree in Kenya a genuine substitute for emitting less carbon in the UK?

hard.q: Analyse the challenges of achieving food security in a world of increasing climate variability.
hard.a: Climate change: shifting rainfall patterns, more extreme events, higher temperatures stressing crops, sea level rise flooding agricultural land, changed growing seasons. Responses needed: drought-resistant crop varieties, diversified supply chains, reduced food waste, sustainable intensification, greenhouse/vertical farming, meat reduction. Multi-pronged strategy required.
hard.hint: Think about all the threats that climate variability poses to food supply, and what each requires as a solution.

hard.q: How does the geography of trade create and maintain global inequality?
hard.a: Developing countries export primary commodities (low value-added, volatile prices); import manufactured goods (high value). Terms of trade have historically moved against primary producers. WTO rules designed by wealthy countries protect their agriculture through subsidies while forcing developing countries to open markets. Geography of comparative advantage reflects colonial inheritance.
hard.hint: Why does a tonne of coffee beans from Ethiopia earn much less than a tonne of packaged coffee from Germany?

hard.q: Critically evaluate the view that borders are the greatest obstacle to global development.
hard.a: For: borders restrict movement of people (migration), goods (tariffs), capital (exchange controls) and knowledge. Removing them could equalise wages and raise development. Against: some borders protect vulnerable industries in developing countries; unlimited migration could destabilise social cohesion; capital mobility can be exploitative. Real issue: who the borders protect and whose movement they restrict.
hard.hint: Capital moves freely across borders (helping rich investors); people from poor countries face huge barriers (helping rich country workers). Are borders neutral?

hard.q: Explain how human-induced land use change is affecting global weather patterns.
hard.a: Deforestation alters albedo (bare soil reflects differently from trees), reduces transpiration (less moisture in atmosphere), disrupts regional rainfall patterns (Amazon creates its own rain). Urban heat islands create local weather. Large-scale land use change can alter jet stream dynamics. Local effects aggregate to regional and global impacts.
hard.hint: If enough land is changed, does that affect weather far away? Think about the Amazon and its rainfall.

hard.q: Assess the long-term sustainability of current freshwater use globally.
hard.a: 70% of freshwater used for agriculture (irrigation); industry 20%; domestic 10%. Aquifers depleted faster than recharged in India, US, Middle East. Rivers diverted (Aral Sea dried up). Climate change intensifies drought. Population growth and dietary changes (meat requires much more water) increase demand. Current trajectory unsustainable without major efficiency improvements.
hard.hint: If aquifers take thousands of years to refill and we're draining them in decades, what does that tell you about sustainability?

hard.q: How does the relationship between urbanisation and economic development vary between world regions?
hard.a: Classical model (Europe/USA): urbanisation followed industrialisation; cities absorbed rural labour into manufacturing. Africa/Asia: urbanisation without equivalent industrialisation β€” people move to cities from poverty, not opportunity; slums grow; informal economy dominates. This 'premature urbanisation' challenges development models built on Western experience.
hard.hint: If people are moving to cities because farming is impossible (drought, land seizure) rather than because of factory jobs, does urbanisation still lead to development?

hard.hint: Follow BODMAS: brackets first. (7) Γ— (4) = 28.

hard.q: What is 6 + 4 Γ— 3 - 2?
hard.hint: BODMAS: multiplication first. 4Γ—3=12. Then: 6+12-2=16.

hard.q: Explain why 2/3 Γ— 3/4 = 1/2.
hard.a: Multiply numerators: 2Γ—3=6. Multiply denominators: 3Γ—4=12. Simplify 6/12 = 1/2.
hard.hint: Multiply straight across top and bottom, then simplify.

hard.q: What is 2/3 Γ· 4?
hard.hint: Dividing by 4 is the same as multiplying by 1/4. 2/3 Γ— 1/4 = 2/12 = 1/6.

hard.q: The nth term of a sequence is 4n - 3. What are the first four terms?
What is the area of a triangle with vertices at (0,0), (6,0) and (0,4)?
hard.a: 12 sq units
hard.hint: Area = Β½ Γ— base Γ— height = Β½ Γ— 6 Γ— 4 = 12.

hard.q: A jar contains a mixture of 1p, 2p and 5p coins in ratio 5:3:2. There are 100 coins. How many 5p coins?
hard.hint: Total parts = 10. Each part = 10 coins. 5p coins = 2 parts = 20.

hard.q: If 3a + 2b = 20 and a = 4, find b.
What is the sum of the interior angles of a pentagon?
Two numbers have a sum of 60 and a difference of 16. What are they?
hard.a: 38 and 22

hard.q: A price was Β£80. After a 15% reduction and a 20% increase, what is the final price?
A cube has volume 125 cmΒ³. What is its surface area?
hard.a: 150 cmΒ²
hard.hint: Side = β›125 = 5 cm. Surface area = 6 Γ— 5Β² = 6 Γ— 25 = 150 cmΒ².

hard.q: What is 10% of 10% of 500?
A train 150 m long passes a 350 m bridge. The train travels at 50 m/s. How long does it take to cross?
hard.a: 10 seconds
hard.hint: Total distance = 150 + 350 = 500 m. Time = 500 Γ· 50 = 10 s.

hard.q: What is 3/5 Γ· 2/3? Give the answer as a mixed number if necessary.
hard.hint: Dividing by 2/3: multiply by 3/2. 3/5 Γ— 3/2 = 9/10.

hard.q: The nth term formula for a sequence is 2nΒ² β’ 1. What is the 5th term?

easy.a: The flow of electric charge (electrons) through a conductor.
easy.hint: It powers lights, computers and appliances.

easy.a: A complete path that allows electric current to flow from a power source, through components and back.
easy.hint: If the path is broken, current stops flowing.

easy.q: Name the components you need for a simple circuit.
easy.a: Battery (power source), wires, and a component (e.g. bulb or buzzer).
easy.hint: Think of the simplest circuit you've made in class.

easy.q: What happens when you break a circuit?
easy.a: The current stops flowing β€” bulbs go out, buzzers stop.
easy.hint: An open switch breaks the circuit.

easy.a: A material that allows electricity to flow through it easily.
easy.hint: Most metals are conductors.

easy.a: A material that does not allow electricity to flow through it.
easy.hint: Plastic, rubber and glass are insulators.

easy.q: Why are wires coated in plastic?
easy.a: The plastic insulates the wire, preventing electric shock and short circuits.
easy.hint: The metal inside carries the current; the plastic keeps you safe.

easy.q: What is a switch in a circuit?
easy.a: A component that opens or closes the circuit, turning the current on or off.
easy.hint: Open switch = no current; closed switch = current flows.

easy.a: E.g. batteries, generators, solar panels, wind turbines.
easy.hint: Think about what powers your phone and your house.

easy.q: What is the function of a battery in a circuit?
easy.a: It provides the electromotive force (voltage) that drives current around the circuit.
easy.hint: Think of a battery as a pump pushing charge around.

easy.a: A form of energy produced by vibrations that travel as waves through a medium.
easy.hint: Pluck a guitar string β€” what does it do?

easy.a: Through vibration of particles in a medium (solid, liquid or gas). It cannot travel in a vacuum.
easy.hint: Sound needs particles to travel β€” no particles, no sound.

easy.q: Does sound travel faster in solids or in air?
easy.a: In solids β€” the particles are closer together, so vibrations transfer more quickly.
easy.hint: You can hear a train approaching by putting your ear to the rail.

easy.a: How high or low a sound is β€” determined by the frequency (vibration rate) of the sound wave.
easy.hint: A violin has higher pitch than a double bass.

easy.q: What affects the pitch of a sound?
easy.a: Frequency of vibrations β€” faster vibrations = higher pitch.
easy.hint: Tighten a guitar string β€” what happens to the pitch?

easy.a: How loud or quiet a sound is β€” determined by the amplitude (energy) of the sound wave.
easy.hint: Pluck a guitar string harder β€” what happens to the volume?

easy.a: E.g. the sun, a candle, a light bulb, a fire, a LED.
easy.hint: Luminous objects produce their own light.

easy.q: Does light travel in straight lines or curves?
easy.a: Straight lines
easy.hint: This is why shadows have sharp edges (when using a point light source).

easy.q: What happens when light hits a mirror?
easy.a: It is reflected β€” it bounces off at the same angle it arrived.
easy.hint: The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.

easy.a: The bending of light as it passes from one medium to another of different density.
easy.hint: A straw in a glass of water appears bent due to refraction.

easy.a: A transparent glass or plastic shape that refracts light, splitting white light into its spectrum of colours.
easy.hint: It produces a rainbow of colours.

easy.q: What colours make up visible white light?
easy.a: Red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet (ROYGBIV)
easy.hint: Remember ROY G BIV.

easy.a: The process of breaking down food into small molecules that can be absorbed into the blood.
easy.hint: It starts in the mouth and ends in the intestines.

easy.a: In the mouth (mechanical chewing and saliva)
easy.hint: Your teeth break food down and saliva contains enzymes.

easy.q: What is the role of the stomach in digestion?
easy.a: It uses acid and muscular churning to break down food further, especially proteins.
easy.hint: The stomach is like a muscular bag that mixes food with acid.

easy.q: Where are nutrients absorbed in the digestive system?
easy.a: In the small intestine
easy.hint: Villi line the small intestine to absorb nutrients into the bloodstream.

easy.q: What is the function of the large intestine?
easy.a: To absorb water from undigested food waste, forming solid faeces.
easy.hint: It recycles water before waste leaves the body.

easy.q: What is the role of enzymes in digestion?
easy.a: Enzymes are biological catalysts that break down large food molecules into smaller ones.
easy.hint: Amylase breaks down starch; protease breaks down proteins.

easy.q: Name two teeth types and their function.
easy.a: Incisors (cut/bite), canines (tear), molars (grind) β€” any two.
easy.hint: Your different types of teeth have different shapes and jobs.

easy.a: The hard outer coating of teeth β€” the hardest substance in the human body.
easy.hint: It protects the inner dentine and pulp.

easy.q: Why is sugary food bad for teeth?
easy.a: Bacteria in the mouth feed on sugar and produce acids that dissolve tooth enamel (dental decay/caries).
easy.hint: The bacteria make acid, which attacks your enamel.

easy.q: What are the three types of teeth in adult humans?
easy.a: Incisors, canines, premolars and molars (technically four types)
easy.hint: Think about the different shapes in your mouth.

easy.q: What does the term 'reversible change' mean? Give an example.
easy.a: A change that can be undone β€” e.g. melting ice (can refreeze), dissolving salt (can evaporate water to recover salt).
easy.hint: Can you get back exactly what you started with?

easy.a: When a solid (solute) mixes completely into a liquid (solvent) to form a solution.
easy.hint: Salt dissolves in water β€” the salt disappears into the water.

easy.a: A mixture formed when a solute dissolves in a solvent β€” e.g. salty water.
easy.hint: You can't see the salt, but it's still there.

easy.a: The substance that dissolves in a solvent β€” e.g. salt in saltwater.
easy.hint: It's the thing being dissolved.

easy.a: The liquid in which a solute dissolves β€” e.g. water in saltwater.
easy.hint: It's the liquid doing the dissolving.

easy.q: How can you separate salt from water?
easy.a: By evaporation β€” heat the solution until the water evaporates, leaving the salt.
easy.hint: What happens to the water when you heat it?

easy.q: How can you separate sand from water?
easy.a: By filtration β€” pour through a filter paper which traps the sand.
easy.hint: Filter paper has tiny holes that let water through but not sand.

easy.q: How can you separate iron filings from sand?
easy.a: By using a magnet β€” iron filings are magnetic; sand is not.
easy.hint: Iron filings are attracted to a magnet; sand is not.

easy.a: A method of separating a liquid from a solution by evaporation and condensation.
easy.hint: Used to get pure water from seawater.

easy.a: A technique for separating mixtures of coloured substances based on how they travel through a medium.
easy.hint: Used to separate ink dyes in paper chromatography.

easy.q: Name three ways heat can be transferred.
easy.a: Conduction, convection and radiation
easy.hint: Heat moves from hot to cold in three ways.

easy.q: What is the Sun's energy source?
easy.a: Nuclear fusion β€” hydrogen atoms fuse to form helium, releasing enormous energy.
easy.hint: The Sun converts hydrogen to helium, releasing energy as light and heat.

easy.q: What is the Earth's atmosphere mainly made of?
easy.a: Nitrogen (78%), oxygen (21%), argon and other gases including COβ‚‚ (0.04%).
easy.hint: Most of what you breathe is nitrogen, not oxygen.

easy.q: What is the difference between a conductor and a semiconductor?
easy.a: Conductors allow charge to flow freely (metals). Semiconductors can conduct under some conditions β€” used in transistors and computer chips.
easy.hint: Silicon is the most common semiconductor.

easy.q: What is the unit of electrical resistance?
easy.a: Ohm (Ξ©)
easy.hint: Named after Georg Ohm, who discovered Ohm's Law.

easy.q: What is the unit of electrical current?
easy.a: Ampere (A)
easy.hint: Named after AndrΓ©-Marie AmpΓ¨re.

easy.q: What is the unit of voltage?
easy.a: Volt (V)
easy.hint: Named after Alessandro Volta, who invented the battery.

easy.q: What is the unit of power?
easy.a: Watt (W)
easy.hint: Named after James Watt. Power = energy per second.

medium.q: Explain the difference between series and parallel circuits.
medium.a: Series: components in one loop; current flows through each in turn; if one breaks the circuit fails. Parallel: components in separate branches; each gets full voltage; if one breaks others continue.
medium.hint: Old Christmas lights were series β€” one bulb out and all went dark. Modern are parallel.

medium.q: Describe how increasing the number of batteries in a circuit affects the brightness of a bulb.
medium.a: More batteries provide greater voltage, increasing the current flowing through the circuit β€” the bulb glows brighter. However, too many batteries can burn out the bulb.
medium.hint: More voltage = more current = more energy transferred through the bulb.

medium.q: Explain how sound is produced and give a musical example.
medium.a: Sound is produced when an object vibrates, creating pressure waves in the surrounding medium. E.g. a guitar string vibrates β†’ air molecules compress and rarefy β†’ ears detect these pressure changes β†’ perceived as sound.
medium.hint: Touch your throat when you speak β€” what do you feel?

medium.q: Describe the effect of medium on the speed of sound.
medium.a: Sound travels fastest in solids (particles closest together), slower in liquids, slowest in gases. Speed in air: 343 m/s. Speed in water: ~1,480 m/s. Speed in steel: ~5,100 m/s.
medium.hint: Why can you hear a train coming by putting your ear to the track?

medium.q: How does a convex lens form an image?
medium.a: A convex lens is thicker in the middle and converges (bends) parallel light rays to a focal point. This is how a magnifying glass works and how the eye focuses light on the retina.
medium.hint: Think about how light bends when it enters a denser material.

medium.q: How does the human eye focus light?
medium.a: The cornea and lens focus light on the retina. The lens changes shape (accommodation) to focus on near or distant objects. The retina detects light and sends signals to the brain via the optic nerve.
medium.hint: Think of the eye as a camera with an adjustable lens.

medium.q: Explain what happens to light when it hits a rough surface vs a smooth surface.
medium.a: Smooth surface: regular (specular) reflection β€” light bounces at consistent angles, producing a clear image (mirror). Rough surface: diffuse reflection β€” light scatters in many directions, no image formed (wall).
medium.hint: Why can you see your reflection in a mirror but not in a piece of paper?

medium.q: Describe the process of digestion from mouth to small intestine.
medium.a: Mouth: teeth mechanically break down food; saliva adds amylase (breaks starch). Oesophagus: peristalsis moves food to stomach. Stomach: acid + protease breaks down proteins; churning. Small intestine: enzymes (lipase, amylase, protease) complete digestion; villi absorb nutrients.
medium.hint: Follow the journey of a sandwich from first bite to absorption.

medium.q: Explain why the villi in the small intestine are designed for absorption.
medium.a: Villi are finger-like projections that massively increase surface area. Each has a thin wall for short diffusion distance, a rich blood supply to carry nutrients away rapidly, and microvilli for even greater surface area.
medium.hint: Think about why surface area matters for absorption.

medium.q: Explain the difference between a physical and a chemical change in terms of particles.
medium.a: Physical: particles rearrange but no new bonds form and no new substances are created (melting ice). Chemical: bonds break and form, creating substances with different properties and usually irreversible (burning wood produces COβ‚‚ and Hβ‚‚O).
medium.hint: Are the original substances still present after the change?

medium.q: Why does sugar dissolve more quickly in hot water than cold water?
medium.a: Higher temperature gives water molecules more kinetic energy, so they move faster and collide more frequently with sugar particles, breaking them away from the crystal and dispersing them more quickly.
medium.hint: Think about how temperature affects particle movement.

medium.q: Describe three separation techniques and explain what each can separate.
medium.a: Filtration: solid from liquid (sand from water). Evaporation: dissolved solid from solution (salt from seawater). Distillation: two liquids with different boiling points (alcohol from water). Magnetism: magnetic from non-magnetic solids.
medium.hint: Each technique works because of a difference in a physical property.

medium.q: Explain chromatography and give an example of what it can separate.
medium.a: Different substances in a mixture travel at different speeds through a stationary medium when carried by a moving solvent. E.g. paper chromatography separates the different coloured pigments in ink or food colouring.
medium.hint: Think about why different substances travel different distances from the origin.

medium.q: Explain what happens to particles at each stage of a change of state.
medium.a: Solid: particles vibrate in fixed positions (strong forces). Liquid: particles move freely but close together (weaker forces). Gas: particles move rapidly, far apart (very weak forces). Changes of state involve transferring energy to overcome attractive forces.
medium.hint: Think about particle arrangement and movement in each state.

medium.q: Why do different materials have different melting and boiling points?
medium.a: Melting/boiling points depend on the strength of attractive forces between particles. Strong forces β†’ high melting/boiling point. Weak forces β†’ low melting/boiling point. E.g. iron melts at 1538Β°C; ice at 0Β°C.
medium.hint: The stronger the forces between particles, the more energy is needed to separate them.

medium.q: Describe two pieces of evidence that the Earth is spherical.
medium.a: The shadow Earth casts on the Moon during a lunar eclipse is always circular. Ships disappear over the horizon hull-first. Different constellations visible from different latitudes. Photos from space. Circumnavigation.
medium.hint: Think about what you would observe if the Earth were flat versus spherical.

medium.q: Explain how the angle of the sun affects the temperature of a place.
medium.a: When the sun is high in the sky, rays are concentrated in a small area (tropics) β€” more energy per mΒ² = warmer. When the sun is low (poles), the same energy is spread over a larger area β€” less energy per mΒ² = colder.
medium.hint: Compare shining a torch straight down versus at an angle β€” what happens to the lit area?

medium.q: What is the difference between renewable and non-renewable energy? Give two examples of each.
medium.a: Renewable: naturally replenished (solar, wind, hydro, tidal, geothermal). Non-renewable: formed over millions of years, will run out (coal, oil, natural gas, nuclear fuel).
medium.hint: Will it run out in our lifetimes if we keep using it at current rates?

medium.q: Explain how solar panels generate electricity.
medium.a: Photovoltaic (PV) cells in solar panels absorb photons of light, which excite electrons and cause them to flow, generating a direct electrical current. Sunlight β†’ electricity directly.
medium.hint: Photovoltaic means light (photo) + electricity (voltaic).

medium.q: Why do electrical wires heat up when current flows through them?
medium.a: Electrons collide with ions in the wire's metal lattice as they flow. These collisions transfer kinetic energy to the metal ions, causing them to vibrate more β€” this is experienced as heat.
medium.hint: Think about what friction does β€” electrical resistance is a form of friction for electrons.

medium.q: Describe the difference between voltage and current in a circuit.
medium.a: Voltage (measured in volts): the electrical potential difference β€” the 'push' driving current around the circuit. Current (measured in amps): the rate of flow of electric charge. Voltage drives current; resistance opposes it.
medium.hint: Voltage is like water pressure; current is like the flow rate of water.

medium.q: Explain what Ohm's Law states.
medium.a: Ohm's Law: Voltage (V) = Current (I) Γ— Resistance (R). For a component with constant resistance, doubling the voltage doubles the current. V = IR.
medium.hint: Think about the three quantities β€” what happens to current if resistance increases?

medium.q: Describe the components of the human digestive system in order.
medium.a: Mouth β†’ oesophagus β†’ stomach β†’ small intestine β†’ large intestine β†’ rectum β†’ anus. Also: liver (bile), pancreas (enzymes), and the appendix.
medium.hint: Follow the path of food from entry to exit.

medium.q: What is the role of bile in digestion?
medium.a: Bile (produced by the liver, stored in the gallbladder) emulsifies fats β€” breaks large fat globules into small droplets, increasing surface area for lipase enzymes to act on.
medium.hint: Bile is like a natural washing-up liquid for fat.

medium.q: Explain the difference between mechanical and chemical digestion.
medium.a: Mechanical: physical breakdown without changing chemical composition β€” chewing (teeth), churning (stomach). Chemical: enzymes break molecular bonds, changing the substances (starch β†’ glucose; proteins β†’ amino acids; fats β†’ fatty acids + glycerol).
medium.hint: Mechanical changes shape; chemical changes what something IS.

medium.q: Describe the role of the nervous system in the human body.
medium.a: The nervous system detects stimuli (sensory), processes information (CNS: brain + spinal cord), and produces responses (motor). Nerve impulses travel as electrical signals along neurones.
medium.hint: Think of it as the body's communication network.

medium.q: What is a reflex action? Why are reflexes useful?
medium.a: A reflex is an automatic, involuntary response to a stimulus, involving the spinal cord β€” e.g. pulling hand away from heat. Useful: faster than conscious response β€” protects body from damage before brain has time to decide.
medium.hint: Think about what happens when you touch something very hot β€” do you wait to think about it?

medium.q: Explain how lenses can correct vision defects.
medium.a: Myopia (short-sightedness): light focuses in front of retina β€” corrected by concave lens (diverges light). Hyperopia (long-sightedness): light focuses behind retina β€” corrected by convex lens (converges light).
medium.hint: Think about whether the eye focuses too strongly or not strongly enough.

medium.q: Describe three properties of light that show it is a wave.
medium.a: Reflection (bounces back), refraction (changes direction in different media), diffraction (bends around obstacles), interference (waves adding/cancelling). Any three.
medium.hint: What behaviours do water waves also show?

medium.q: Why are some materials transparent and others opaque?
medium.a: Transparent materials allow photons of visible light to pass through without being significantly absorbed or scattered (glass, air). Opaque materials absorb or reflect most visible light (metal, wood). Translucent materials scatter light (frosted glass).
medium.hint: Think about what the material does to photons when they hit it.

medium.q: Explain how a compass needle shows that the Earth has a magnetic field.
medium.a: A compass needle is a small magnet. Earth has a large magnetic field (generated by its liquid iron core). The needle aligns with Earth's field, its north pole pointing towards Earth's magnetic south pole (near geographic north).
medium.hint: Why does a freely suspended magnet always align north-south?

medium.q: Describe the difference between weight and mass and how each is measured.
medium.a: Mass: amount of matter, measured in kg with a balance/scales β€” constant everywhere. Weight: gravitational force on mass, measured in Newtons with a spring scale/newton meter β€” varies with gravity.
medium.hint: Would a 10 kg weight feel the same on the Moon?

medium.q: Explain three factors that affect the rate of dissolving.
medium.a: Temperature: higher = faster. Particle size: smaller = faster (more surface area). Stirring: faster = increases contact between solute and solvent. Concentration: unsaturated solution dissolves faster than near-saturated.
medium.hint: Think about what you do when you make sugary tea β€” how do you make the sugar dissolve faster?

medium.q: What is a food web and why is it more realistic than a food chain?
medium.a: A food web shows all feeding relationships in an ecosystem β€” animals usually eat more than one thing and are eaten by more than one predator. A food chain shows only one linear pathway β€” oversimplified.
medium.hint: What do foxes eat, and what eats foxes? These interconnections form a web.

medium.q: Describe two effects of habitat destruction on biodiversity.
medium.a: Population collapse of specialist species dependent on that habitat. Increased competition as organisms concentrate in remaining areas. Extinction of endemic species found nowhere else. Loss of ecosystem services (pollination, water purification).
medium.hint: Think about both the direct effects on species and the knock-on effects through food webs.

medium.q: Explain what is meant by 'selective breeding' and give an agricultural example.
medium.a: Humans choose organisms with desired characteristics to reproduce, over generations increasing the frequency of those traits. E.g. dairy cows selectively bred for high milk yield; wheat bred for disease resistance.
medium.hint: It's the same mechanism as natural selection but the 'selector' is human rather than the environment.

medium.q: Describe how antibiotic resistance develops in bacteria.
medium.a: Random mutations create bacteria with natural resistance. When antibiotics kill susceptible bacteria, resistant ones survive and reproduce (natural selection). Overuse of antibiotics accelerates this β€” resistant bacteria multiply when others are killed off.
medium.hint: Think about natural selection operating on a bacterial population β€” who survives antibiotic treatment?

medium.q: Explain the difference between a series circuit and a parallel circuit using the concept of current.
medium.a: Series: current is the same throughout the circuit (same path). Parallel: total current from the battery splits between branches β€” each branch receives part of the total current, but voltage across each branch is the same as battery voltage.
medium.hint: In a series circuit, everything is in one loop. In parallel, the current has choices of which path to take.

medium.q: Describe how sound intensity (loudness) decreases with distance.
medium.a: Sound waves spread out in all directions from the source. As they spread, the energy is distributed over an increasingly large area (sphere), so energy per unit area (intensity) decreases β€” inversely with the square of distance (inverse square law).
medium.hint: Think about a ripple in a pond spreading outward β€” the wave height decreases as it spreads.

medium.q: Why do we see coloured objects as their particular colour?
medium.a: Objects absorb some wavelengths of light and reflect others. The wavelengths reflected enter our eyes β€” we see those wavelengths as colour. E.g. a red apple reflects red wavelengths and absorbs others.
medium.hint: A black object absorbs all wavelengths; a white object reflects all.

medium.q: Explain how temperature affects the rate of chemical reactions.
medium.a: Higher temperature gives particles more kinetic energy β€” they move faster and collide more frequently and with more energy. More successful collisions per second = faster reaction rate. Approximately doubling every 10Β°C rise.
medium.hint: Think about collision theory β€” what needs to happen for particles to react?

medium.q: Describe the structure of the atom.
medium.a: Central nucleus containing positively charged protons and neutral neutrons; negatively charged electrons orbit in shells (energy levels) around the nucleus. Atom is mostly empty space β€” nucleus is tiny relative to the electron cloud.
medium.hint: The nucleus is to the atom what a pea is to a football stadium.

medium.q: What is the difference between an element, a compound and a mixture?
medium.a: Element: one type of atom (e.g. Oβ‚‚). Compound: atoms of different elements chemically bonded (e.g. Hβ‚‚O). Mixture: substances combined but not bonded β€” can be separated (e.g. air, seawater).
medium.hint: Can it be separated by physical means? If yes, it's a mixture. If no, it's a compound (or element).

medium.q: Explain how DNA controls the characteristics of an organism.
medium.a: DNA is a double helix carrying coded instructions (genes) for making proteins. Different proteins determine cell type and function, growth and development, and physical characteristics (phenotype). The sequence of bases in DNA determines which proteins are made.
medium.hint: DNA β†’ protein β†’ characteristic. Think about how instructions make a product.

medium.q: What is the difference between sexual and asexual reproduction?
medium.a: Sexual: two gametes (egg + sperm) fuse; genetic variation in offspring. Asexual: one parent; offspring genetically identical (clones). Sexual: slower but adaptable to change. Asexual: faster but no variation.
medium.hint: Is there genetic mixing? Does it take one parent or two?

medium.q: Describe one advantage and one disadvantage of renewable energy.
medium.a: Advantage: inexhaustible supply; lower carbon emissions. Disadvantage: intermittent (sun/wind not always available), high initial cost, large land area required, remote from demand.
medium.hint: Think about reliability, cost and environmental impact.

medium.q: Explain why scientists conduct repeat experiments.
medium.a: To check reliability β€” random errors may affect a single result but average out over many repeats. Multiple results allow calculation of a mean, identify outliers, and provide confidence that results represent a real effect rather than a one-off chance.
medium.hint: Is one result enough to be sure? What if something went wrong that one time?

medium.q: Describe two ways evolution can be observed in the fossil record.
medium.a: Gradual morphological change over geological time in rock strata (e.g. horse fossils showing gradual size increase); transitional fossils showing intermediate features between ancestral and descendant forms (Archaeopteryx: bird + dinosaur features).
medium.hint: Think about what you'd see in a sequence of fossils from old rock layers to new.

hard.q: Analyse the evidence supporting the theory of evolution by natural selection.
hard.a: Fossil record: gradual change over time. Comparative anatomy: homologous structures (human hand/bat wing/dolphin flipper β€” same bones). Molecular: DNA similarities between related species. Observed: antibiotic resistance, finch beak changes (Darwin's finches). All consistent with common descent and selection.
hard.hint: Think about multiple independent lines of evidence all pointing to the same conclusion.

hard.q: Why is the scientific method considered the most reliable way of understanding the natural world?
hard.a: It is systematic: observation β†’ hypothesis β†’ prediction β†’ controlled experiment β†’ analysis β†’ peer review β†’ replication. Peer review catches errors; replication builds confidence; falsifiability prevents unfalsifiable claims from persisting. Self-correcting over time.
hard.hint: What makes science different from opinion or belief?

hard.q: Explain the relationship between genes, proteins and phenotype.
hard.a: Genes (DNA sequences) code for specific proteins. Proteins determine cell structure and function β€” including enzymes regulating biochemistry, structural proteins, and signalling molecules. Phenotype (observable characteristics) emerges from how proteins build and regulate the organism's development and function.
hard.hint: Think about DNA as a recipe book for proteins, and proteins as the molecules that build and run the organism.

hard.q: Evaluate the claim that renewable energy can completely replace fossil fuels in the next 20 years.
hard.a: Possible in theory: solar and wind now cheapest electricity sources; electric vehicles growing; storage improving. Challenges: grid intermittency (storage unsolved at scale); industrial processes (steel, cement) hard to decarbonise; political/economic resistance; developing countries still need cheap energy; timeline very challenging though directionally correct.
hard.hint: Think about the technical barriers (storage, industrial heat) as well as the economic and political ones.

hard.q: Explain what is meant by 'conservation of energy' and apply it to a falling ball.
hard.a: Energy cannot be created or destroyed β€” only transferred between forms. Falling ball: at rest (top) β†’ maximum gravitational potential energy (GPE), zero kinetic energy (KE). As it falls: GPE converts to KE. At lowest point: maximum KE. Energy transferred to thermal (sound) on impact.
hard.hint: The total energy stays the same β€” it just changes form.

hard.q: Describe the ethical issues surrounding genetic engineering and cloning.
hard.a: Genetic engineering: designer babies (where to draw the line?), unforeseen ecological effects of GM crops, corporate control of food supply. Cloning: human cloning raises identity/rights issues; therapeutic cloning (stem cells) vs reproductive cloning. All involve balancing scientific progress against unintended consequences and human dignity.
hard.hint: Think about who benefits, who decides, and what could go wrong.

hard.q: Explain how modern medicine exploits our understanding of the immune system.
hard.a: Vaccination: introduce weakened pathogen β†’ immune system produces antibodies + memory cells β†’ rapid response on re-exposure. Monoclonal antibodies: target specific proteins on cancer cells or pathogens. Immunosuppressants: prevent rejection of transplanted organs by damping the immune response.
hard.hint: Think about how each application uses the immune system's natural mechanisms.

hard.q: Critically evaluate the statement: 'correlation proves causation'.
hard.a: Correlation shows two variables change together β€” but this could be coincidence, confounding (a third factor causing both), or reverse causation. Causation requires: controlled experiment ruling out alternatives, plausible mechanism, dose-response relationship, consistency across studies. E.g. ice cream sales correlate with drowning rates β€” both caused by hot weather.
hard.hint: Can you think of a correlation that is clearly not causal?

hard.q: Explain how the theory of plate tectonics changed our understanding of the Earth.
hard.a: Before: continents seen as fixed. Wegener (1912) proposed continental drift β€” continents fit together, shared fossils. Mechanism discovered (1960s): ocean floor spreading, convection in mantle. Now: explains distribution of earthquakes, volcanoes, mountain formation, rock types, fossil distribution. A unifying theory for Earth science.
hard.hint: Think about what plate tectonics explains that no previous theory could.

hard.q: Why does the size of a cell limit how large an organism can be without specialised organ systems?
hard.a: Cells exchange materials (oxygen, nutrients, waste) via diffusion. Diffusion rate depends on surface area : volume ratio. As cells grow larger, volume grows faster than surface area, reducing the ratio β€” diffusion too slow to supply the cell's interior. Specialised organs (circulatory, respiratory) overcome this by distributing materials internally.
hard.hint: Why doesn't the human body have one giant cell? What limits cell size?

hard.q: Explain the concept of 'sustainability' in the context of fishing quotas.
hard.a: Fish stocks reproduce at a maximum sustainable yield (MSY). If you remove more than the reproductive rate, population declines to extinction. Quotas limit catches to below MSY, allowing the population to reproduce and maintain itself. Properly implemented quotas are sustainable; overfishing leads to stock collapse (e.g. Grand Banks cod).
hard.hint: Think about the rate of removal versus the rate of reproduction.

hard.q: How does the electromagnetic spectrum demonstrate that different types of radiation are fundamentally the same?
hard.a: All electromagnetic radiation: travels at the speed of light (3Γ—10βΈ m/s) in vacuum; transverse waves; obeys same physical laws; differs only in wavelength/frequency/energy. Radio waves β†’ microwaves β†’ infrared β†’ visible β†’ UV β†’ X-rays β†’ gamma β€” all part of the same spectrum, just different frequencies.
hard.hint: What do radio waves, X-rays and visible light have in common? They're all transverse electromagnetic waves.

hard.q: Describe the long-term consequences of biodiversity loss for human wellbeing.
hard.a: Food security: fewer pest-resistant crop species; loss of pollinators (bees). Medicine: 25% of pharmaceuticals derived from plants; unknown future medicines lost with extinct species. Ecosystem services: water purification, carbon sequestration, flood prevention all require biodiversity. Cultural: aesthetic, spiritual value of nature. Economic: ecotourism.
hard.hint: Think beyond the intrinsic value of wildlife to the concrete services that biodiversity provides to humans.

hard.q: Explain the concept of 'emergent properties' in biology, using the human brain as an example.
hard.a: Emergent properties: system-level properties that cannot be predicted from the properties of components alone. Example: individual neurones are simple switches β€” but billions connected create consciousness, memory, emotion, creativity. The system exhibits properties greater than the sum of its parts.
hard.hint: Can you be conscious with a single neurone? Where does consciousness 'come from'?

hard.q: Evaluate the risks and benefits of nuclear power in addressing climate change.
hard.a: Benefits: low-carbon, reliable base load, high energy density, long operational life. Risks: radioactive waste (thousands of years storage), catastrophic failure risk (Chernobyl, Fukushima), high construction costs and time, uranium supply finite, proliferation risk. In a climate emergency: low-carbon benefit may outweigh other risks β€” debate continues.
hard.hint: Think about the risk-risk trade-off: nuclear accidents versus climate change deaths.

hard.q: Explain how the human microbiome affects health.
hard.a: Trillions of microorganisms (bacteria, fungi, viruses) live in/on the human body, especially in the gut. Functions: digesting food (fibre β†’ short-chain fatty acids), competing with pathogens, training the immune system, producing vitamins (K, B12), influencing mood (gut-brain axis). Disruption linked to inflammatory diseases.
hard.hint: Think of the gut microbiome as an organ β€” what do its residents do for you?

hard.q: How does climate change affect the distribution of species?
hard.a: Warming shifts habitats poleward and to higher altitudes. Species track suitable climate conditions or face extinction. Marine species migrate to cooler waters. Phenological mismatch (e.g. caterpillar peak no longer aligned with bird chick hatching). Not all species can migrate β€” specialists are most vulnerable.
hard.hint: Think about which species can adapt fast enough and which cannot.

hard.q: Describe the evidence that the universe began with the Big Bang.
hard.a: Expansion: Hubble (1929) found galaxies receding (redshift) β€” run time backwards β†’ dense origin. CMB: cosmic microwave background radiation β€” afterglow of early hot universe. Light element ratios: Big Bang nucleosynthesis predicts H:He ratio = 75:25 β€” matches observations.
hard.hint: Three independent pieces of evidence: expansion, CMB, element ratios.

hard.q: Explain what 'natural selection' is and distinguish it from 'evolution'.
hard.a: Evolution: change in heritable characteristics of populations over generations β€” the fact. Natural selection: the mechanism β€” variation exists; some variants better suited to environment; survive and reproduce more; offspring inherit favourable traits; over time, population changes. Natural selection is the HOW of evolution.
hard.hint: Evolution is the what (populations change over time); natural selection is one of the why/how mechanisms.

hard.q: What is the role of the immune system in distinguishing 'self' from 'non-self'?
hard.a: Body cells display MHC (Major Histocompatibility Complex) markers β€” recognised as 'self' by T-cells. Foreign cells or pathogens lack these markers and are attacked. Autoimmune diseases occur when this system malfunctions and attacks 'self' cells. Organ transplants are rejected because donor MHC differs.
hard.hint: Think about how the immune system identifies what belongs in your body and what doesn't.

hard.q: Explain how genetic mutations can be both harmful and beneficial.
hard.a: Most mutations are neutral (no phenotypic effect). Harmful: sickle-cell anaemia, cystic fibrosis (cause disease). Beneficial: sickle-cell trait (one copy) provides malaria resistance; bacteria develop antibiotic resistance. Same mutation can be beneficial or harmful depending on environment.
hard.hint: Think about sickle-cell disease β€” harmful in two copies, but why does it persist in malaria-endemic areas?

hard.q: How does the study of deep-sea organisms challenge our assumptions about life requirements?
hard.a: Deep-sea organisms live without sunlight: chemosynthesis (bacteria use chemical energy from hydrothermal vents) supports food chains. Extremophiles survive crushing pressure, boiling temperatures, total darkness. Expands definition of 'habitable' environments β€” relevant to the search for life beyond Earth.
hard.hint: We assumed all life needs sunlight β€” what does chemosynthesis tell us?

hard.q: Evaluate the statement: 'Science is objective.'
hard.a: For: data collection/analysis uses standardised methods; peer review challenges bias; replication tests reliability. Against: researchers choose what to study (funding bias), interpret data through theoretical frameworks, personal/cultural biases affect hypothesis formation, historically some science served racist/colonial agendas. Science aspires to objectivity but is practised by humans.
hard.hint: Think about the difference between the scientific method as a tool and scientists as humans with biases.

hard.q: Describe the possible consequences of antibiotic resistance becoming widespread.
hard.a: Routine surgery becomes dangerous (post-operative infection); chemotherapy would be impossible (immune compromise). Childhood infections (meningitis, sepsis) become untreatable. Global spread via travel and agriculture (antibiotics in farming). Estimated 10 million deaths/year by 2050 in worst case β€” comparable to cancer deaths today.
hard.hint: Think about which current medical practices depend on antibiotics to prevent infection.

hard.q: Explain how the discovery of DNA's structure changed biology.
hard.a: Watson, Crick, Franklin, Wilkins (1953): double helix model explained how DNA stores information (base pair sequences = genetic code) and replicates (strands separate β†’ each serves as template). United genetics, biochemistry, evolution β€” explained how hereditary information is stored, expressed and inherited.
hard.hint: Before 1953, scientists knew heredity existed but didn't know the molecular mechanism. What changed?

hard.q: How do scientists use isotopes in medicine?
hard.a: Radioactive tracers: inject radioactive isotope (e.g. I-131 for thyroid, technetium-99m for bone scans) β†’ emits gamma rays detectable by scanner β†’ shows organ function. PET scanning: F-18 labels glucose β†’ highlights metabolically active tissue (cancer, brain activity). Radiotherapy: targeted gamma rays destroy cancer cells.
hard.hint: Think about how the properties of radioactive isotopes (known decay rate, detectable emission) make them useful.

hard.q: Critically evaluate the theory of spontaneous generation and how it was disproved.
hard.a: Spontaneous generation: life arises from non-living matter spontaneously (maggots from meat). Disproved: Pasteur (1859) swan-neck flask experiment β€” broth sterilised and sealed didn't develop microbes; breaking the seal did. Showed microbes come from air, not generated spontaneously. Established germ theory.
hard.hint: Think about how Pasteur controlled his experiment to isolate the variable being tested.

hard.q: Describe how the carbon cycle connects plants, animals, the atmosphere and the oceans.
hard.a: Atmosphere: COβ‚‚. Plants absorb COβ‚‚ (photosynthesis) β†’ organic compounds in biomass. Animals eat plants β†’ COβ‚‚ released via respiration. Dead organisms decomposed β†’ COβ‚‚ returned. Ocean absorbs COβ‚‚. Burning fossil fuels releases stored carbon. Feedback: more COβ‚‚ β†’ more plant growth (up to a point).
hard.hint: Carbon moves between living organisms, the atmosphere, the ocean and the Earth's crust in a continuous cycle.

hard.q: Explain why we need to use models in science and what their limitations are.
hard.a: Models (particle model, DNA structure, planetary model of atom, climate models) simplify complex reality to make it understandable, testable and predictive. Limitations: simplify and omit factors; predictions valid only within the model's assumptions; can become outdated as understanding improves (Bohr model replaced by quantum mechanics).
hard.hint: Is the planetary model of an atom (electrons orbiting like planets) accurate? If not, why is it still useful?

hard.q: Explain the concept of 'half-life' and how it is used in carbon dating.
hard.a: Half-life: time for half of a radioactive isotope to decay. C-14 has a half-life of ~5,730 years. Living organisms incorporate C-14 at a known ratio. After death: C-14 decays, C-12 stays constant. Measuring C-14:C-12 ratio determines time since death. Reliable for up to ~50,000 years.
hard.hint: Think about C-14 as a clock that starts ticking when an organism dies.

hard.q: How might life exist elsewhere in the universe, based on what we know about the requirements for life on Earth?
hard.a: Life on Earth requires: liquid water, carbon-based chemistry, energy source (sunlight or chemical), amino acids. Potentially habitable: planets in the Goldilocks zone around other stars; Europa (Jupiter's moon, liquid water ocean under ice); Enceladus (Saturn's moon, hydrothermal vents). Life may exist in chemosynthetic forms without sunlight.
hard.hint: Earth-based life requirements may not be universal β€” think about the extreme environments where life exists on Earth.

easy.q: What is a modal verb? Give three examples.
easy.a: Verbs expressing possibility, necessity or obligation β€” e.g. can, could, may, might, will, would, shall, should, must, ought to.
easy.hint: Modal verbs express how likely or necessary something is.

easy.a: 'Can' means having the ability. 'May' expresses permission or possibility. 'Can I go?' (ability) vs 'May I go?' (requesting permission).
easy.hint: 'Can you swim?' (ability). 'May I swim here?' (permission).

easy.q: What is a complex sentence? Give an example.
easy.a: A sentence containing a main clause and at least one subordinate clause β€” e.g. 'Although it was raining, she went outside.'
easy.hint: The subordinate clause cannot stand alone as a sentence.

easy.q: What is a compound sentence? Give an example.
easy.a: Two main clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction (FANBOYS) β€” e.g. 'She was tired, but she kept running.'
easy.hint: Both parts could stand alone as sentences.

easy.a: For, And, Nor, But, Or, Yet, So β€” the coordinating conjunctions.
