easy.hint: These are the words that join two equal clauses.

easy.a: E.g. 'Although the weather was cold, the children played outside.'
easy.hint: The clause starting with 'although' depends on the main clause.

easy.q: What is the difference between a colon and a semicolon?
easy.a: Colon: introduces a list, quotation or explanation. Semicolon: joins two closely related independent clauses.
easy.hint: Colon introduces; semicolon joins.

easy.q: What is an abstract noun? Give two examples.
easy.a: A noun you cannot see or touch β€” e.g. happiness, courage, freedom, justice, love.
easy.hint: You can't hold abstract nouns in your hand.

easy.q: What is a concrete noun? Give two examples.
easy.a: A noun you can see, touch or physically experience β€” e.g. table, dog, rain, bread.
easy.hint: You can point to or pick up concrete nouns.

easy.q: What is the difference between 'who' and 'whom'?
easy.a: 'Who' is the subject of a verb ('Who did this?'). 'Whom' is the object ('To whom did you give it?'). Test: replace with 'he' (subject) or 'him' (object).
easy.hint: If you'd use 'him', use 'whom'. If you'd use 'he', use 'who'.

easy.q: What is a determiner? Give four examples.
easy.a: A word placed before a noun to specify it β€” e.g. the, a, an, this, those, my, some, any, every.
easy.hint: It specifies which one or how many.

easy.q: What is a possessive pronoun? Give examples.
easy.a: A pronoun showing ownership β€” e.g. mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs, its.
easy.hint: Not to be confused with possessive adjectives (my, your, his...) which go before a noun.

easy.q: Punctuate correctly: she asked him where are you going tonight
easy.a: She asked him, 'Where are you going tonight?'
easy.hint: Identify the direct speech and punctuate accordingly.

easy.q: Convert to reported speech: 'I will call you tomorrow,' he said.
easy.a: He said that he would call me the following day.
easy.hint: Tense shifts back; pronouns change; tomorrow β†’ the following day.

easy.q: What is the superlative form of 'good'?
easy.a: Best
easy.hint: Good β†’ better β†’ best. This is an irregular comparative.

easy.q: What is the comparative form of 'bad'?
easy.a: Worse
easy.hint: Bad β†’ worse β†’ worst. Irregular comparative.

easy.q: What is a gerund? Give an example.
easy.a: A verb form ending in -ing used as a noun β€” e.g. 'Swimming is good exercise.' (Swimming is the subject.)
easy.hint: It looks like a participle but functions as a noun.

easy.q: What is an infinitive? Give an example.
easy.a: The base form of a verb, usually with 'to' β€” e.g. to run, to think, to be.
easy.hint: 'I want to go home.' β€” 'to go' is the infinitive.

easy.q: What is a split infinitive? Give an example.
easy.a: When an adverb is placed between 'to' and the verb β€” e.g. 'to boldly go'. Traditionally avoided but now widely accepted.
easy.hint: 'To boldly go' splits the infinitive 'to go' with 'boldly'.

easy.a: Using someone else's words or ideas without acknowledgement and presenting them as your own β€” academically dishonest.
easy.hint: Always credit your sources.

easy.a: A list of sources used in or relevant to a piece of writing β€” books, articles, websites.
easy.hint: It appears at the end of a piece of non-fiction writing.

easy.a: A word or phrase formed by rearranging the letters of another β€” e.g. 'listen' β†’ 'silent'.
easy.hint: The same letters in a different order.

easy.q: What is ambiguity? Give an example.
easy.a: When language has more than one possible meaning β€” e.g. 'I saw the man with the telescope' (who had the telescope?). Good writers avoid unintended ambiguity.
easy.hint: Is there more than one way to interpret the sentence?

easy.a: Specialised technical language used by a particular profession or group β€” e.g. medical, legal or computer jargon.
easy.hint: A doctor might say 'myocardial infarction' rather than 'heart attack'.

easy.q: What is an ellipsis and what are its three uses?
easy.a: Three dots (...). Uses: 1) show omission from a quotation; 2) indicate trailing off in dialogue; 3) create suspense in narrative.
easy.hint: Think about the different effects it creates in different contexts.

easy.a: The central argument of an essay, stated clearly (usually at the end of the introduction), telling the reader what will be argued.
easy.hint: It answers the question: 'What is this essay going to argue?'

easy.q: What is the purpose of a topic sentence in a paragraph?
easy.a: To introduce the main idea of the paragraph and signal to the reader what the paragraph will be about.
easy.hint: Think of it as the paragraph's title sentence.

easy.q: What is the difference between 'fewer' and 'less'?
easy.a: Fewer: for countable nouns ('fewer people'). Less: for uncountable nouns ('less water'). Common error: 'less people' should be 'fewer people'.
easy.hint: Can you count it? If yes, use fewer.

easy.a: A subordinate clause that functions as an adverb β€” telling when, where, how, why or under what condition the main action occurs.
easy.hint: 'When she arrived' in 'When she arrived, the party began' is an adverbial clause of time.

easy.q: Write a sentence using a colon to introduce a list.
easy.a: E.g. 'She had everything she needed: courage, intelligence and luck.'
easy.hint: The colon promises the reader a list is coming.

easy.q: What is the function of the apostrophe in 'it's'?
easy.a: It replaces the missing letter 'i' in 'it is' β€” a contraction apostrophe.
easy.hint: If you can replace it with 'it is', use 'it's'. If not, use 'its' (possessive).

easy.a: A unit of writing focused on one idea or aspect, beginning on a new line and often indented or separated by a blank line.
easy.hint: New paragraph when topic, time, place or speaker changes (TTPS).

easy.q: What is the effect of the dash in creative writing?
easy.a: Creates dramatic pause, adds an afterthought or asides β€” or introduces a sudden shift in thought. More informal and dramatic than brackets.
easy.hint: How does a dash change the rhythm of a sentence compared to commas or brackets?

easy.q: What is a relative clause? Give an example.
easy.a: A subordinate clause that modifies a noun, beginning with who, which, that, whose, where or when β€” e.g. 'The house that Jack built.'
easy.hint: It adds information about the noun it follows.

easy.q: What is the difference between restrictive and non-restrictive relative clauses?
easy.a: Restrictive: essential information β€” no commas ('The man who stole it was caught'). Non-restrictive: extra information β€” commas ('My brother, who lives in Spain, is coming to visit').
easy.hint: Can you remove the clause without changing which person/thing is meant?

easy.q: What is the present participle? Give an example.
easy.a: The -ing form of a verb, used to form continuous tenses or as an adjective β€” e.g. 'running', 'thinking', 'the running water'.
easy.hint: In 'She was running', 'running' is the present participle.

easy.q: What is the past participle? Give an example.
easy.a: The form used in perfect tenses (often -ed or irregular) β€” e.g. 'eaten', 'broken', 'written', 'walked'.
easy.hint: Used with 'has/have/had' β€” 'She has eaten'; 'He had broken the glass.'

easy.q: What is a double negative? Why should it be avoided in formal writing?
easy.a: Using two negative words in one clause β€” 'I didn't do nothing.' In standard English this is illogical (a double negative implies positive). Avoided in formal writing though common in dialects.
easy.hint: If you didn't do nothing, then you did do something!

easy.q: What is the difference between prose and poetry?
easy.a: Prose: continuous written language, not divided into poetic lines, follows grammatical sentences. Poetry: arranged in lines and stanzas, often uses rhyme/rhythm/meter, concentrates meaning more densely.
easy.hint: A novel is prose; a sonnet is poetry.

easy.q: What is a stanza in poetry?
easy.a: A group of lines in a poem, arranged together β€” the poem's equivalent of a paragraph.
easy.hint: Like a paragraph, it groups related ideas together.

easy.a: The pattern of end rhymes in a poem, labelled with letters (ABAB, AABB, ABCABC etc.).
easy.hint: In ABAB: lines 1 and 3 rhyme, lines 2 and 4 rhyme.

easy.a: A metrical pattern with 10 syllables per line: five iambs (unstressed-STRESSED), as used by Shakespeare ('Shall I COMPARE thee TO a SUM-mer's DAY').
easy.hint: da-DUM da-DUM da-DUM da-DUM da-DUM β€” five beats per line.

easy.q: What is the difference between a short story and a novel?
easy.a: Length: short stories are brief (< ~15,000 words), focus on one event/character/theme. Novels: long, complex, multiple characters/subplots/themes. Short stories: tight and focused; novels: expansive.
easy.hint: Think about the scope β€” a short story can cover a single afternoon; a novel can span generations.

easy.a: A non-fiction account of a person's life, written by someone else.
easy.hint: An autobiography is written by the subject themselves.

easy.a: A first-person account of a person's own life story, written by the subject.
easy.hint: Auto = self; bio = life; graph = write.

easy.q: What is a synonym and an antonym for 'brave'?
easy.a: Synonym: courageous, bold, fearless, valiant. Antonym: cowardly, timid, fearful.
easy.hint: Synonyms share meaning; antonyms are opposites.

easy.a: An opening technique designed to immediately engage the reader β€” a shocking fact, intriguing question, dramatic action, or compelling statement.
easy.hint: What would make you read on after the first sentence?

easy.q: What is the climax of a story?
easy.a: The point of highest tension or drama β€” the decisive moment in the narrative.
easy.hint: In a thriller: the moment the hero confronts the villain.

easy.a: The final resolution of a story's plot β€” what happens after the climax, tying up loose ends.
easy.hint: French for 'unknotting' β€” the untangling of the plot.

easy.q: What is the difference between dialogue and monologue?
easy.a: Dialogue: conversation between two or more people. Monologue: one character speaking alone, revealing thoughts and feelings.
easy.hint: Di = two; mono = one.

medium.q: Explain how modal verbs can express degrees of certainty. Give examples.
medium.a: Must/will (strong certainty). Should/ought to (expectation). Can/may (possibility). Might/could (weaker possibility). E.g. 'It will rain' (certain); 'It might rain' (possible). Writers choose modals deliberately to show how confident they are.
medium.hint: Think about the spectrum from 'definitely' to 'possibly'.

medium.q: Describe the conventions of a newspaper article. List five features.
medium.a: Headline (grabs attention), byline (author's name), lead paragraph (answers who/what/where/when/why/how), inverted pyramid structure (most important information first), quotes, formal register, third person, present tense for headline, sub-headings.
medium.hint: Think about how a newspaper article is structured from most to least important information.

medium.q: Explain what is meant by 'formality register' and give an example of the same information in two different registers.
medium.a: Register = level of formality. Formal: 'I am writing to express my dissatisfaction regarding...' (letter to headteacher). Informal: 'I'm not happy about...' (text to friend). Same meaning; different vocabulary, grammar and tone.
medium.hint: Think about how you'd tell a friend about something versus how you'd report it officially.

medium.q: What is a subordinate clause and what are the different types?
medium.a: A clause that depends on the main clause. Types: adverbial (when/because/if/although β€” telling when/why/condition); relative (who/which/that β€” adding info about noun); nominal (that + clause acting as noun β€” 'I know that she went').
medium.hint: Think about what function the clause serves β€” is it like an adverb, an adjective, or a noun?

medium.q: Explain what 'pathetic fallacy' is and analyse an example.
medium.a: Pathetic fallacy: using weather/nature to reflect human emotion or events. E.g. 'A storm broke as they buried him' β€” the storm mirrors grief and turmoil. The technique creates atmosphere and links the natural world to human experience without stating feelings directly.
medium.hint: How does the weather reinforce rather than simply describe the scene's mood?

medium.q: Describe the difference between a static and a dynamic character.
medium.a: Dynamic: changes significantly during the story (develops, learns, transforms). Static: remains largely unchanged (may be used as a foil). Most protagonists are dynamic; many antagonists or minor characters are static.
medium.hint: Think about which characters learn something and which do not.

medium.q: Explain three ways a writer can create and sustain narrative tension.
medium.a: Short sentences (urgency); withholding information (mystery); multiple threats (overwhelm); ticking clock (time pressure); dramatic irony (audience knows more than character); cliffhangers; setting (confined/threatening space).
medium.hint: Think about what makes you unable to stop reading.

medium.q: What is the difference between first-person and third-person limited narration?
medium.a: First person (I): narrator IS a character, highly subjective, cannot know others' thoughts, very intimate. Third-person limited (he/she): narrator outside story but limited to one character's perspective. Third person limited is slightly less intimate but allows more flexibility.
medium.hint: Both access one consciousness β€” but one from inside, one from outside.

medium.q: Explain the effect of starting a sentence with a participle phrase.
medium.a: A participle phrase at the start creates a fronted adverbial describing the character's simultaneous action or state β€” e.g. 'Running as fast as she could, she reached the door.' Creates immediacy, describes simultaneous action, varies sentence structure.
medium.hint: Think about how it changes the emphasis compared to 'She ran as fast as she could and reached the door.'

medium.q: What is the difference between an argument essay and a narrative essay?
medium.a: Argument: non-fiction, presents evidence and reasoning to support a thesis, analytical structure (introduction, body paragraphs, conclusion). Narrative: tells a story, may be fiction or creative non-fiction, uses descriptive/literary techniques, follows plot structure.
medium.hint: One tries to convince; the other tries to engage through story.

medium.q: Explain how to use evidence effectively in a non-fiction essay.
medium.a: Introduce evidence with context; quote accurately (in inverted commas); explain what the evidence shows (analysis); connect to your argument (how it supports your thesis). Avoid simply listing evidence without explanation.
medium.hint: Think: introduce, evidence, explain, link (PEEL or similar structure).

medium.q: What is the effect of varying sentence length in prose fiction?
medium.a: Long sentences: slow pace, detail, contemplation, complexity. Short sentences: urgency, impact, drama. Varying: creates rhythm and prevents monotony. Writers use this deliberately β€” a short sentence after several long ones delivers maximum impact.
medium.hint: Read a thriller chase scene aloud β€” what do the sentences look like?

medium.q: Explain what is meant by 'authorial voice' and how it is created.
medium.a: The distinctive personality and perspective that comes through in an author's writing β€” through diction (word choice), syntax (sentence structure), tone, use of humour/irony, what is described and what is omitted, pace and rhythm.
medium.hint: Why do you know immediately whether a paragraph was written by Roald Dahl or Charles Dickens?

medium.q: Describe three purposes of reading non-fiction text types.
medium.a: To inform (report, textbook, encyclopaedia), to persuade (advertisement, opinion column, manifesto), to instruct (recipe, manual), to entertain (travel writing, memoir), to analyse (essay, review), to advise (guide, advice column).
medium.hint: Think about why writers write non-fiction and what they want their readers to do.

medium.q: What is the difference between a 'biased' and a 'balanced' source?
medium.a: Biased: presents one perspective selectively, omitting evidence that contradicts it, using loaded language. Balanced: presents multiple perspectives, uses neutral language, acknowledges uncertainty.
medium.hint: Think about why you should read multiple news sources about the same event.

medium.q: Explain how to write an effective opening paragraph for a persuasive essay.
medium.a: Hook: dramatic statistic, rhetorical question, bold claim. Context: brief background. Thesis: clear statement of your position. Preview: optional indication of main arguments. Confident, formal register.
medium.hint: Think about what makes you want to read more after the first paragraph.

medium.q: What is the difference between 'showing' and 'telling' in fiction? Give an example of each.
medium.a: Telling: 'She was angry' β€” states the emotion directly. Showing: 'She slammed the door, hands shaking, jaw clenched' β€” reader infers the emotion from physical detail. Showing is generally more powerful; telling can be used for efficiency.
medium.hint: What physical signs of anger could you describe instead of naming the emotion?

medium.q: Explain what 'free indirect discourse' is in narrative fiction.
medium.a: A technique blending the narrator's voice with the character's thoughts/speech without quotation marks or 'he thought' β€” e.g. 'She walked in. Well, here she was at last.' (the italics show her thought but in third person). Jane Austen used it extensively.
medium.hint: How can a third-person narrator suddenly seem to speak in a character's voice?

medium.q: Describe how punctuation affects the reading of a poem.
medium.a: End-stopped lines (punctuation at line end): distinct thoughts, measured pace. Enjambment (no punctuation): ideas flow across lines, creates continuity or ambiguity. Caesura (mid-line pause): breaks rhythm, creates contrast. Heavy punctuation = controlled; light = flowing.
medium.hint: Read the poem aloud β€” where are you forced to pause? Where does the meaning spill over?

medium.q: What is an epistolary form in writing? Give an example.
medium.a: Writing composed of letters, diary entries, or other documents. E.g. Bram Stoker's 'Dracula' (diaries, letters, newspaper cuttings); Samuel Richardson's 'Pamela' (letters). Gives intimacy, multiple perspectives, can create unreliable narration.
medium.hint: Think about how reading someone's private letters or diary makes you feel as a reader.

medium.q: Explain what makes good descriptive writing. Include three specific techniques.
medium.a: Specific vocabulary (not just 'big' but 'towering', 'monolithic'); varied sentence structure; multiple senses (not just visual); figurative language (simile, metaphor, personification); precise verbs; avoiding clichΓ©; creating atmosphere through selective detail.
medium.hint: Think about what professional writers do that amateur writers forget.

medium.q: What is the 'rule of three' in rhetoric and writing? Give examples.
medium.a: Groups of three items have a satisfying, memorable rhythm: 'I came, I saw, I conquered.' 'Life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness.' 'Friends, Romans, countrymen.' Used in speeches, persuasive writing and literature for emphasis and memorability.
medium.hint: Why do three feel complete where two feels insufficient and four feels cluttered?

medium.q: Explain the difference between a theme and a symbol in literature.
medium.a: Theme: a central idea or message (e.g. power corrupts). Symbol: a specific object/action/place representing a wider concept (e.g. the green light in Gatsby = unattainable dreams). Symbols can embody themes β€” they make abstract themes concrete.
medium.hint: A symbol is a thing; a theme is an idea. Symbols can carry themes.

medium.q: What is dramatic irony? How does it create tension or humour?
medium.a: When the audience knows something a character doesn't. Tension: we know the villain is hiding when the hero relaxes (horror). Humour: we know the 'surprise party' when the guest of honour is oblivious. Tension comes from what might happen; humour from the gap between perception and reality.
medium.hint: Think about Shakespeare's comedies (audiences know the disguises) versus tragedies (audiences know the fate).

medium.q: Explain how tone can be conveyed in writing without directly stating it.
medium.a: Through: diction (Latinate = formal; Anglo-Saxon = direct; emotional words = passionate); sentence length (short = urgent, direct; long = reflective, elaborate); punctuation (!!! = excitement; ... = uncertainty); figurative language; what is described vs omitted.
medium.hint: Think about how you can tell from the words alone whether a speaker is sarcastic, warm or threatening.

medium.q: What is the 'hero's journey' (monomyth) and how does it apply to a story you know?
medium.a: Campbell's model: ordinary world β†’ call to adventure β†’ refusal β†’ mentor β†’ threshold β†’ tests β†’ ordeal β†’ reward β†’ road back β†’ resurrection β†’ return. Apply e.g. Harry Potter: Muggle world (ordinary) β†’ Hogwarts letter (call) β†’ Voldemort (ordeal) β†’ wizarding world saved (return).
medium.hint: Think about the stages and match them to events in a familiar story.

medium.q: Explain the effect of an unreliable narrator on the reading experience.
medium.a: Creates active reading β€” we must question everything. Layers of meaning emerge between what the narrator claims and what we infer. Creates dramatic irony. Can be disturbing (we're implicated in a villain's perspective) or humorous. Forces us to construct an alternative truth.
medium.hint: How do you feel when you realise mid-way through that you can't trust the narrator?

medium.q: Describe the features of a good counter-argument in a persuasive essay.
medium.a: State the opposing view fairly and charitably (strongest version, not a straw man). Acknowledge what is valid. Refute: explain why your position is still stronger (evidence, logic). Don't dismiss β€” engage seriously. This builds credibility and anticipates reader objections.
medium.hint: Think about why addressing a counter-argument actually STRENGTHENS rather than weakens your case.

medium.q: What is the difference between deductive and inductive reasoning?
medium.a: Deductive: start with a general premise, draw specific conclusion ('All humans die; Socrates is human; therefore Socrates will die' β€” valid if premises are true). Inductive: from specific observations to general conclusion ('I've seen 100 swans and they were all white, therefore all swans are white' β€” strong but not certain).
medium.hint: Deductive: certainty from premises. Inductive: probability from observation.

medium.q: Explain what 'semantic change' is in the history of English, with examples.
medium.a: Words change meaning over time. Amelioration: meaning improves ('nice' originally meant foolish). Pejoration: meaning worsens ('villain' originally just meant farm worker). Broadening: meaning expands ('dog' used to mean a specific breed). Narrowing: meaning restricts ('meat' once meant any food).
medium.hint: Think about what words meant 500 years ago versus now.

medium.q: Describe the purpose of a 'controlled assessment' in writing.
medium.a: A piece of writing completed under specific conditions (time limit, no help) to assess independent writing ability. Tests: grammar, structure, vocabulary, ideas, style. Demonstrates what you can do without assistance.
medium.hint: Think about what distinguishes assessed writing from classroom practice writing.

medium.q: What is the difference between a dynamic and a static character?
medium.a: Dynamic: changes significantly through the story (develops morally, emotionally, intellectually). Static: remains essentially unchanged. Protagonists are usually dynamic; antagonists may be static. Character arcs are the journeys dynamic characters take.
medium.hint: Think about a character who learns something important versus one who never changes.

medium.q: How do writers use contrast in their work? Give two examples.
medium.a: Structural contrast: joyful opening / tragic ending. Character contrast (foil): Gatsby's dreams vs Tom's cynical reality. Tonal contrast: serious argument interrupted by comedy. Imagery contrast: warm home / cold outside. All create meaning through juxtaposition.
medium.hint: Things are defined partly by what they are NOT β€” contrast highlights this.

medium.q: Explain the conventions of writing a formal email.
medium.a: Subject line (clear and specific); formal greeting (Dear Mr/Ms + surname); formal language (no slang/contractions); paragraphed structure; clear purpose stated early; professional sign-off (Yours sincerely/Kind regards); full name and contact details.
medium.hint: Think about how this differs from a text message or informal email.

medium.q: What is the purpose of a 'twist ending' in a story?
medium.a: To recontextualise everything the reader has experienced β€” revealing that their assumptions were wrong. Effect: shock, surprise, re-reading (to find foreshadowing clues), raising questions about perspective and reliability. Works best when both surprising AND inevitable in retrospect.
medium.hint: Think about 'The Sixth Sense' β€” how does the ending change your understanding of everything before it?

medium.q: Explain what is meant by 'writing for different audiences'. Give an example.
medium.a: Different audiences require different vocabulary, tone, complexity and assumed knowledge. E.g. explaining gravity: to a 7-year-old (simple metaphor, no jargon); to a GCSE student (Newton's law, some formulas); to a physicist (general relativity, tensors). Same content, radically different treatment.
medium.hint: Think about how you'd describe your weekend to a 5-year-old versus to a teacher.

medium.q: What is 'implication' in language and how do writers use it?
medium.a: Implication: meaning suggested but not directly stated. Writers use this for subtlety, irony, characterisation. E.g. a character who always arrives exactly on time when others are late implies obsessive punctuality without stating it. What is NOT said can be as significant as what is.
medium.hint: Think about a character who never says they're sad but whose actions all convey sadness.

medium.q: Explain how repetition is used as a rhetorical device.
medium.a: Repetition creates emphasis, rhythm, memorability and emotional force. Types: anaphora (repeated opening), epistrophe (repeated ending), anadiplosis (end of one clause = start of next), refrain. 'Never give up, never surrender, never yield' β€” the repetition of 'never' makes the commitment feel absolute.
medium.hint: Why does repetition feel powerful rather than just redundant?

medium.q: What is a 'stream of consciousness' narrative technique? Give an example.
medium.a: Unedited flow of thoughts, images and feelings mimicking the actual flow of human thought β€” not grammatically organised. James Joyce and Virginia Woolf used this. E.g. Mrs Dalloway: 'What a lark! What a plunge! For so it had always seemed to her...' β€” rapid, associative, private.
medium.hint: Think about how your thoughts actually flow β€” not in neat sentences but in fragments and jumps.

medium.q: Explain what makes a successful introduction to a piece of extended writing.
medium.a: 1) Hook: engage the reader. 2) Context: frame the topic. 3) Thesis: state your argument/purpose. 4) Signpost: indicate structure. The introduction should be approximately 10% of the whole piece and leave the reader wanting to know more.
medium.hint: Think about what the reader needs to know before diving into your main argument.

medium.q: What is the difference between an 'open' and a 'closed' ending in fiction?
medium.a: Closed ending: all plot strands resolved β€” the reader knows what happened to everyone. Open ending: ambiguous or unresolved β€” the reader must interpret or imagine what follows. Open endings often create more thought-provoking, lasting impressions.
medium.hint: How does an unresolved ending make you feel differently about a story than a neat resolution?

medium.q: Explain how punctuation can change the meaning of a sentence. Give an example.
medium.a: 'Woman without her man is nothing.' vs 'Woman: without her, man is nothing.' Same words; entirely opposite meaning depending on where punctuation is placed.
medium.hint: Think about other examples where a comma or colon changes everything.

hard.q: Analyse how Dickens uses language to critique Victorian society in 'Oliver Twist'.
hard.a: Dickens uses social realism to expose workhouse conditions (gruel scene); ironic narrative voice ('Please, sir, I want some more' β€” the shock of such a small request); caricatured villains (Fagin as exploitation); contrasted settings (slums vs wealth). His language transforms social criticism into compelling narrative.
hard.hint: Think about specific language choices and how they serve Dickens's social purpose.

hard.q: Evaluate the view that all texts are political.
hard.a: For: all writing reflects values about power, identity, society β€” even choosing what to describe is a political act; genre conventions reflect dominant culture. Against: some writing aspires to purely aesthetic, universal concerns. Conclusion: texts always make implicit ideological choices (who speaks, whose story, what is normalised) even without explicit political intent.
hard.hint: Think about what is in a text AND what is absent β€” both reflect choices.

hard.q: What is the difference between structuralism and post-structuralism in literary theory?
hard.a: Structuralism (Saussure, LΓ©vi-Strauss): texts have underlying structures (binary oppositions, narrative grammar) that produce meaning β€” meaning is in the system. Post-structuralism (Derrida): meaning is not fixed β€” language is unstable, texts are full of contradictions and gaps, meaning is deferred indefinitely (diffΓ©rance).
hard.hint: Structuralism: meaning is findable in the structure. Post-structuralism: meaning is never stable.

hard.q: Analyse the use of irony in Swift's 'A Modest Proposal'.
hard.a: Swift proposes eating Irish babies to solve poverty β€” a horrifying literal proposal. The irony works because: the tone is calmly rational and detached (like a government document), making the horror more disturbing; the real target is British indifference to Irish suffering; the reader must work to understand what Swift actually believes.
hard.hint: Think about the gap between what Swift says and what he means β€” and how the manner of saying it makes the point.

hard.q: Explain the concept of 'implied author' in narrative theory.
hard.a: Booth's concept: the 'implied author' is not the real author but the version of the author implied by the text β€” their apparent values, intelligence, moral stance as inferred from the narrative choices. Readers construct an image of who made these choices even when the actual author is unknown.
hard.hint: Think about the difference between an author's real opinions and what their novel seems to value.

hard.q: Evaluate the argument that literature can change the world.
hard.a: For: 'Uncle Tom's Cabin' influenced abolition movement; 'The Jungle' improved food safety laws; 1984/Brave New World shaped political discourse; literature builds empathy. Against: direct causal effects are hard to prove; literature preaches to the converted; action requires more than reading. Conclusion: literature can shift attitudes over time; rarely creates immediate direct change.
hard.hint: Think about cases where literature is credited with social change β€” and then question whether literature caused the change or reflected already-changing attitudes.

hard.q: What is 'aporia' in rhetoric and literary theory?
hard.a: Aporia: expressing genuine doubt or uncertainty β€” 'I scarcely know how to begin.' As a rhetorical device, it can be performative (pretending uncertainty while actually being certain) or genuine (acknowledging the limits of knowledge). In deconstructive criticism, aporia refers to moments where a text contradicts itself.
hard.hint: Think about the difference between a speaker who pretends not to know where to start (false modesty) and one who genuinely doesn't.

hard.q: Critically analyse the narrative structure of a film or novel you know well.
hard.a: E.g. 'The Shawshank Redemption': non-chronological narrator (Red narrates retrospectively, creating dramatic irony); rising action through Andy's small acts of resistance; climax (escape); denouement (reunion). Structure creates hope despite oppression; retrospective narration assures us of survival.
hard.hint: Think about how the order of events, choice of narrator, and story's shape all create meaning.

hard.q: Explain Bakhtin's concept of 'heteroglossia' and its application to the novel.
hard.a: Heteroglossia: the presence of multiple social voices, registers and ideologies within a text. The novel is uniquely suited to heteroglossia β€” characters speak differently based on class, education, region. Unlike lyric poetry (single voice), the novel juxtaposes voices, allowing meaning to arise from their interaction.
hard.hint: Think about how characters in a novel all speak differently β€” and how that creates meaning.

hard.q: How do writers use intertextuality to enrich their texts? Analyse one example.
hard.a: Intertextuality: references to other texts add layers of meaning for readers who recognise the source. E.g. 'Wide Sargasso Sea' (Rhys) rewrites 'Jane Eyre' from Bertha's perspective β€” reversing the colonial gaze of the original. Readers who know BrontΓ« experience a completely transformed reading.
hard.hint: Does knowing the source text change how you read the new text? What does it add?

hard.q: Explain what is meant by 'narrative reliability' and how writers manipulate it.
hard.a: Reliability concerns how much we can trust the narrator's account. Writers manipulate it through: internal contradiction, revealed motivation (biased narrator), limited knowledge, psychological disturbance, or meta-fictional signals. Unreliability forces active reading and raises epistemological questions about truth.
hard.hint: Think about what different types of narrator limitation look like and why writers choose them.

hard.q: Analyse how the Romantic poets used nature differently from Victorian poets.
hard.a: Romantics: nature as sublime, transcendent, healing spiritual force β€” contrast to industrial society (Wordsworth's 'spots of time'; Keats's 'odes'). Victorian: nature seen with scientific eye (post-Darwin β€” Tennyson's 'Nature, red in tooth and claw'); industrial damage to nature; nature as moral comfort or threat.
hard.hint: What changed between 1800 and 1850 in terms of how humans understood nature? How did Darwin change poetry?

hard.q: What is 'defamiliarisation' (Shklovsky) and how can writers use it in their own work?
hard.a: Making familiar things seem strange to restore fresh perception β€” cutting through habitual, automatic seeing. Techniques: describe familiar objects from an alien perspective; use unusual syntax; describe in excessive technical detail; present from a child's uncomprehending perspective.
hard.hint: Try describing a chair as if you've never seen one before β€” what do you notice?

hard.q: Explain the concept of 'narrative closure' and when writers deliberately avoid it.
hard.a: Narrative closure: resolution of conflicts, satisfaction, completion. Writers avoid it to: reflect life's ambiguity; invite reader interpretation; suggest ongoing struggle; create political point (resolution would be false given circumstances); modernist/postmodernist distrust of neat endings.
hard.hint: Why might a novel about injustice choose NOT to end with justice being served?

hard.q: What is the difference between syntax and semantics in linguistic analysis?
hard.a: Syntax: the rules governing sentence structure β€” word order, grammatical relations. Semantics: the study of meaning β€” what words and sentences mean. A sentence can have correct syntax but be semantically anomalous: 'Colourless green ideas sleep furiously' (Chomsky) β€” grammatically perfect, meaningless.
hard.hint: Think about sentences that follow all the grammar rules but still make no sense.

hard.q: Evaluate the claim that fiction is 'lies that tell the truth'.
hard.a: Fictional events are invented (lies) but the emotional, psychological and social truths they convey can be more profound than factual accounts. E.g. 'The Kite Runner' (invented story, real Afghan experience); 'To Kill a Mockingbird' (fictional trial, real racial injustice). 'Truth' here means emotional and moral authenticity.
hard.hint: Think about why a made-up story can make you understand something real better than a documentary.

hard.q: Analyse the use of symbolism in a text of your choice.
hard.a: E.g. 'Animal Farm' (Orwell): the farm = Russia; Boxer = the working class; the pigs = Bolshevik leaders; 'All animals are equal, but some animals are more equal than others' = corruption of revolutionary ideals. Symbolism allows political allegory to function across historical periods.
hard.hint: Think about what each element represents beyond its literal meaning.

hard.q: Explain the concept of 'voice' in memoir writing and how it distinguishes memoir from fiction.
hard.a: Voice in memoir is the author's actual personality β€” the specific sensibility, humour, pain, wonder that belongs to one real person. Unlike fiction (author creates a persona), memoir voice IS the author. The tension in memoir: voice must be authentic (real self) but crafted (shaped for narrative effect).
hard.hint: Think about what makes a memoir feel genuine rather than performed.

hard.q: Describe three examples of where language choices reveal ideology in non-fiction texts.
hard.a: Passive voice: 'Mistakes were made' (hides agent β€” often used in political discourse to evade accountability). Nominalisation: 'the government's intervention' vs 'the government intervened' β€” process becomes a static thing. Euphemism: 'collateral damage' for civilian deaths. All shape perception by foregrounding/hiding agency and impact.
hard.hint: Think about the difference between describing an action and disguising it as a noun.

hard.q: What is 'genre hybridisation' and why do contemporary writers use it?
hard.a: Mixing genres that are conventionally kept separate β€” e.g. crime + literary fiction ('The Secret History'); science fiction + realism ('Never Let Me Go'). Reasons: defamiliarises expectations, allows exploration of themes not available in single genre, appeals to multiple audiences, questions genre conventions.
hard.hint: Think about what you expect from a genre and how subverting those expectations creates meaning.

hard.q: Explain the purpose and techniques of satire as a literary form.
hard.a: Satire: using irony, exaggeration, parody or ridicule to critique society, power or human folly. Techniques: hyperbole, irony (literal meaning vs intended), parody (imitation mocking the original), juxtaposition, understatement. Examples: Swift, Orwell, Private Eye. Goal: expose and critique through laughter rather than direct argument.
hard.hint: Why is satire sometimes more powerful than direct criticism? What can it do that argument can't?

hard.q: Analyse how language change reflects social change, using one example from the history of English.
hard.a: E.g. gender-neutral language: 'they' as singular pronoun now widely accepted (reflected non-binary identity recognition); 'Ms' adopted (reflects women's independence from marital status definition). Language both reflects and shapes social change β€” once a term exists, it makes a concept thinkable and communicable.
hard.hint: Think about words that didn't exist 50 years ago because the concept didn't need expressing β€” what do new words reveal about social change?

hard.q: Critically evaluate New Criticism's approach to texts (close reading only, no context).
hard.a: New Criticism (1930sβ€“60s): focus on the text itself β€” close reading, irony, ambiguity, tension. Context (biography, history) is the 'intentional fallacy' (author's intent is unknowable/irrelevant). Strengths: rigorous, text-centred, develops close-reading skills. Weaknesses: context does matter (reading Camus without Algeria; Toni Morrison without slavery is impossible).
hard.hint: Can you fully understand '1984' without knowing about totalitarianism in the 1940s?

hard.q: Explain what 'narrative distance' is and how it can be varied.
hard.a: How close the narrator is, psychologically and emotionally, to the events narrated. Close: intimate access to thought/feeling (free indirect discourse, stream of consciousness). Distant: objective, surface-level reporting with little interiority. Writers vary this for effect β€” distance for irony; closeness for empathy.
hard.hint: Think about how a documentary feels different from a first-person diary of the same events.

hard.q: What is the difference between 'story time' and 'discourse time' in narrative theory?
hard.a: Story time: chronological duration of events in the world of the story. Discourse time: how long it takes the narration to cover those events. Novel tricks: years summarised in one page (summary); one minute expanded to 50 pages (scenic/real-time). Controlling this ratio creates pace.
hard.hint: Think about novels that spend 100 pages on one day, or a film that covers a decade in 2 minutes.

hard.q: Analyse how rhyme scheme contributes to meaning in a specific poem.
hard.a: E.g. Shakespeare Sonnet 18: ABAB CDCD EFEF GG β€” alternating rhyme in first 12 lines creates a structured, controlled argument; the final couplet (GG) makes a decisive, memorable conclusion ('So long as men can breathe, or eyes can see, / So long lives this...'). Rhyme links ideas and gives closure.
hard.hint: Think about how the sound of rhyme reinforces the logic of an argument.

hard.q: Explain how academic writing differs from creative writing in its use of language.
hard.a: Academic: impersonal/objective register; hedged language ('evidence suggests'); passive voice; citation of sources; Latin/Greek vocabulary; formal syntax; no figurative language; deductive structure. Creative: voice/persona; metaphor, imagery; syntactic experimentation; emotional language; sensory detail; structure varies by purpose.
hard.hint: Take a sentence from each type and compare the vocabulary, grammar and tone.

hard.q: What is 'lyric poetry' and how does it differ from narrative and dramatic poetry?
hard.a: Lyric: first-person expression of emotion, thought or perception β€” subjective, present moment (ode, elegy, sonnet). Narrative: tells a story (epic, ballad). Dramatic: a character speaks (dramatic monologue, verse drama). Lyric is the most common form; its hallmark is intensity of individual feeling.
hard.hint: Think about what each form primarily does: express, narrate, or dramatise.

hard.q: Evaluate the role of metaphor in conceptual thought (Lakoff and Johnson's 'conceptual metaphor theory').
hard.a: Lakoff/Johnson: abstract concepts are understood through concrete metaphors β€” we 'understand' time by conceptualising it as a physical resource ('spending time', 'wasting time', 'time is money'). Metaphors are not just literary devices but cognitive structures shaping how we think. Language reveals underlying conceptual frameworks.
hard.hint: Why do we 'attack' arguments or 'defend' positions? What metaphor underlies how we think about debate?

hard.q: What is the 'uncanny' (Freud's Unheimlich) and how do writers use it?
hard.a: The uncanny is the eerie feeling when something familiar becomes strange β€” the German word means both homely and un-homely. Writers create it through: familiar objects behaving wrongly (dolls, doubles), uncanny repetition, blurring of alive/inanimate. Kafka, Poe and horror fiction exploit it extensively.
hard.hint: Think about why a doll that looks almost but not quite human is more disturbing than one that's obviously fake.

hard.q: Explain the role of genre conventions in reader expectations and authorial creativity.
hard.a: Genre conventions (detective fiction: crime committed, investigation, revelation) create expectations that authors can fulfil (satisfy) or subvert (surprise). Subversion creates meaning through contrast β€” the genre's absence is felt. Too much fulfilment = formula. Too much subversion = failure to communicate. Art lies in the interplay.
hard.hint: Why is a detective novel without a resolution unsatisfying? Why is one with exactly the expected solution boring?

hard.q: Analyse how Orwell uses language to satirise political discourse in 'Animal Farm' or '1984'.
hard.a: Animal Farm: the gradual corruption of the Seven Commandments mirrors the corruption of revolutionary language in totalitarianism. 'All animals are equal but some are more equal than others' satirises Stalinist doublespeak. 1984: Newspeak (restricted vocabulary prevents thought), doublethink (holding contradictory beliefs), slogans ('War is Peace') β€” all demonstrate language as a tool of oppression.
hard.hint: How does controlling language control thought? What does Orwell warn us about?

easy.q: What was the ancient Silk Road used for?
easy.a: Trading goods (silk, spices, porcelain, gold) between China, Central Asia, the Middle East and Europe.
easy.hint: It connected East and West through trade.

easy.a: E.g. Egypt, Greece, Rome, Mesopotamia, India (Indus Valley), China, Maya, Aztec
easy.hint: Ancient civilisations developed thousands of years ago.

easy.q: What was ancient Mesopotamia known as?
easy.a: 'The cradle of civilisation' β€” in modern Iraq, between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers.
easy.hint: It was home to the Sumerians, Babylonians and Assyrians.

easy.q: What was the Code of Hammurabi?
easy.a: One of the earliest written legal codes, from ancient Babylon (~1750 BC), setting out laws and punishments.
easy.hint: It is one of the first examples of a written law system.

easy.q: What is the significance of the year 1066 in English history?
easy.a: The Norman Conquest β€” William the Conqueror defeated Harold II at the Battle of Hastings and became King of England.
easy.hint: One of the most famous dates in British history.

easy.a: A scientist who studies the past through excavating and analysing physical remains, artefacts and structures.
easy.hint: They dig up the past.

easy.q: Name three things we can learn from ancient Egyptian artefacts.
easy.a: Religion (beliefs in afterlife, gods), daily life (food, clothing, tools), writing system (hieroglyphics), burial practices, trade.
easy.hint: Think about what objects tell us about how people lived and believed.

easy.q: What was the role of a pharaoh in ancient Egypt?
easy.a: The pharaoh was the absolute ruler, considered a god on Earth, responsible for maintaining order (Ma'at), protecting Egypt, and serving as intermediary between gods and people.
easy.hint: In ancient Egypt, the king was also a god.

easy.a: Trained fighters (often slaves or prisoners) who fought in arenas for public entertainment in ancient Rome.
easy.hint: They fought in places like the Colosseum.

easy.q: What was the purpose of the Roman forum?
easy.a: A public space at the centre of Roman cities used for commerce, political life, public speeches, temples and courts.
easy.hint: It was the heart of Roman public life β€” like a town centre.

easy.q: Name two Roman gods and their domains.
easy.a: Jupiter (king of gods/sky), Mars (war), Venus (love), Neptune (sea), Diana (hunting), Mercury (messengers) β€” any two.
easy.hint: Roman gods were borrowed from Greek mythology.

easy.q: What was the ancient Greek city-state called?
easy.a: A polis (plural: poleis)
easy.hint: Each Greek city-state had its own laws, army and government.

easy.a: E.g. Socrates, Plato, Aristotle, Heraclitus, Pythagoras
easy.hint: They shaped Western thought for over 2000 years.

easy.q: What was the significance of the Library of Alexandria?
easy.a: One of the largest libraries in the ancient world (founded ~3rd century BC in Egypt), attempting to collect all human knowledge.
easy.hint: Its destruction is seen as a great loss to human knowledge.

easy.a: The largest Roman amphitheatre, built in Rome (completed 80 AD), seating up to 80,000 spectators for gladiatorial contests.
easy.hint: It is the most recognisable Roman building still standing.

easy.a: A Roman general, politician and dictator who conquered Gaul and Britain. Assassinated on the Ides of March (15 March, 44 BC).
easy.hint: 'Et tu, Brute?' are his alleged dying words.

easy.a: A wooden horse used by the Greeks to sneak soldiers inside the walls of Troy, ending the Trojan War.
easy.hint: It was a gift that concealed an army.

easy.a: A collection of traditional stories explaining the origins of the world, natural phenomena, and cultural traditions, often involving gods and heroes.
easy.hint: Greek myths include stories of Zeus, Hercules and Odysseus.

easy.a: An ancient Greek poet (8th century BC) credited with writing the Iliad (Trojan War) and the Odyssey (Odysseus's journey).
easy.hint: The Iliad and Odyssey are two of the oldest epic poems.

easy.q: Name two famous structures from ancient Rome that still exist.
easy.a: Colosseum, Pantheon, Hadrian's Wall, Pont du Gard, aqueducts, Roman roads β€” any two.
easy.hint: Roman engineering was so good that many structures survived 2000 years.

easy.q: What did the ancient Greeks contribute to mathematics?
easy.a: Pythagoras (right-angle triangles), Euclid (geometry), Archimedes (pi, levers). Laid foundations of Western mathematics.
easy.hint: You still use Pythagoras's theorem today.

easy.q: What is the difference between BC and AD?
easy.a: BC = Before Christ; AD = Anno Domini (year of the Lord). Years in BC count backwards; AD counts forwards from the birth of Christ.
easy.hint: 2000 BC is further in the past than 100 BC.

easy.q: What was the reign of Augustus Caesar significant for?
easy.a: Augustus (27 BC β€“ 14 AD) was the first Roman Emperor, beginning the Pax Romana (200 years of relative peace), building many Roman monuments and expanding the empire.
easy.hint: He transformed Rome from a republic into an empire.

easy.q: Name a famous ancient Greek monument that still stands.
easy.a: The Parthenon (temple to Athena, Athens) or the Temple of Olympian Zeus.
easy.hint: The Parthenon stands on the Acropolis in Athens.

easy.q: What is archaeology's main limitation compared to written history?
easy.a: Archaeology can reveal physical evidence (tools, buildings, bones) but cannot directly tell us what people thought, believed, or said β€” we must infer this from artefacts.
easy.hint: What can an object tell you that a diary entry can?

easy.a: A stone wall (73 miles) built across northern Britain by Emperor Hadrian (122 AD) to mark the northern frontier of the Roman Empire.
easy.hint: It still partly stands across northern England.

easy.a: An elaborate burial structure (like a pyramid) containing the pharaoh's mummified body and possessions for use in the afterlife.
easy.hint: The Egyptians believed the body needed to be preserved for the afterlife.

easy.a: A Roman city near Naples buried by the eruption of Vesuvius in 79 AD, preserved almost perfectly under ash and pumice.
easy.hint: Its sudden burial preserved a snapshot of Roman daily life.

easy.q: What is the significance of the invention of writing?
easy.a: Writing allowed record-keeping, complex administration, accumulation of knowledge across generations, legal codes and literature β€” making complex civilisations possible.
easy.hint: Without writing, history before writing is called 'prehistory'.

easy.a: Ra (sun), Isis (magic/healing), Osiris (death/afterlife), Horus (sky), Anubis (embalming), Thoth (writing) β€” any two.
easy.hint: Egyptians worshipped many gods associated with natural forces.

easy.a: A stone coffin, often decorated, used in ancient Egypt (and elsewhere) to hold a mummified body.
easy.hint: It protected the mummy inside.

easy.q: Name the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.
easy.a: Great Pyramid of Giza (only surviving), Hanging Gardens of Babylon, Colossus of Rhodes, Lighthouse of Alexandria, Temple of Artemis, Statue of Zeus, Mausoleum at Halicarnassus.
easy.hint: Only the Pyramid still stands.

easy.q: What did Romans use aqueducts for?
easy.a: To transport water over long distances from rivers and springs to cities β€” supplying baths, fountains and homes.
easy.hint: Roman aqueducts used gravity to move water.

easy.a: A decree (196 BC) written in three scripts (hieroglyphic, demotic, Greek), which allowed scholars to decode Egyptian hieroglyphics after its discovery in 1799.
easy.hint: It was the key to understanding ancient Egyptian writing.

easy.q: Why was the River Nile important to Egypt's survival?
easy.a: It provided water for drinking and irrigation, its annual floods deposited rich fertile silt for farming, fish for food, papyrus reeds for writing/building, and a transport route.
easy.hint: Egypt would be desert without the Nile.

easy.q: What is the Islamic Golden Age?
easy.a: A period (8thβ€“13th centuries) when the Islamic world led the world in science, mathematics, medicine, philosophy and art, centred on Baghdad.
easy.hint: Think about what the Islamic world preserved and discovered during Europe's Middle Ages.

easy.q: Who built the Great Wall of China?
easy.a: Multiple Chinese rulers over centuries, with Emperor Qin Shi Huang linking earlier walls (around 221 BC) and later Ming dynasty emperors extending it.
easy.hint: It wasn't built all at once by one person.

easy.a: Long, narrow wooden ships with shallow draught, allowing Vikings to sail across oceans and also up rivers β€” enabling long-distance exploration and raiding.
easy.hint: Their design allowed both ocean voyaging and river navigation.

easy.q: Name the Norse god of thunder.
easy.a: Thor
easy.hint: Thursday is named after Thor.

easy.a: A medieval Norse prose narrative, recording history and legends of Viking-age heroes and kings.
easy.hint: Sagas are the main source of Viking history.

easy.q: What is the significance of the year 1215?
easy.a: King John signed the Magna Carta, limiting royal power and establishing that the king must obey the law.
easy.hint: A foundational document for English democracy.

easy.q: What were medieval castles built for?
easy.a: Military defence, control of surrounding territory, symbol of power, administrative centre for a region.
easy.hint: Think about why someone would need a defensible stronghold.

easy.a: A series of religious wars (1095β€“1291) in which European Christians attempted to reclaim the Holy Land from Muslim control.
easy.hint: Pope Urban II called the First Crusade in 1095.

easy.a: King Richard I of England (1189β€“1199), famous for his role in the Third Crusade.
easy.hint: He spent most of his reign abroad fighting in the Crusades.

easy.a: A hierarchical system of land ownership and duties: king β†’ lords β†’ knights β†’ serfs. Each level provided military service or labour in exchange for land and protection.
easy.hint: Think of a pyramid β€” the king owned all land; serfs at the bottom did the work.

easy.q: Name two famous buildings in ancient Greece.
easy.a: Parthenon (Athens), Temple of Delphi, Temple of Olympian Zeus, Theatre of Epidaurus β€” any two.
easy.hint: Greek buildings influenced Western architecture forever.

easy.q: What is the significance of the year 776 BC in Greek history?
easy.a: The first recorded Olympic Games, held at Olympia in honour of Zeus.
easy.hint: The ancient Greeks held these games every four years.

easy.a: The 'Roman Peace' β€” roughly 200 years of relative peace and stability across the Roman Empire (27 BC β€“ 180 AD).
easy.hint: It allowed Roman culture and trade to flourish.

easy.q: What were the causes of the fall of the Western Roman Empire?
easy.a: Military overextension, economic problems, political instability, Germanic invasions, and social decay. The Western Empire fell in 476 AD.
easy.hint: Think about internal weakness and external pressure combining.

easy.a: King of the Franks and Holy Roman Emperor (crowned 800 AD), who united much of Western Europe and promoted Christianity and learning.
easy.hint: He is called the 'Father of Europe'.

medium.q: Compare the political systems of ancient Athens and ancient Sparta.
medium.a: Athens: direct democracy (adult male citizens voted on laws), emphasis on arts/philosophy, navy-based power. Sparta: military oligarchy (ephors and kings), rigorous military training (agoge) from age 7, no democracy, agriculture-based. Both: Greek city-states, enslaved populations (Helots in Sparta).
medium.hint: Think about how each was governed and what it valued.

medium.q: Explain the significance of the Roman Republic's downfall and the rise of the Empire.
medium.a: Republic: two Consuls, Senate, separation of powers. Fell: civil wars (Marius/Sulla; Caesar/Pompey); Julius Caesar's dictatorship; his assassination β†’ Octavian (Augustus) became first emperor. Significance: end of republican principles, absolute power concentrated, 500 years of empire.
medium.hint: What constitutional principles did the Republic have, and how were they eroded?

medium.q: Describe the main contributions of ancient Greece to Western civilisation.
medium.a: Democracy (Athens), philosophy (Socrates, Plato, Aristotle), mathematics (Pythagoras, Euclid), science (Archimedes, Hippocrates), literature (Homer, Sophocles), architecture (Doric/Ionic/Corinthian columns), Olympic Games.
medium.hint: Think about government, thought, science, art and culture.

medium.q: Why did Alexander the Great's empire collapse so quickly after his death?
medium.a: No clear heir β€” he died young (32) without naming a successor. His generals (Diadochi) fought civil wars to divide the empire. No administrative system could hold such a vast, diverse territory without his unifying leadership.
medium.hint: What does it say about an empire when it depends entirely on one person's talent?

medium.q: Describe the causes and consequences of the Black Death in medieval Europe.
medium.a: Causes: Yersinia pestis bacteria, transmitted by rat fleas, spread via trade routes from Asia. Consequences: ~30β€“60% of European population died; labour shortage, higher wages, peasant empowerment; questioned Church authority; art became death-obsessed; eventually weakened feudalism.
medium.hint: Think about what happens to society when a third of the workforce dies suddenly.

medium.q: Explain how the Byzantine Empire preserved and transmitted classical knowledge.
medium.a: After Western Rome fell (476 AD), the Eastern (Byzantine) Empire survived until 1453. Scholars preserved Greek texts; Constantinople's fall sent scholars fleeing to Italy, bringing manuscripts. This contributed to the Italian Renaissance.
medium.hint: What happened to the Greek texts when Western Rome fell? Where were they kept?

medium.q: Why was the Silk Road important beyond just trade?
medium.a: Spread of religions (Buddhism, Islam, Christianity along routes); exchange of technologies (paper, printing, compass from China); spread of diseases (plague); cultural exchange (art, music, food). More than goods β€” it was a vector for ideas.
medium.hint: What travels along a trade route besides merchandise?

medium.q: Compare primary and secondary source types used by historians of ancient history.
medium.a: Primary: inscriptions, coins, pottery, buildings, contemporary texts (Homer, Herodotus β€” though biased). Secondary: modern archaeological analysis, interpretive histories. Challenge for ancient history: few written records, mostly elite perspective, potential for significant gaps.
medium.hint: What sources survive from 3000 years ago, and how reliable are they?

medium.q: Explain why the Maya civilisation is remarkable.
medium.a: Independently developed: complex writing system, accurate calendar (more precise than European), sophisticated mathematics (zero), advanced astronomy, monumental architecture (Chichen Itza, Tikal), without metal tools or the wheel. Peak c.250β€“900 AD.
medium.hint: Think about what they achieved without technologies Europeans consider essential.

medium.q: Describe the Islamic Golden Age's contributions to science.
medium.a: Al-Khwarizmi: algebra (algorithms named after him). Ibn al-Haytham: optics. Ibn Sina (Avicenna): medical encyclopaedia used in Europe for 600 years. Astronomy: improved star charts. Preserved and extended Greek knowledge while Europe was in the 'Dark Ages'.
medium.hint: Think about what knowledge was kept alive and extended in Baghdad while Europe's learning declined.

medium.q: Why did the Mongol Empire become the largest contiguous land empire in history?
medium.a: Military innovation: horse archers, mobility, disciplined command. Psychological terror: cities that surrendered were spared; those that resisted were destroyed (creating a reputation that made many surrender). Merit-based promotion. Trade networks preserved after conquest.
medium.hint: Think about military strategy, reputation and administrative skill.

medium.q: Explain the historical significance of Magna Carta to the development of democracy.
medium.a: First formal limit on royal power (1215): king subject to law, taxation with consent (clause 14), right to trial by peers. Long-term: influenced Parliamentary development, English Bill of Rights (1689), US Constitution, Universal Declaration of Human Rights. A direct line from 1215 to modern democracy.
medium.hint: Think about the principle that rulers are accountable to law β€” where does that idea lead over centuries?

medium.q: Describe how the printing press changed the course of the Reformation.
medium.a: Luther's 95 Theses (1517) printed and distributed across Germany within weeks β€” previously impossible. Allowed reformers to bypass Church control of manuscripts. Mass printing spread vernacular Bibles, making scripture accessible without priests. Information control ended; Reformation became unstoppable.
medium.hint: How was information controlled before printing, and who lost control when printing democratised it?

medium.q: Why was the Renaissance an intellectual revolution?
medium.a: Recovered and built on classical Greek/Roman learning; shift from God-centred to human-centred thinking (humanism); observation and experiment over doctrine; art celebrated the human body; science began to diverge from theology. A fundamental change in how Europeans understood themselves and nature.
medium.hint: What changed about how people asked questions and where they looked for answers?

medium.q: Compare the treatment of conquered peoples by the Roman Empire and the Mongol Empire.
medium.a: Romans: generally incorporated conquered peoples as citizens or subjects; allowed local religions and customs; built infrastructure. Mongols: offered peace to those who submitted quickly; destroyed resistant cities; ruled through existing administrative structures but extracted tribute.
medium.hint: Think about integration versus extraction β€” what did each empire want from its conquests?

medium.q: Explain how we know about the ancient past when there was no writing.
medium.a: Archaeology: tools, pottery, buildings, human remains. Scientific dating: carbon-14 (up to 50,000 years), dendrochronology, stratigraphy (rock layers). DNA analysis: human migration patterns. Cave art. Comparative anthropology: studying similar present-day cultures.
medium.hint: What can physical objects tell us about the past that writing cannot?

medium.q: Why is the history of ancient Rome relevant to understanding modern Western society?
medium.a: Legal systems (Roman law underpins civil law in Europe); language (Latin basis of Romance languages, legal/scientific vocabulary); architecture (domes, arches, columns); democracy (Republic model); calendar (Julian β†’ Gregorian); Christianity (spread via Roman Empire).
medium.hint: Think about what Roman structures and ideas survived the empire's fall.

medium.q: Describe three ways in which the Norman Conquest transformed English society.
medium.a: Language: Old English + Norman French β†’ modern English. Land: Anglo-Saxon nobility replaced by Normans; Domesday Book (1086) quantified all land. Feudalism: systematised land holding. Architecture: stone castles and cathedrals. Religion: church reform, close ties to Rome.
medium.hint: Think about language, land, power and buildings.

medium.q: Why do historians disagree about the causes of Rome's fall?
medium.a: Gibbon (1776): Christianity weakened Roman virtues. Modern theories: economic decline, plague, climate change, migration pressure, political instability β€” probably a combination. The fact of disagreement shows that 'simple causes' for complex events are always oversimplifications.
medium.hint: What does historians' disagreement about Rome's fall tell us about how we should explain historical events?

medium.q: Explain how trade networks shaped the ancient world.
medium.a: Trade spread: technologies (metalworking, agriculture), religions (Buddhism/Islam along Silk Road), diseases (plagues), languages. Wealth from trade funded empires. Cultural diffusion: Greek culture spread with Alexander's trade routes; Roman culture spread with roads. Economic interdependence made civilisations dependent on each other.
medium.hint: Think about all the non-commercial things that travel alongside goods.

medium.q: Describe the life of an enslaved person in ancient Rome.
medium.a: Enslaved people: captured in war, born to enslaved parents, or bought in slave markets. No legal rights. Work: agriculture (most common), mining (most dangerous), domestic (cooking, cleaning, teaching), skilled work (doctors, teachers). Could be freed (manumission). Rome's economy depended on enslaved labour.
medium.hint: Think about what it means to be considered property rather than a person.

medium.q: Why is studying indigenous American civilisations important for a balanced view of world history?
medium.a: European history often ignores sophisticated non-European civilisations that existed contemporaneously. Maya, Aztec, Inca β€” all had complex mathematics, astronomy, architecture, governance, religion independent of European influence. Challenges idea that 'civilisation' = European.
medium.hint: What assumptions about the world are challenged when you learn that complex civilisations existed in the Americas for thousands of years before European contact?

medium.q: Explain the concept of 'historical continuity' using the example of religion in ancient Rome.
medium.a: Roman religion evolved β€” absorbed Greek gods, then spread Middle Eastern religions (Mithraism, Christianity). When Christianity became official (313 AD), it preserved many Roman structures (church hierarchy paralleled imperial administration) and festivals (Christmas = Saturnalia). Religious continuity despite dramatic change.
medium.hint: What stayed the same as Rome changed from pagan to Christian?

medium.q: Describe how Greek democracy was limited by modern standards.
medium.a: Limited to adult male citizens. Women: excluded. Slaves (~1/3 of population): excluded. Metics (resident foreigners): excluded. Perhaps only 10β€“20% of Athens's population could vote. No representative democracy (citizens voted directly but only citizens) β€” radical for its time but highly unequal.
medium.hint: Who was excluded from Athenian democracy and why does that matter?

medium.q: Compare the roles of religion in ancient Egyptian and ancient Greek society.
medium.a: Egypt: religion inseparable from state β€” pharaoh was god, all aspects of life religiously ordered, focused on afterlife and maintaining cosmic order (Ma'at). Greece: polytheistic with gods who had very human personalities, more distance from the divine, philosophy developed alongside religion, less absolute.
medium.hint: Think about whether religion and state were separate, and how each society related to its gods.

medium.q: How did the introduction of iron change ancient societies?
medium.a: Iron was harder and more abundant than bronze. Cheaper iron tools and weapons: more farmers could afford iron ploughs (agricultural revolution), more soldiers could be equipped (military democratisation). Disrupted Bronze Age civilisations, contributed to the Bronze Age collapse (~1200 BC).
medium.hint: Think about what happens when a better material becomes cheap enough for everyone to use.

medium.q: Why were ancient trade routes difficult and dangerous?
medium.a: Long distances, varied terrain (mountains, deserts), banditry/piracy, weather, disease, political barriers (taxes/tolls, war), lack of maps. Death rate on long journeys was significant. This is why trade goods were expensive.
medium.hint: Think about all the physical and human obstacles between a trader's starting point and their destination.

medium.q: Explain the legacy of Alexander the Great's conquests.
medium.a: Cultural: 'Hellenism' β€” Greek language and culture spread across Middle East and Central Asia. Cities founded (Alexandria: 20+ cities). Fusion cultures: Greco-Buddhist art in India. Scientific: Library of Alexandria. Trade: new routes opened. His empire's division created successor states that spread Greek culture for centuries.
medium.hint: Think about what happened AFTER Alexander died β€” his cultural legacy outlasted his political one.

medium.q: What is 'historical determinism' and why do many historians reject it?
medium.a: The view that history follows predetermined patterns or inevitable laws. Rejected because: human agency (individual decisions matter), contingency (historical accidents change outcomes), and the same conditions can produce different outcomes in different contexts β€” no universal law predicts human history reliably.
medium.hint: Was World War II inevitable? Or did specific human decisions make it happen?

medium.q: Describe how the Roman Catholic Church dominated life in medieval Europe.
medium.a: Church controlled: education (only institution running schools), hospitals, recorded births/deaths/marriages, courts (for clergy), art, architecture, and determined what was spiritually acceptable. Excommunication (exclusion) was a devastating political weapon. Pope could challenge monarchs.
medium.hint: Think about what the Church did that today is done by the state, universities and hospitals.

hard.q: Evaluate the extent to which the ancient Athenian 'democracy' deserves that name.
hard.a: Strong case for: citizens directly voted on laws (direct democracy), annual rotation of magistrates, accountability through ostracism. Strong case against: women, slaves (~30% of population), and foreigners excluded. Perhaps 15% of Athenians were citizens. A meaningful democracy for citizens but deeply exclusionary by modern standards. Word 'democracy' originated there; the reality was highly restricted.
hard.hint: Who got to participate, and what was the significance of who was left out?

hard.q: Critically assess the claim that Rome 'civilised' the peoples it conquered.
hard.a: Roman argument (and modern echo): roads, laws, urban life, stable governance spread widely. Critique: imposed by military violence; destroyed existing cultures; extracted wealth; enslaved millions; the narrative silences conquered peoples' perspectives. The 'civilising' claim often justified exploitation. Legacy is genuinely mixed.
hard.hint: Who is telling the story, and what does 'civilisation' mean to the conquered versus the conqueror?

hard.q: To what extent was religion the primary driver of the Crusades?
hard.a: Religious motivations: reclaim Jerusalem, Pope's call, spiritual rewards, genuine faith. Non-religious: political (Pope asserting authority over kings), economic (access to trade routes, wealth), social (younger sons needing land/adventure), military (channelling European knightly violence externally). Religion provided justification; material interests provided momentum.
hard.hint: Think about the gap between what people said motivated the Crusades and what actually drove them.

hard.q: How did the Islamic Golden Age challenge Eurocentric narratives of intellectual history?
hard.a: Between 750β€“1250 AD, when European learning declined, Islamic scholars preserved Greek texts AND extended them: algebra, optics, medicine, astronomy. European Renaissance depended on Islamic transmission of classical knowledge. This shows that intellectual progress is not exclusively European β€” it is global and reciprocal.
hard.hint: Where did Leonardo and Copernicus get their mathematics? How did those ideas reach Renaissance Italy?

hard.q: Evaluate the historical significance of the printing press versus writing itself as turning points.
hard.a: Writing (~3200 BC): enabled civilisation itself β€” administration, laws, accumulated knowledge, history. Printing (~1440 AD): democratised writing, ended Church/elite information monopoly, enabled Reformation and scientific revolution. Both transformative, but printing's effects were faster and broader. Writing created civilisation; printing transformed it.
hard.hint: Think about who could access information before and after each invention.

hard.q: Explain how gender shapes our understanding of ancient history.
hard.a: Most ancient written sources were produced by elite men β€” women's experiences are largely invisible. Archaeology can partially fill gaps (burial goods, household artefacts). Feminist historiography asks: what did women do, own, control? It reveals a more complex picture of ancient societies than male-authored texts suggest.
hard.hint: What sources do we have for women's lives in ancient Greece or Rome? What don't we have?

hard.q: Assess the view that the fall of Rome led to the 'Dark Ages' in Europe.
hard.a: Conventional narrative: Western Rome fell (476 AD), learning declined, barbarian chaos. Revisionist: 'Dark Ages' reflects bias of surviving elite Roman sources. Continuity existed: local kingdoms, church preserved literacy, trade continued at lower level, Byzantium flourished. 'Dark Ages' applies to written records from that period, not necessarily to living standards.
hard.hint: Does 'we have few written records' mean 'it was a dark period for people living then'?

hard.q: How do we balance acknowledging great historical achievements while condemning the methods used to achieve them?
hard.a: Roman roads, Greek philosophy, Egyptian pyramids β€” all achievements of societies that practised slavery, conquered by violence, and were deeply unequal. We can: describe the achievement honestly, acknowledge the human cost, resist both simplistic celebration and simplistic condemnation. Context is essential; so is the voices of those who suffered.
hard.hint: Can the Parthenon be beautiful AND built by enslaved people? How do you hold both truths?

hard.q: Why is there so much scholarly debate about the historicity of the Trojan War?
hard.a: Homer's Iliad (8th century BC) describes war centuries earlier (~1200 BC). Archaeological evidence (Hisarlik, Turkey) suggests a real city was destroyed c.1250 BC. But: Homer was mythologising centuries later; oral tradition distorts; the 'war' may be many campaigns compressed into one story. Evidence: suggestive but not conclusive.
hard.hint: Think about the gap between when Homer wrote and when the war supposedly happened, and what that means for reliability.

hard.q: Explain why the concept of 'progress' in history is problematic.
hard.a: Linear progress (barbarism β†’ civilisation β†’ modern Western society) is a Western, post-Enlightenment narrative. Problems: ignores sophisticated non-Western civilisations; 'progress' for whom? Colonial 'progress' meant destruction for the colonised. History has many trajectories, not one upward line. The idea of progress often legitimises current power structures.
hard.hint: Was the move from Roman Empire to medieval Europe 'progress'? Who decides what counts?

hard.q: How does the study of ancient trade networks challenge traditional notions of historical isolation?
hard.a: Roman gold coins found in India; Chinese silk in Roman graves; Indian cotton in Egypt; wheat from North Africa feeding Rome. Ancient peoples were interconnected through trade far more than traditional school history suggests. 'Civilisations in isolation' is a myth β€” globalisation is ancient, not modern.
hard.hint: Think about what physical objects from across the ancient world tell us about contact and connection.

hard.q: Evaluate the significance of literacy in ancient societies.
hard.a: Writing enabled: laws (Hammurabi), administration (taxation records), religion (Torah, Qur'an), history (Herodotus), science, literature. But literacy was elite and exclusive β€” most ancient people were illiterate. This means written history represents only a small, privileged fraction of ancient experience.
hard.hint: If only 5% of ancient Greeks could read, what does that mean for what their written sources represent?

hard.q: Assess the long-term impact of Alexander the Great's conquests on world history.
hard.a: Hellenistic culture (Greek language, art, philosophy) spread from Greece to India, creating a shared cultural zone for centuries. Koine Greek became the language of early Christianity (New Testament). Alexandria's Library was the greatest ancient centre of learning. Though his empire dissolved, the cultural legacy outlasted any political achievement.
hard.hint: Think about cultural rather than political legacy β€” what survived Alexander's death?

hard.q: Why is it important to include non-Western perspectives in the history curriculum?
hard.a: Half of human history occurs outside Europe. Eurocentric curricula: distort historical reality, serve national/imperial myths, exclude the majority of humanity's experience, imply that progress = Westernisation. Including e.g. Islamic Golden Age, Mali Empire, Chinese inventions: gives a truer picture and develops genuinely global citizens.
hard.hint: What assumptions are built into a curriculum that only covers European history?

hard.q: Explain the concept of 'collective memory' and how it shapes understanding of the past.
hard.a: Collective memory: shared narrative of the past within a social group β€” constructed, maintained through monuments, education, ritual, media. Not the same as accurate history β€” selects, distorts, mythologises. E.g. British collective memory of WWII emphasises heroic resistance; less emphasis on empire, collaboration in occupied territories.
hard.hint: Think about the difference between what a nation remembers and what historians document.

hard.q: Why do we have much more historical evidence from elites than from ordinary people?
hard.a: Elites: more likely to be literate, commission monuments/texts, be subjects of other people's writing, have elaborate burials. Ordinary people: rarely literate, leave few material remains, not considered worth recording. Archaeology helps partially β€” can recover everyday objects β€” but literacy bias in sources is structural.
hard.hint: Think about what determines whether a person's story is remembered after they die.

hard.q: Assess the degree to which ancient Egypt was a theocracy.
hard.a: Strong case: pharaoh was literally divine; religion permeated every aspect of state (calendar, taxation, law, architecture); priests had vast power; the purpose of the state was maintaining Ma'at (cosmic order) on behalf of the gods. Qualifications: pharaohs made practical political decisions not purely religious ones; bureaucracy operated in secular spheres.
