hard.hint: Can a state be both a religious institution and a practical political entity? Where does theocracy begin and end?

hard.q: Explain how colonialism distorted the historical record of non-European civilisations.
hard.a: Colonisers often destroyed local records (Spanish burning Maya codices), imposed their own frameworks ('barbarous peoples'), collected artefacts without consent (British Museum), trained local elites in Western frameworks that dismissed indigenous history. 20th century decolonisation involved recovering and revaluing suppressed histories.
hard.hint: Think about what happens to a culture's history when another culture defines what counts as history.

hard.q: How does the study of pre-Columbian Americas challenge assumptions about the uniqueness of 'Western progress'?
hard.a: Independently: Maya developed zero, accurate calendar; Aztec had sophisticated urban planning (Tenochtitlan larger than contemporary London); Inca's agricultural terracing and road network; all without iron tools or the wheel. Demonstrates: 'civilisation' is not one path but emerges independently across human societies given time and resources.
hard.hint: If the Americas were 'discovered' in 1492, what were the millions of people living there before then?

hard.q: Critically evaluate the claim that war is the driving force of historical change.
hard.a: For: WWII reshaped the world order; conquests spread civilisations (Alexander, Rome); wars produced technological innovation (internet from ARPANET). Against: economic forces, disease (Black Death), intellectual movements (Enlightenment), trade, social reform β€” all drive change without war. War is one driver among many; often destroys rather than creates.
hard.hint: Think about the biggest changes in the last 200 years β€” which were caused by war and which by other forces?

hard.q: Explain the relationship between geography and the rise of civilisation.
hard.a: Rivers (Nile, Tigris-Euphrates, Indus, Yellow River) provided: irrigation, transport, fertile soil. Mediterranean sea enabled Greek and Phoenician trade networks. The Fertile Crescent had wild ancestors of crop plants. Jared Diamond (Guns, Germs and Steel): geography not racial superiority explains why Eurasia developed faster.
hard.hint: Think about what physical advantages the Fertile Crescent had that, say, the Amazon didn't.

hard.q: How does examining coins help historians understand ancient economies?
hard.a: Coins reveal: metalwork technology, artistic standards, political messages (images of rulers = propaganda), trade extent (coins found far from origin = trading partners), inflation (debased coinage = economic problems), economic stability or collapse.
hard.hint: Think about what a coin tells you beyond just its monetary value.

hard.q: Evaluate the contribution of women to intellectual history, recognising that their contributions have been systematically obscured.
hard.a: Hypatia of Alexandria (mathematician/philosopher, murdered 415 AD); Hildegard of Bingen (medieval composer/scientist/theologian); women scientists obscured by male contemporaries (Rosalind Franklin/DNA; Lise Meitner/nuclear fission). Systematic exclusion from education and institutions meant contributions were fewer β€” but those who overcame barriers were exceptional.
hard.hint: Think about why women's contributions appear less in the historical record β€” is it because they contributed less, or because their contributions were recorded less?

hard.q: What does the history of pandemics tell us about human societies' ability to respond to crises?
hard.a: Plague of Athens (430 BC): democrated governance challenged. Black Death (1347): social upheaval, questioning of institutions. Spanish Flu (1918): suppressed by wartime censorship. COVID-19 (2020): global cooperation challenged by nationalism. Pattern: pandemics expose existing inequalities and test institutional resilience. Societies adapt but unevenly.
hard.hint: Think about what each pandemic revealed about the societies it hit β€” their strengths and vulnerabilities.

easy.a: The process by which the world's economies, cultures and populations have become increasingly interconnected through trade, communication and technology.
easy.hint: Your smartphone was probably designed in the US, made in China with parts from many countries.

easy.a: E.g. Amazon, Apple, McDonald's, Nike, Toyota, NestlΓ©, Shell
easy.hint: Companies that operate in many countries.

easy.a: The exchange of goods and services between people, businesses or countries.
easy.hint: Countries import what they need and export what they produce.

easy.a: A good or service brought into a country from another country.
easy.hint: The UK imports bananas (can't grow them) and exports financial services.

easy.a: A good or service sold to another country.
easy.hint: The UK exports whisky (from Scotland) and financial services.

easy.a: Gross Domestic Product β€” the total value of goods and services produced in a country in a year.
easy.hint: It is used to measure the size and health of a country's economy.

easy.q: What is the difference between a developed and a developing country?
easy.a: Developed: high income, educated population, strong services, long life expectancy (e.g. UK, Germany). Developing: lower income, fewer services, shorter life expectancy (e.g. Somalia, Haiti).
easy.hint: Think about income, healthcare, education and infrastructure.

easy.a: E.g. UK, Germany, Japan, USA, France, Australia
easy.hint: More Economically Developed Countries have high incomes.

easy.a: E.g. Somalia, Haiti, Bangladesh, Ethiopia, Cambodia
easy.hint: Less Economically Developed Countries have lower incomes.

easy.a: A direction measured in degrees from north (0Β°/360Β°), going clockwise.
easy.hint: North = 0Β°, East = 90Β°, South = 180Β°, West = 270Β°.

easy.q: What is a six-figure grid reference?
easy.a: A precise location on an OS map using three horizontal digits and three vertical digits, locating a 100 m Γ— 100 m square.
easy.hint: More precise than four-figure β€” go along then up, each with three digits.

easy.a: A low-lying area between hills or mountains, often with a river running through it.
easy.hint: V-shaped (river) or U-shaped (glacier).

easy.a: A narrow, steep-sided valley cut by a river through rock.
easy.hint: Like a canyon β€” deep and narrow.

easy.a: Where a river falls over a sudden drop in its bed, often where it crosses from hard to soft rock.
easy.hint: Niagara Falls is one of the world's most famous.

easy.a: A curve or bend in a river, formed by erosion on the outside and deposition on the inside of the bend.
easy.hint: Rivers snake through flat land in meanders.

easy.a: The increase in the proportion of a population living in urban areas.
easy.hint: More than 50% of the world's population now lives in cities.

easy.a: The movement of people from one place to another to live.
easy.hint: International migration crosses borders; internal migration is within a country.

easy.a: A consistent wind blowing from subtropical high pressure zones towards the equatorial low pressure β€” northeast in the Northern Hemisphere, southeast in the Southern.
easy.hint: They drove sailing ships from Europe to the Americas.

easy.a: A moderate climate with warm summers and mild winters, neither extreme hot nor extreme cold.
easy.hint: Western Europe (including the UK) has a temperate climate.

easy.a: A violent rotating column of air extending from a storm to the ground β€” extremely destructive in a narrow path.
easy.hint: Common in 'Tornado Alley' in the USA.

easy.a: Rain made acidic (pH < 5.6) by sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides (from burning fossil fuels), which dissolve in water vapour.
easy.hint: Acid rain damages trees, lakes and buildings.

easy.a: A region of the stratosphere containing ozone (Oβ‚ƒ), which absorbs most of the sun's harmful ultraviolet radiation.
easy.hint: The hole in the ozone layer (from CFCs) allowed more UV radiation to reach Earth's surface.

easy.q: What is photosynthesis and why is it important for geography?
easy.a: Plants convert COβ‚‚ and water using sunlight into glucose and oxygen. Important: forests are carbon sinks, regulating the carbon cycle and climate.
easy.hint: Deforestation removes this carbon sink, contributing to climate change.

easy.a: A forest of cone-bearing, needle-leafed evergreen trees (pine, spruce, fir) adapted to cold temperatures, found in high latitudes (taiga biome).
easy.hint: The world's largest biome stretches across Russia, Canada and Scandinavia.

easy.a: A forest of broad-leaved trees that shed their leaves in autumn, growing in temperate regions.
easy.hint: Most forests in England are deciduous.

easy.a: An underwater ecosystem built by calcium carbonate structures secreted by coral polyps, found in warm, shallow tropical seas.
easy.hint: The Great Barrier Reef (Australia) is the world's largest.

easy.q: What are the threats to coral reefs?
easy.a: Ocean warming (bleaching), acidification (COβ‚‚ absorption), pollution, physical damage (anchors, divers), overfishing, runoff from land.
easy.hint: Coral bleaching occurs when warmer water causes corals to expel their symbiotic algae.

easy.a: Coastal tropical forests growing in saltwater, with distinctive root systems above the waterline. Vital for coastal protection and fish nurseries.
easy.hint: Mangroves grow where land meets sea in tropical regions.

easy.a: A semi-arid band across Africa between the Sahara Desert (north) and tropical forest (south), from Senegal to Ethiopia.
easy.hint: It is at serious risk from desertification and climate change.

easy.a: When all people consistently have physical and economic access to sufficient, nutritious food for a healthy life.
easy.hint: The opposite β€” food insecurity β€” means people don't know where their next meal will come from.

easy.q: Name two countries with high food insecurity.
easy.a: E.g. Yemen, Somalia, South Sudan, Ethiopia, Haiti, Syria
easy.hint: Often affected by conflict, drought, or poverty.

easy.a: A flat area of land formed by river deposits (alluvium) over time, very fertile.
easy.hint: The Ganges plain and the Nile Valley are famous alluvial plains.

easy.a: A raised bank of sediment on either side of a river in its lower course, built up by repeated flooding.
easy.hint: Natural levees rise above the flood plain when rivers deposit sediment at their banks.

easy.a: A stream or river that flows into a larger river.
easy.hint: The Thames has many tributaries including the Lea and Wandle.

easy.q: What is the difference between erosion and weathering?
easy.a: Weathering: breakdown of rock in place (no movement). Erosion: removal and transport of weathered material by a moving agent (water, wind, ice).
easy.hint: Weathering happens first; erosion carries the material away.

easy.a: Hydraulic action (water pressure), abrasion (rock grinding), attrition (rocks wearing each other down), solution (chemical dissolving) β€” any two.
easy.hint: Think about different ways a river or sea wears rock away.

easy.a: A coastal landform of deposited sand or shingle extending from the shore into the sea, with a curved (hooked) end.
easy.hint: Spits form where longshore drift transports material past a break in the coast.

easy.a: The zig-zag movement of material along a beach by waves that arrive at an angle and swash material up the beach and backwash carries it down the shore.
easy.hint: Groynes are built to interrupt longshore drift and keep beach material in place.

easy.q: What is a headland and bay?
easy.a: Headland: a point of harder rock that projects into the sea. Bay: a curved indentation where softer rock has eroded faster on either side.
easy.hint: Differential erosion: soft rock erodes faster, forming bays; hard rock remains, forming headlands.

easy.q: What are sea arches and sea stacks?
easy.a: Arch: formed when caves erode through a headland. Stack: when the arch collapses, leaving an isolated column of rock.
easy.hint: Think about the Old Man of Hoy (Scotland) β€” a famous sea stack.

easy.a: The large-scale removal of forest, especially tropical rainforest, usually for farming, logging or development.
easy.hint: The Amazon loses an area of forest equivalent to a football field every second.

easy.a: Loss of biodiversity; COβ‚‚ released (climate change); soil erosion; local rainfall reduction; displacement of indigenous communities; flooding.
easy.hint: Think about what forests do for the climate, soil and biodiversity.

easy.a: Managing forests so that timber is harvested at a rate that allows the forest to regenerate, maintaining biodiversity and environmental services.
easy.hint: For every tree cut, plant two or more.

easy.a: Farming that uses high inputs (fertilisers, pesticides, machinery) to maximise yield from a relatively small area.
easy.hint: Opposite of extensive farming β€” which uses large areas with low inputs.

easy.a: Farming that uses large areas of land with low inputs per hectare β€” e.g. sheep farming in upland Britain, cattle ranching in the American West.
easy.hint: Low inputs, low yields per hectare, large areas.

easy.a: Farming without synthetic fertilisers or pesticides, using natural methods to maintain soil health and control pests.
easy.hint: Organic food is more expensive but has lower chemical inputs.

easy.q: What is the difference between a city and a suburb?
easy.a: City: the central urban area with high density, commerce, services. Suburb: residential areas on the outskirts of a city, lower density, typically housing.
easy.hint: People often live in suburbs but commute to the city for work.

easy.a: An area outside towns and cities, characterised by low population density and farming or natural land use.
easy.hint: Villages and the countryside are rural.

easy.a: The transitional zone at the edge of a city where urban and rural land uses meet and sometimes conflict.
easy.hint: Think of the edge of a city where houses give way to fields.

easy.q: Name two problems caused by traffic congestion in cities.
easy.a: Air pollution, wasted time, increased accident risk, noise pollution, economic costs (delayed goods), carbon emissions.
easy.hint: Think about what happens when too many cars use the same roads.

easy.a: A zone of protected open land around a city, where development is restricted to prevent urban sprawl.
easy.hint: London's green belt prevents the city from growing into surrounding countryside.

medium.q: Explain the difference between voluntary and forced migration, with examples.
medium.a: Voluntary: economic migrants choosing to move for better opportunities (Polish workers in UK). Forced: people displaced against their will by war, persecution, famine, environmental disaster (Syrian refugees, Rohingya). Distinction blurs: is famine 'forcing' people if there is technically no alternative?
medium.hint: Think about the degree of choice β€” but also consider how much choice exists for someone facing starvation.

medium.q: Describe the impacts of migration on both origin and destination countries.
medium.a: Origin: brain drain (lose skilled workers), remittances sent back (economic benefit), population decrease. Destination: fills labour gaps, cultural enrichment, pressure on services (housing, schools, hospitals), demographic change.
medium.hint: Think about both sides β€” who benefits and who loses in each country?

medium.q: Explain how development can be measured using multiple indicators.
medium.a: GDP/GNI per capita (income), HDI (combines income + life expectancy + education), infant mortality rate, literacy rate, access to clean water, COβ‚‚ emissions, Gini coefficient (inequality). Single measures miss dimensions β€” HDI better captures human wellbeing than GDP alone.
medium.hint: Think about whether money alone tells you how good a country is to live in.

medium.q: Describe the formation of coastal cliffs through erosion.
medium.a: Waves attack the cliff base through hydraulic action, abrasion and solution. A wave-cut notch forms at the waterline. The overhang becomes unsupported and collapses. The process repeats, cliffs retreat, leaving a wave-cut platform at the base.
medium.hint: Think about where the sea is most powerful and what happens to the cliff over time.

medium.q: Explain the formation of a river delta.
medium.a: As a river meets the sea, it slows and deposits sediment it has been carrying. Sediment builds up faster than waves can remove it, creating a fan-shaped landform at the mouth. Examples: Nile, Mississippi, Ganges-Brahmaputra.
medium.hint: Think about what happens when a fast-moving river suddenly slows down β€” where does its load go?

medium.q: Describe the causes and consequences of urban heat islands.
medium.a: Causes: dark surfaces absorb heat, lack of vegetation (no evapotranspiration cooling), waste heat from vehicles/buildings/industry, tall buildings trap air. Consequences: higher temperatures (3β€“5Β°C warmer), increased cooling energy demand, health risks (heat stress), altered local rainfall patterns.
medium.hint: Think about what cities are made of versus what countryside is made of, and how each affects temperature.

medium.q: Explain how the global distribution of fossil fuels has shaped geopolitics.
medium.a: Oil concentrated in Middle East, Russia, Venezuela, Nigeria β†’ OPEC cartel, oil price manipulation. US energy policy shaped by oil dependence. Gulf Wars, Russia-Europe gas disputes, Nigerian oil conflicts all linked to fossil fuel geography. Energy security is a major driver of international politics.
medium.hint: Think about why countries fight over oil-rich regions and why energy-poor nations are more dependent on energy-rich ones.

medium.q: Describe two strategies used to manage rivers to reduce flood risk.
medium.a: Hard: embankments/levees (raise banks), channelisation (straighten river to increase speed), flood control reservoirs, flood barriers (Thames Barrier). Soft: afforestation (intercepts rain), managed retreat (allow flooding of marginal land), sustainable drainage, floodplain restoration.
medium.hint: Think about both fighting floods with engineering and working with natural processes.

medium.q: Explain the difference between weather and climate, and why climate prediction is possible but weather prediction is limited.
medium.a: Weather: short-term atmospheric conditions (hours/days) β€” chaotic system, sensitive to initial conditions, accurate prediction beyond ~10 days almost impossible. Climate: average patterns over decades β€” driven by stable forcing factors (solar radiation, ocean circulation, greenhouse gases), predictable using physics-based models.
medium.hint: Think about why we can confidently say 'summers will be hotter by 2100' but can't predict next Tuesday's weather beyond a week.

medium.q: Describe the impacts of sea level rise on different types of coastal areas.
medium.a: Low-lying deltas (Bangladesh, Nile): flooding, saltwater intrusion, displacement of millions. Pacific island nations (Tuvalu, Maldives): entire nations at risk of disappearing. Developed coasts (UK, Netherlands): costly coastal defence. Wetlands and mangroves: submerged, removing coastal protection and biodiversity.
medium.hint: Think about which coastlines are most vulnerable and what the consequences are for each.

medium.q: Explain the concept of 'trade deficit' and 'trade surplus'.
medium.a: Trade deficit: country imports more than it exports in value. Trade surplus: exports exceed imports. UK: large trade deficit (imports many goods, exports services). Germany: large surplus (manufacturing powerhouse). Neither is automatically good or bad β€” depends on what is being traded.
medium.hint: Think about whether it matters if a country buys more than it sells to other countries.

medium.q: Describe the geographic distribution of tropical cyclones and explain why they form there.
medium.a: Form over tropical oceans (8Β°β€“20Β° N/S) with surface temperatures above 26Β°C. Sea evaporates, releasing latent heat. Rising air rotates (Coriolis effect). Self-reinforcing spiral develops. Found: Caribbean, Bay of Bengal, South China Sea, Western Pacific.
medium.hint: Think about the energy source (warm water) and the rotation mechanism (Coriolis effect).

medium.q: Explain how the distribution of water on Earth creates inequality.
medium.a: 97.5% of water is salt water. 2.5% fresh, but 70% locked in ice caps. Only 0.75% accessible as groundwater and surface water. Uneven distribution: Middle East/sub-Saharan Africa water-scarce; Canada/Brazil water-rich. Water scarcity affects billions, particularly in LEDC tropical/subtropical zones.
medium.hint: Think about how much fresh water there actually is, where it is, and whether it matches where people live.

medium.q: Describe the formation of glacial landforms in the UK.
medium.a: During ice ages, glaciers carved: U-shaped valleys (Borrowdale), corries/cirques (cwms in Wales), arΓtes (knife-edge ridges), hanging valleys, ribbon lakes (Windermere), drumlins and moraines (deposited material). All evidence of glacial erosion and deposition.
medium.hint: Think about what a huge, heavy, slow-moving river of ice does to a landscape over thousands of years.

medium.q: Explain how population pyramids reveal information about a country's development stage.
medium.a: Wide base, narrow top (Stage 1/2): high birth rate, high death rate, low life expectancy β†’ LEDC. Narrower base, wide middle (Stage 3): falling birth rate, older population β†’ middle income. Near-rectangular or top-heavy (Stage 4): low birth rate, low death rate, ageing population β†’ MEDC.
medium.hint: Think about what different shapes at different parts of the pyramid tell you about births, deaths and life expectancy.

medium.q: What are the advantages and disadvantages of wind energy?
medium.a: Advantages: renewable, no COβ‚‚ when operating, increasingly cheap, can be offshore or rural, no water needed. Disadvantages: intermittent (no wind = no power), visual impact, noise, bird strike risk, transmission from remote locations, not always where demand is.
medium.hint: Think about why wind energy is growing rapidly despite some significant limitations.

medium.q: Explain the concept of the 'multiplier effect' in economic development.
medium.a: When a new industry arrives, it creates jobs. Workers earn income and spend locally β†’ more demand for services β†’ more jobs created. This 'multiplies' the economic impact of the initial investment. The multiplier is higher when money stays in the local economy.
medium.hint: Think about what happens to the money that a new factory worker earns β€” where does it go?

medium.q: Describe the challenges of waste management in rapidly growing cities.
medium.a: Volume outpaces infrastructure: open dumps, informal waste picking, plastic entering waterways, health impacts (disease vectors), methane from landfill (climate), e-waste toxicity. Solutions: recycling infrastructure, waste-to-energy, composting, formal waste economy, consumer reduction.
medium.hint: Think about what happens when millions of people produce rubbish faster than a city can collect and dispose of it.

medium.q: Explain what is meant by 'food miles' and evaluate its usefulness as an environmental measure.
medium.a: Food miles: distance food travels from producer to consumer. More miles = more transport emissions. Limitation: not just distance β€” method of transport (ship vs air: vast difference), growing method (heated UK greenhouse uses more energy than Spanish outdoor farm despite shorter distance), seasonality. Food miles alone is an oversimplification.
medium.hint: Think about whether a tomato grown in a heated UK greenhouse really has a smaller carbon footprint than one grown in Spain and shipped.

medium.q: Describe two environmental impacts of intensive agriculture.
medium.a: Eutrophication: fertiliser runoff enriches water, causing algal blooms that deplete oxygen, killing fish. Pesticide accumulation: bioaccumulation in food chains. Soil degradation: compaction, loss of organic matter. Water extraction: depleting aquifers. Loss of hedgerows and biodiversity.
medium.hint: Think about what happens when chemicals designed to boost food production enter the wider environment.

medium.q: Explain the difference between hard and soft coastal management approaches.
medium.a: Hard: sea walls (reflect waves), groynes (trap beach material), rock armour/rip-rap (absorb energy), revetments. High cost, may shift erosion elsewhere. Soft: beach nourishment (add sand), managed retreat (planned flooding), dune restoration. More sustainable, less costly, but less certain.
medium.hint: Hard = fight the sea. Soft = work with it. What are the trade-offs?

medium.q: Describe how cities in developing countries differ from those in developed countries.
medium.a: Developing: rapid growth (urbanisation without industrialisation), large informal economy, slum settlements (favelas, shanty towns), poor infrastructure, pollution, but often vibrant economies. Developed: slower growth, car-dependent suburbs, gentrification, homelessness. Both face inequality; different manifestations.
medium.hint: Think about Mumbai vs London β€” both are major cities but what are the differences in their challenges?

medium.q: Explain what 'fair trade' is and evaluate its effectiveness.
medium.a: Fair trade: minimum price guarantee + social premium for communities. Benefits: direct income boost, community investment, women empowered. Limitations: small share of global trade, certified producers often cooperatives not poorest farmers, higher retail price reduces demand, doesn't address systemic trade inequality.
medium.hint: Is paying more for a fair trade banana enough to address global trade inequality?

medium.q: Describe the geographic pattern of natural hazard vulnerability.
medium.a: Tectonic: Ring of Fire, Mediterranean, Himalayan belt (earthquakes/volcanoes). Tropical storms: 8Β°β€“20Β° latitude, warm ocean zones. Floods: river floodplains, low-lying coasts. Droughts: sub-Saharan Africa, Mediterranean, Australia. Vulnerability is not just about location but development level β€” poor countries suffer most.
medium.hint: Think about both WHERE hazards occur and who suffers most when they do.

medium.q: Explain the relationship between population growth and environmental pressure.
medium.a: More people β†’ more food demand (deforestation, water use), more energy (COβ‚‚), more waste, more land use. But: population growth concentrated in LEDCs with low consumption per person. Rich countries with declining populations have far higher environmental footprints. Total impact = population Γ— consumption per person.
medium.hint: A US citizen uses ~50x more resources than a Malawian. Who is causing more environmental pressure?

medium.q: Describe how rivers are managed for multiple uses and the conflicts that arise.
medium.a: Uses: water supply, irrigation, recreation, fishing, transport, flood control, hydroelectric power. Conflicts: dams for HEP flood farmland; irrigation reduces flow for downstream users; recreation conflicts with industrial extraction; flood control walls change sedimentation patterns. River management requires balancing competing stakeholders.
medium.hint: Think about all the different things people want from the same river β€” and how those wants conflict.

medium.q: Explain the causes and human consequences of drought.
medium.a: Causes: climate variability, jet stream changes, La NiΓ±a, deforestation, overuse of groundwater. Human consequences: crop failure β†’ food insecurity, water shortage β†’ disease (waterborne), migration to cities, economic collapse, political instability, famine.
medium.hint: Follow the chain from lack of rain to human suffering.

medium.q: Evaluate the effectiveness of overseas development aid in reducing global inequality.
medium.a: Benefits: emergency relief saves lives, infrastructure investment (roads, schools), technical expertise. Criticism: creates dependency, diverts resources to donor-preferred projects, tied aid forces recipient to buy from donor country, corruption diverts funds, doesn't address structural trade inequality. Most effective: targeted, long-term, community-led.
medium.hint: Think about the difference between giving food to people who are starving and helping them grow their own food.

medium.q: Describe and explain the pattern of global atmospheric circulation.
medium.a: Equator: intense heating β†’ low pressure (ITCZ) β†’ rising air β†’ diverges towards poles. 30Β° N/S: descends β†’ high pressure (subtropical highs) β†’ trade winds towards equator, westerlies towards poles. 60Β° N/S: cold/warm air meets β†’ low pressure. Poles: cold, high pressure, easterlies.
medium.hint: Think about where air rises (equator, 60Β°) and where it sinks (30Β°, poles) and what this creates.

medium.q: Explain how the concept of 'ecological footprint' differs between countries.
medium.a: Ecological footprint measures land area needed to supply a person's resources and absorb waste. USA: ~8.1 gha; UK: ~5.1 gha; China: ~3.7 gha; India: ~1.2 gha; global average: ~2.8 gha; Earth's biocapacity: ~1.6 gha. Most rich countries use 3β€“5Γ— their fair share.
medium.hint: Think about how consumption levels relate to environmental impact.

medium.q: Describe two ways that technology has changed the geography of economic activity.
medium.a: Internet: enables remote working (decentralises offices), e-commerce (challenges high street retail geography), global supply chains more complex. Automation: reduces labour advantage of LEDCs (key reason for offshoring), may reshape manufacturing geography. Both: disrupt established geographic patterns of production and employment.
medium.hint: Think about where work was done 30 years ago versus where it is done now, and why.

medium.q: Explain what is meant by the 'urban hierarchy' and how it relates to service provision.
medium.a: Urban hierarchy: settlement sizes from hamlet β†’ village β†’ town β†’ city β†’ conurbation β†’ megacity. Higher in hierarchy: more services (more varied, more specialised), larger sphere of influence (catchment area), more people travel to access them. Low-order settlements have fewer, more basic services.
medium.hint: Think about why you'd travel to a city for a specialist hospital but use a local GP in a small town.

medium.q: What is the relationship between transport infrastructure and economic development?
medium.a: Good transport: reduces transaction costs, enables market integration, facilitates labour mobility, allows specialisation. Poor transport (landlocked countries, poor roads): adds cost to exports, limits market access, constrains development. Infrastructure investment often precedes development; but causation can run both ways.
medium.hint: Why are landlocked countries often among the poorest? What does being near a port mean for trade?

medium.q: Explain what is meant by 'environmental determinism' and why modern geographers reject it.
medium.a: Environmental determinism: geography/climate determines human culture and development (e.g. tropical climates make people 'lazy', temperate climates create industriousness). Rejected: racist overtones, ignores human agency and institutions, countless exceptions (tropical Singapore, temperate but poor Moldova). Geography influences but does not determine.
medium.hint: If tropical climate caused laziness, why is Singapore one of the world's most productive economies?

medium.q: Describe the challenges of providing adequate housing in rapidly growing cities.
medium.a: Scale: millions arrive faster than formal housing can be built. Cost: poor migrants cannot afford formal housing. Land: city land owned/expensive. Result: informal settlements (slums) emerge. Solutions: self-help schemes, site-and-service, slum upgrading, social housing. All require political will, funding and time.
medium.hint: Think about what happens when a city grows by 1 million people in a decade and formal house building can't keep up.

hard.q: Critically evaluate the concept of 'development' and whether it is a value-neutral term.
hard.a: Development often means 'becoming like a Western market economy' β€” measuring GDP/HDI reflects Western economic values. Alternative frameworks: Amartya Sen's capabilities approach (human freedom), Bhutan's Gross National Happiness, post-development theory (development as a Western imposition). The term is not neutral β€” it encodes assumptions about what 'better' looks like.
hard.hint: Who defined what 'developed' means? Do all cultures want the same thing from development?

hard.q: Explain how the geography of climate change impacts is unjust, relating it to who is responsible.
hard.a: Highest COβ‚‚ emitters historically: USA, Europe, China (industrialised nations). Worst affected: low-lying developing countries (Bangladesh, Pacific islands), Sub-Saharan Africa (drought). The countries least responsible for emissions suffer most. This 'climate injustice' raises ethical obligations for adaptation finance from rich nations.
hard.hint: Think about who caused the problem and who is paying the price.

hard.q: Analyse the political geography of water rights conflicts.
hard.a: Water doesn't respect borders. Nile: Ethiopia's Grand Renaissance Dam vs Egypt's existential water security. Jordan River: Israel/Palestine/Jordan competing claims. Colorado River: overallocated between US states and Mexico. As climate change reduces freshwater, these conflicts will intensify β€” water as a 'conflict resource' growing.
hard.hint: Think about why water creates conflict: it's necessary for life, unevenly distributed, and crosses political boundaries.

hard.q: Evaluate the sustainability of current agricultural systems in feeding a growing world population.
hard.a: Industrial agriculture: high yields but: topsoil depletion, water overuse, biodiversity loss, antibiotic resistance, fossil fuel dependency. 10 billion people by 2050 requires 50β€“70% more food. Options: sustainable intensification, agroecology, diet shift (less meat), food waste reduction, gene editing. No single solution β€” requires transformation across all areas.
hard.hint: Think about whether current farming methods can be scaled up or whether they're already at their limit.

hard.q: How does the geopolitics of the Arctic region illustrate broader themes of resource competition and sovereignty?
hard.a: Melting ice reveals: oil/gas reserves, new shipping routes, fish stocks. Competing claims: Russia (majority Arctic continental shelf claim), US, Canada, Norway, Denmark. Russia asserting military presence. Legal framework (UNCLOS) inadequate for new territory. Microcosm of how climate change creates new geopolitical flashpoints.
hard.hint: Think about all the things that become valuable when ice melts, and who has claims on them.

hard.q: Critically assess whether megacities are sustainable.
hard.a: Environmental unsustainability: energy/water intensity, heat islands, waste, pollution. Economic: agglomeration economies are efficient (services, labour markets). Social: inequality extreme (slums alongside luxury). Sustainability depends entirely on governance and investment β€” Singapore/Singapore (city-state) vs Lagos/Karachi (chronic underfunding). Megacities are neither inherently sustainable nor unsustainable.
hard.hint: Think about whether the problem is cities being big or cities being badly planned and underfunded.

hard.q: Explain how globalisation has transformed the geography of production in the last 50 years.
hard.a: Offshoring: manufacturing moved from high-wage (US, UK) to low-wage (China, Bangladesh, Vietnam). Global supply chains: Apple iPhone made with components from 40+ countries. Services relocated (call centres to India). Digital economy: some production/services can be anywhere. Creates 'geography of exploitation' alongside efficiency gains.
hard.hint: Think about where your clothes are made and why that location was chosen.

hard.q: Evaluate the claim that borders are the greatest obstacle to global development.
hard.a: For: restrict movement of people (migration bans prevent workers from going where wages are highest), create tariff barriers, limit spread of ideas. Against: some protection for developing industries, prevent exploitation, maintain cultural identity, unlimited migration may destabilise. Real question: who can cross borders freely (capital, goods) vs who cannot (poor people).
hard.hint: Capital moves freely; poor people face walls. What does this asymmetry tell you?

hard.q: How do physical geography constraints affect economic development? Use two contrasting examples.
hard.a: Landlocked (Ethiopia/Central Asia): transportation costs 50% higher; limited trade access; economic disadvantage. Coastal/river-based (Singapore/Netherlands): low-cost trade, port economy. Mountains: barrier and resource (tourism, hydro). None of these is deterministic β€” but all create constraints or advantages that require different strategies to address.
hard.hint: Compare what it takes to export a tonne of goods from Switzerland versus the Netherlands.

hard.q: Explain what 'just transition' means in geography and why it is contentious.
hard.a: Just transition: ensuring the shift to a low-carbon economy is fair β€” workers in fossil fuel industries get retraining and support, not just unemployment. Contentious: unions want to slow the transition; environmentalists want faster change; developing countries argue they shouldn't bear costs of transitions for problems created by rich countries.
hard.hint: Think about the coal miners of South Wales or Appalachia β€” what do they deserve when the industry ends?

hard.q: Analyse how the geography of disease intersects with global inequality.
hard.a: Tropical diseases (malaria, Chagas, schistosomiasis) kill millions in LEDCs with little pharmaceutical research (not profitable). COVID-19 vaccine distribution: rich countries vaccinated first. Healthcare infrastructure determines whether diseases become endemic or are controlled. Geographic vulnerability + structural inequality = 'diseases of poverty'.
hard.hint: Why do diseases that kill millions in Africa receive less research funding than conditions affecting thousands in rich countries?

hard.q: Describe and explain the concept of 'planetary boundaries', applying it to two specific boundaries.
hard.a: RockstrΓ¶m's nine planetary boundaries mark safe operating limits for Earth systems. 1) Climate change: atmospheric COβ‚‚ safe boundary ~350 ppm; currently ~420 ppm β€” exceeded. 2) Biodiversity loss: safe level ~10 extinctions per million species per year; current rate 100β€“1000Γ— higher β€” massively exceeded. Beyond boundaries: risk of irreversible Earth system change.
hard.hint: Think about what happens to the Earth system when these boundaries are crossed.

hard.q: Evaluate the evidence that the world is approaching a 'water crisis'.
hard.a: Water use has grown 6Γ— in the past century. 2 billion people currently live in water-stressed areas. Key aquifers (Ogallala, Arabian) depleted faster than recharged. Climate change: shifts rainfall patterns, increases evaporation, melts glaciers (short-term increase, long-term collapse). Demand from agriculture (70%), industry, urbanisation all rising. Trajectory: unsustainable without fundamental efficiency improvements.
hard.hint: Think about the supply side (where freshwater comes from and whether it's replenishing) and the demand side (how much we use and whether that's growing).

hard.q: How does the geography of renewable energy resources create new dependencies and inequalities?
hard.a: Renewable transition requires: cobalt (Congo), lithium (Chile/Bolivia/Argentina β€” the Lithium Triangle), rare earth metals (China has 85% of processing capacity). New resource dependencies replacing oil dependencies. Communities near mines may face environmental damage similar to fossil fuel extraction. Rich countries may design systems that maintain their advantage.
hard.hint: Think about whether the green energy transition creates a new version of the old resource geopolitics.

hard.q: Explain how coastal management decisions reflect political, economic and social priorities.
hard.a: Hard defences (sea walls) protect property values but are expensive and may displace erosion elsewhere. Managed retreat (allow coastline to move) is often most sustainable but requires compensating landowners and displacing communities. Who decides: central government, local authority, community? Each reflects different values β€” property rights vs ecosystem services vs community tradition.
hard.hint: Think about who has the power to make decisions about coastlines and what interests each decision-maker serves.

hard.q: Assess the view that rapid urbanisation in Sub-Saharan Africa is fundamentally different from the historical urbanisation of Europe.
hard.a: Different: urbanisation without industrialisation (primate city development without manufacturing jobs); speed (London took 200 years to grow to 8 million; Lagos took 30); colonial legacy (infrastructure designed for extraction, not urban growth); demographics (still young, high-growth populations). Similar: slum formation, inequality, rural-urban migration drivers. Requires different policy responses.
hard.hint: Think about whether policies designed for 19th-century European cities make sense for 21st-century African cities.

hard.q: Explain the tension between national sovereignty and global environmental governance.
hard.a: Climate change requires collective action beyond national borders β€” but nations guard sovereignty over energy policy, land use, emissions. UNFCCC, Paris Agreement: voluntary commitments β€” no enforcement mechanism. Rich nations resist binding targets (economic cost); poor nations resist caps on development (moral unfairness). A global commons problem with no global government.
hard.hint: Think about why the tragedy of the commons is so hard to solve when the commons is the entire atmosphere.

hard.q: How does the geography of forced displacement create long-term geopolitical challenges?
hard.a: 30+ million refugees; 80+ million internally displaced. Concentrated in unstable regions: Syria, DRC, Myanmar, South Sudan. Regional burden: Turkey, Jordan, Lebanon host millions (disproportionate to size/wealth). Integration challenges: camps become permanent cities. Political backlash in host countries. Climate change will create further displacement (projected 200+ million by 2050).
hard.hint: Think about the scale, the distribution of responsibility, and why displacement tends to create more instability.

hard.q: Critically evaluate the Rostow model of development and alternatives to it.
hard.a: Rostow (1960): five stages from traditional society to high consumption β€” linear, Westernised. Critiques: doesn't explain all trajectories (Korea vs Philippines at same starting point took different paths); ignores dependency theory (external factors like colonialism); ignores environment; doesn't predict which stage countries are in. Alternative: dependency theory, world systems theory (Wallerstein), capability approach (Sen), post-development.
hard.hint: Why does the Rostow model fit US experience quite well but struggle to explain sub-Saharan African development?

hard.q: Explain how 'smart cities' technology could address urban sustainability challenges, and what the risks are.
hard.a: Opportunities: real-time traffic management reduces congestion and emissions; smart meters reduce energy waste; sensors detect infrastructure failure; AI optimises waste collection routes; data enables better planning. Risks: surveillance capitalism, data privacy, exclusion of tech-poor populations, infrastructure vulnerability to cyber attack, corporate control of public goods.
hard.hint: Think about who designs smart cities and in whose interest they are run.

hard.q: Describe how the concept of 'environmental justice' challenges traditional geographical approaches to hazard management.
hard.a: Environmental justice recognises that hazard impacts are unequally distributed by race, class and gender. Traditional hazard management: physical risk assessment, engineering solutions. Environmental justice adds: who decides where hazardous facilities go? Who is evacuated first? Who rebuilds? Black communities in New Orleans were disproportionately affected by Katrina β€” not just because of geography but because of systemic racism.
hard.hint: Think about whether geographical location alone explains who suffers most from hazards β€” or whether social factors compound the risk.

hard.q: Assess how satellite technology has transformed geographical knowledge and its geopolitical implications.
hard.a: Transformed: global mapping (Google Earth), climate monitoring (ice loss, deforestation measured), humanitarian response (disaster assessment), precision agriculture, weather forecasting, GPS navigation. Geopolitical: military surveillance, anti-satellite weapons (China, US, Russia), GPS dependence creates vulnerability, monitoring of human rights abuses. Satellites both democratise information and concentrate power.
hard.hint: Think about who controls satellites and what advantages that gives them.

hard.q: Why is the concept of 'resilience' increasingly central to geography and how is it applied to cities?
hard.a: Resilience: capacity to absorb shocks, adapt and recover. Applied to cities: diverse economies (not dependent on one industry), redundant infrastructure (multiple transport routes), social cohesion, adaptive governance, ecological buffers (green infrastructure). Cities that are resilient to: climate events, economic shocks, pandemics, social unrest. The concept bridges physical and human geography.
hard.hint: Think about what made some cities cope better with COVID-19 or recent floods than others.

hard.q: Evaluate the geopolitical significance of control over the internet infrastructure.
hard.a: Internet runs on physical infrastructure: undersea cables (most global internet), data centres, satellite networks. Control: US companies dominate cloud (AWS, Google, Microsoft); China building parallel infrastructure; undersea cables key vulnerability (sabotage/intelligence). Internet sovereignty vs open internet: China's 'Great Firewall', Russia's 'RuNet'. Who controls infrastructure controls information flows.
hard.hint: Think about what it means that most of the world's internet traffic passes through undersea cables that could be cut.

hard.q: How does the concept of 'spatial inequality' manifest differently at local, national and global scales?
hard.a: Local: within-city inequalities (rich neighbourhoods vs slums share the same city). National: regional inequalities (northern England vs London; coastal China vs interior). Global: MEDC/LEDC wealth gap. Common drivers: agglomeration economies, historical factors, infrastructure access, political power. Spatial inequality self-reinforces β€” resources concentrate where resources already are.
hard.hint: Think about how inequalities at different scales look similar in mechanism even if different in scale.

easy.hint: It shows how energy flows between many different organisms.

easy.q: What are the three states of matter?
easy.a: Solid, liquid, gas
easy.hint: Water exists as ice (solid), water (liquid), and steam (gas).

easy.q: What type of rock is formed from cooled lava?
easy.a: Igneous rock
easy.hint: Magma cools and solidifies to form this type of rock.

easy.a: An animal that hunts and eats other animals
easy.hint: Lions, wolves, and sharks are examples.

easy.q: What organ pumps blood around the body?
easy.a: The heart
easy.hint: This muscular organ beats about 60β€“100 times per minute in humans.

easy.q: What is the role of the lungs?
easy.a: To take in oxygen and remove carbon dioxide from the blood
easy.hint: Gas exchange occurs in tiny air sacs called alveoli.

easy.a: The stage of physical development where a child matures into an adult
easy.hint: It is triggered by hormones and usually occurs between ages 8-16.

easy.q: What does the skeletal system do?
easy.a: Supports the body, protects organs, and allows movement
easy.hint: It also produces blood cells in the bone marrow.

easy.a: The curved path a planet or moon takes around another object
easy.hint: Earth's orbit around the Sun takes 365.25 days.

easy.q: What is the Sun made of?
easy.a: Mainly hydrogen and helium gas
easy.hint: Nuclear fusion of hydrogen into helium releases the Sun's energy.

easy.q: What is a year on Earth based on?
easy.a: Earth's orbit around the Sun (365.25 days)
easy.hint: Every 4 years we add an extra day (leap year) to account for the extra 0.25.

easy.a: Does not let light through
easy.hint: You cannot see through an opaque material. A brick wall is opaque.

easy.a: Any one of: solar, wind, hydro, geothermal, tidal
easy.hint: Renewable sources won't run out and often produce little pollution.

easy.a: The natural environment where an organism lives
easy.hint: It provides food, shelter, and other needs for the organism.

easy.q: What is the process by which plants make food?
easy.a: Photosynthesis
easy.hint: Photo = light, synthesis = making. Plants use light to make glucose.

easy.a: A change that cannot be undone
easy.hint: Burning wood or baking a cake are irreversible changes.

easy.a: A change that can be undone
easy.hint: Melting ice is reversible β€” it can refreeze.

easy.q: What force keeps planets in orbit around the Sun?
easy.a: Gravity
easy.hint: The Sun's massive gravitational pull keeps planets in their orbits.

easy.a: Jupiter or Saturn (also Uranus and Neptune are ice giants)
easy.hint: These large planets are made mostly of gas, with no solid surface.

easy.a: The force of gravity acting on an object's mass
easy.hint: Weight is measured in Newtons, not kilograms.

easy.q: What is the difference between mass and weight?
easy.a: Mass is the amount of matter; weight is the gravitational force on that mass
easy.hint: Your mass stays the same on the Moon, but your weight decreases.

easy.q: What does a spring balance (force meter) measure?
easy.a: Force (in Newtons)
easy.hint: It works by measuring how much a spring stretches under a force.

easy.a: A simple machine using a wheel and rope to change the direction or magnitude of a force
easy.hint: A single pulley changes the direction of force; multiple pulleys reduce the effort needed.

easy.q: What is the nearest planet to Earth?
easy.a: Venus (on average)
easy.hint: Although Mars gets closer at times, Venus is closest on average.

easy.q: Name the gas that makes up most of Earth's atmosphere.
easy.a: Nitrogen (about 78%)
easy.hint: Oxygen makes up about 21%; the remaining 1% includes argon and COβ‚‚.

easy.a: A natural satellite that orbits a planet
easy.hint: Our Moon orbits Earth, but other planets have moons too.

medium.q: Why does Earth experience seasons?
medium.a: Because Earth's axis is tilted (23.5Β°) relative to its orbit around the Sun
medium.hint: When the Northern Hemisphere tilts towards the Sun, it experiences summer.

medium.q: How long does it take the Moon to orbit Earth?
medium.a: Approximately 27.3 days (a lunar month)
medium.hint: This is why we see different phases of the Moon over about 4 weeks.

medium.q: What are the phases of the Moon?
medium.a: New moon β†’ crescent β†’ quarter β†’ gibbous β†’ full moon β†’ gibbous β†’ quarter β†’ crescent β†’ new moon
medium.hint: The Moon's appearance changes as different portions are lit by the Sun.

medium.q: Explain how a lever reduces the effort needed to lift a heavy object.
medium.a: By placing the load close to the fulcrum and applying force further away, a small effort can lift a large load (mechanical advantage).
medium.hint: The longer the effort arm compared to the load arm, the greater the mechanical advantage.

medium.q: Why do objects fall at the same speed in a vacuum (ignoring air resistance)?
medium.a: Gravity accelerates all objects equally regardless of mass (9.8 m/sΒ² on Earth)
medium.hint: Galileo demonstrated this β€” a feather and a hammer fall at the same rate in a vacuum.

medium.q: What is the difference between a solute, solvent, and solution?
medium.a: Solute: the substance that dissolves; solvent: the liquid it dissolves in; solution: the resulting mixture
medium.hint: Salt (solute) dissolves in water (solvent) to make brine (solution).

medium.q: How does a parachute slow a falling person?
medium.a: It increases the surface area, which increases air resistance and reduces the downward acceleration.
medium.hint: Greater air resistance balances more of the gravitational force.

medium.q: What happens to light when it passes from air into glass?
medium.a: It slows down and bends (refracts) towards the normal
medium.hint: Refraction occurs when light changes speed as it moves between media.

medium.q: Explain the life cycle of a frog.
medium.a: Egg β†’ tadpole β†’ froglet β†’ adult frog
medium.hint: This process of changing form is called metamorphosis.

medium.q: What is the difference between a herbivore, carnivore, and omnivore?
medium.a: Herbivore: eats only plants; carnivore: eats only animals; omnivore: eats both plants and animals
medium.hint: Humans are omnivores β€” we can eat both.

medium.q: Why is the Sun larger in appearance during sunset?
medium.a: This is an optical illusion; the Sun's apparent size doesn't actually change β€” it's perceived as larger near the horizon due to surrounding reference objects.
medium.hint: Compare the Sun at sunset to the Moon β€” the Moon effect is similar.

medium.q: Explain what happens when iron rusts.
medium.a: Iron reacts with oxygen and water (moisture) to form iron oxide (rust) β€” an irreversible chemical change.
medium.hint: Rust is a new substance (iron oxide). Can you reverse this?

medium.q: What is the difference between a physical and chemical change?
medium.a: Physical: no new substance formed (e.g. melting); chemical: new substance(s) formed (e.g. burning)
medium.hint: Physical changes are usually reversible; chemical changes usually aren't.

medium.q: How does the Moon cause tides on Earth?
medium.a: The Moon's gravity pulls on Earth's oceans, creating a bulge of water on the side facing the Moon (and another on the opposite side), causing tides.
medium.hint: High tides occur on the side of Earth facing the Moon and the side facing away.

medium.q: What is the carbon cycle?
medium.a: The process by which carbon moves between the atmosphere, living organisms, and the Earth through photosynthesis, respiration, combustion, and decomposition.
medium.hint: Plants absorb COβ‚‚; animals respire COβ‚‚; decomposers break down organisms releasing COβ‚‚.

medium.q: Explain why it is warmer in summer than in winter.
medium.a: In summer, Earth is tilted towards the Sun, so sunlight hits more directly and days are longer, providing more energy per day.
medium.hint: It's not about distance from the Sun β€” it's about the angle and duration of sunlight.

medium.q: What are the differences between series and parallel circuits?
medium.a: Series: components in one loop; if one breaks, all stop. Parallel: components in separate branches; if one breaks, others continue.
medium.hint: Christmas tree lights used to be in series β€” one broken bulb stopped all.

medium.q: What is natural selection?
medium.a: The process by which organisms with favourable traits are more likely to survive and reproduce, passing those traits to offspring.
medium.hint: Darwin described this as 'survival of the fittest'.

medium.q: How does exercise affect the heart rate?
medium.a: Exercise increases heart rate because muscles need more oxygen and glucose; the heart pumps faster to deliver more blood.
medium.hint: Your breathing also increases during exercise β€” why might that be?

medium.q: What is filtration used for?
medium.a: To separate an insoluble solid from a liquid (e.g. sand from water)
medium.hint: The filter paper allows the liquid through but traps the solid particles.

medium.q: Why is evaporation used to separate a soluble solid from a liquid?
medium.a: Heating the solution causes the liquid to evaporate, leaving the dissolved solid behind.
medium.hint: This is how sea salt is obtained β€” seawater evaporates, leaving salt crystals.

medium.q: What is distillation?
medium.a: A technique that separates liquids with different boiling points by evaporating and then condensing the vapour.
medium.hint: Pure water can be obtained from a solution by distillation.

medium.q: Explain how a shadow changes in size and direction throughout the day.
medium.a: In the morning and evening, shadows are long (Sun is low); at midday, shadows are shortest (Sun is high). Direction changes as the Sun moves from east to west.
medium.hint: Think about the angle of the sunlight relative to the object.

medium.q: What is the difference between translucent and transparent materials?
medium.a: Transparent allows light to pass through clearly (e.g. glass); translucent allows light but scatters it so objects can't be clearly seen (e.g. frosted glass).
medium.hint: Can you see clearly through each type of material?

medium.q: What is gestation?
medium.a: The period of development inside the womb before birth
medium.hint: In humans, gestation is approximately 9 months.

medium.q: Why do we see the Moon shine at night?
medium.a: The Moon does not produce its own light; it reflects sunlight.
medium.hint: The Moon is like a mirror reflecting the Sun's light towards Earth.

medium.q: How do humans change their environment, and what effects can this have?
medium.a: Deforestation, pollution, farming, and building β€” these can destroy habitats, reduce biodiversity, and cause climate change.
medium.hint: Think about deforestation or plastic pollution.

medium.q: What is the difference between weight and mass? Give the unit for each.
medium.a: Mass: amount of matter, measured in kg or g. Weight: gravitational force on that mass, measured in Newtons (N).
medium.hint: On the Moon, your mass stays the same but your weight is about 1/6 of that on Earth.

medium.q: Explain how a rainbow forms.
medium.a: Raindrops act as tiny prisms, refracting and reflecting white sunlight, splitting it into its spectrum of colours (red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet).
medium.hint: Light bends as it enters and exits each raindrop, different colours bending by different amounts.

medium.q: What is photosynthesis and what are its reactants and products?
medium.a: Photosynthesis: COβ‚‚ + Hβ‚‚O + light energy β†’ glucose + Oβ‚‚. Plants make food from carbon dioxide and water using sunlight.
medium.hint: Reactants go in (COβ‚‚ and water); products come out (glucose and oxygen).

medium.q: How does insulation help save energy in a home?
medium.a: Insulation reduces heat transfer through walls, roofs, and windows, keeping the home warmer in winter and cooler in summer, reducing energy use.
medium.hint: Materials like loft insulation or double glazing trap air, which is a poor conductor.

medium.q: What is biodiversity?
medium.a: The variety of living organisms in an area or ecosystem
medium.hint: High biodiversity means many different species living in an area.

medium.q: What is adaptation?
medium.a: A feature of an organism that makes it better suited to its environment
medium.hint: A polar bear's thick fur is an adaptation to cold Arctic conditions.

medium.q: Why do some animals hibernate?
medium.a: To conserve energy during winter when food is scarce and temperatures are low
medium.hint: Hibernating animals slow their heart rate and metabolism.

medium.q: What causes an eclipse of the Sun (solar eclipse)?
medium.a: The Moon passes between the Earth and the Sun, blocking the Sun's light (or part of it) from reaching Earth.
medium.hint: A total eclipse is when the Moon completely covers the Sun's disc.

medium.q: What is chromatography used for?
medium.a: To separate mixtures of dissolved substances (e.g. inks) based on how far they travel through a material
medium.hint: Used in forensics and food testing to identify components of a mixture.

medium.q: Name two uses of magnets.
medium.a: Any two of: fridge magnets, electric motors, compasses, MRI scanners, maglev trains, speakers, door catches
medium.hint: Magnets are used in many electrical devices.

medium.q: What is an electromagnet?
medium.a: A magnet created by passing electric current through a coil of wire around an iron core; it can be switched on and off.
medium.hint: Unlike permanent magnets, this type can be turned off.

medium.q: What is the difference between a star and a planet?
medium.a: Stars produce their own light through nuclear fusion; planets orbit stars and reflect the star's light.
medium.hint: The Sun is a star; Earth is a planet.

medium.q: Explain the water cycle in three steps.
medium.a: 1. Evaporation (water vapour rises from oceans/rivers). 2. Condensation (vapour cools to form clouds). 3. Precipitation (rain or snow falls back to Earth).
medium.hint: The energy from the Sun drives this cycle.

medium.q: What is a force diagram (free body diagram)?
medium.a: A diagram showing all the forces acting on an object as arrows, indicating direction and relative size.
medium.hint: Larger arrows represent bigger forces; balanced forces are equal arrows in opposite directions.

medium.q: What is terminal velocity?
medium.a: The constant maximum speed reached when air resistance equals the downward force of gravity
medium.hint: A skydiver reaches this when forces are balanced and acceleration stops.

medium.q: Why does ice float on water?
medium.a: Ice is less dense than liquid water because its crystal structure spaces molecules further apart.
medium.hint: Most substances are denser as solids, but water is unusual.

medium.q: What is the difference between reproduction in mammals and birds?
medium.a: Mammals give birth to live young (viviparous, usually); birds lay eggs (oviparous).
medium.hint: There are exceptions, like platypuses, which are egg-laying mammals.

medium.q: Describe what happens to particles in a solid when it is heated to its melting point.
medium.a: Particles vibrate more vigorously, gaining enough energy to break free from fixed positions, allowing them to flow β€” the solid becomes a liquid.
medium.hint: At the melting point, energy goes into breaking bonds rather than raising temperature.

medium.q: What is the function of chlorophyll in plants?
medium.a: It absorbs light energy (mainly red and blue wavelengths) and uses it to power photosynthesis.
medium.hint: Chlorophyll also makes plants appear green because it reflects green light.

medium.q: What is compost, and how does it form?
medium.a: Compost is decomposed organic material (e.g. food scraps, leaves). It forms when microorganisms break down organic matter.
medium.hint: Decomposers like bacteria and fungi break down the material over time.

medium.q: How do vaccines protect us from disease?
medium.a: They introduce a weakened or inactive form of a pathogen, prompting the immune system to produce antibodies without causing disease, so the body is prepared if exposed later.
medium.hint: Think of it as training the immune system to recognise and fight a specific germ.

medium.q: What is pollination and why is it important?
medium.a: The transfer of pollen from the male part of a flower to the female part, enabling fertilisation and seed production. Important for plant reproduction and food crops.
medium.hint: Bees and wind are common pollinators.

medium.q: Explain the difference between renewable and non-renewable energy.
medium.a: Renewable: will not run out and is replenished naturally (e.g. solar, wind). Non-renewable: finite supply that will eventually run out (e.g. coal, oil, gas).
medium.hint: Fossil fuels took millions of years to form β€” they cannot be replaced quickly.

hard.q: Explain why the inner planets (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars) are rocky and the outer planets are gas giants.
hard.a: The solar wind from the young Sun blew lighter gases away from the inner Solar System; only rocky, heavier materials condensed close to the Sun. Further out, lighter gases (hydrogen, helium) could remain.
hard.hint: Think about what the early Sun did to lighter elements in the inner Solar System.

hard.q: What is the Doppler effect, and how is it used to detect whether stars are moving towards or away from us?
hard.a: The Doppler effect: apparent change in wave frequency when the source moves relative to the observer. Stars moving away have red-shifted light (longer wavelengths); moving towards show blue shift.
hard.hint: Like a car horn changing pitch as it passes β€” the same principle applies to light.

hard.q: Describe the process of natural selection using an example.
hard.a: E.g. peppered moths: before industrial revolution, light moths survived on pale lichen; dark moths were eaten. After pollution darkened trees, dark moths survived better and bred more, increasing in frequency.
hard.hint: Which trait gives a survival advantage changes when the environment changes.

hard.q: Why is antibiotic resistance a serious global health concern?
hard.a: Overuse/misuse of antibiotics kills susceptible bacteria but allows resistant variants to survive and reproduce. These resistant bacteria spread, making infections harder to treat.
hard.hint: Natural selection applies here β€” bacteria evolve resistance when repeatedly exposed to antibiotics.

hard.q: Explain how the greenhouse effect works and how human activity enhances it.
hard.a: Greenhouse gases (COβ‚‚, methane) absorb infrared radiation emitted by Earth's surface and re-emit it back, warming Earth. Human activities (burning fossil fuels, deforestation) increase COβ‚‚ levels, enhancing the effect.
hard.hint: The natural greenhouse effect is essential; the enhanced greenhouse effect is causing global warming.

hard.q: A student mixes baking soda and vinegar. Give three pieces of evidence that a chemical change has occurred.
hard.a: Any three: bubbling (gas produced), temperature change, irreversibility, new smell, new substance (COβ‚‚) formed
hard.hint: What are the signs that a new substance has been created?

hard.q: Explain why it is colder at the top of a mountain despite being closer to the Sun.
hard.a: The atmosphere is thinner at altitude and absorbs less radiated heat from Earth's surface. Temperature is mainly governed by proximity to the warm Earth surface, not proximity to the Sun.
hard.hint: The Sun heats Earth's surface, which then heats the air above it.

hard.q: Compare and contrast sexual and asexual reproduction.
hard.a: Sexual: two parents, genetic variation, e.g. mammals. Asexual: one parent, genetically identical offspring (clones), e.g. bacteria, some plants. Sexual reproduction creates variation; asexual is faster but creates no variety.
hard.hint: Think about the number of parents and the genetic similarity of offspring.

hard.q: What is the difference between a physical and chemical property? Give one example of each.
hard.a: Physical: can be observed without changing the substance (e.g. melting point, colour, density). Chemical: describes how a substance reacts or changes to form new substances (e.g. flammability, reactivity with acid).
hard.hint: Does observing or measuring the property change the substance?

hard.q: Explain how muscles work in pairs (antagonistic muscles) to move a limb.
hard.a: Muscles can only pull (contract), not push. So they work in pairs: when the bicep contracts to bend the arm, the tricep relaxes, and vice versa.
hard.hint: Think about what happens to your bicep and tricep when you bend and straighten your elbow.

hard.q: Why is the sky blue and sunsets red?
hard.a: Blue light scatters more in the atmosphere (Rayleigh scattering) so it spreads across the sky. At sunset, sunlight travels through more atmosphere, scattering away blue light and leaving red/orange wavelengths.
hard.hint: Shorter wavelengths (blue) scatter more easily; longer wavelengths (red) pass through more atmosphere.

hard.q: Explain what happens to a metal rod when it is heated, at a particle level.
hard.a: Particles in the rod vibrate with more energy and move slightly further apart, causing the rod to expand (thermal expansion). Electrons carry this kinetic energy through the metal quickly.
hard.hint: Think about how particles change their movement and spacing when given more energy.

hard.q: A ball is thrown upwards. Describe all forces acting on it at the top of its trajectory.
hard.a: At the top: gravity acts downwards (weight = mg). Air resistance acts upwards (opposing motion, which is zero/turning point). The ball is momentarily stationary but gravity is still acting.
hard.hint: Gravity always acts. What about air resistance when velocity is momentarily zero?

hard.q: What are trophic levels and why does energy decrease at each level?
hard.a: Trophic levels are feeding stages in a food chain: producers, primary consumers, secondary consumers, etc. Energy decreases because organisms use energy for respiration, movement, and heat at each level (~90% is lost).
hard.hint: Why can an ecosystem support more herbivores than carnivores?

hard.q: Explain what causes the aurora borealis (Northern Lights).
hard.a: Charged particles from the Sun (solar wind) are deflected to the poles by Earth's magnetic field, where they collide with atmospheric gases, exciting them to emit coloured light.
hard.hint: It involves solar wind, Earth's magnetic field, and atmospheric gases.

hard.q: How does the kidney regulate the water content of the body?
hard.a: Kidneys filter blood and adjust the amount of water reabsorbed depending on how hydrated you are. ADH (antidiuretic hormone) tells kidneys to retain more water when dehydrated.
hard.hint: Think about why you produce more/less concentrated urine on a hot day.

hard.q: What would happen to life on Earth if the Sun suddenly disappeared?
hard.a: Earth would drift into space (no gravity to orbit). Temperatures would plummet. Photosynthesis would stop, killing plants, then all life that depends on them. Within days, most life would perish.
hard.hint: Consider what the Sun provides: gravity for orbits, light for photosynthesis, heat for temperature.

hard.q: Why are viruses not classified as living organisms?
hard.a: Viruses cannot reproduce independently β€” they need a host cell's machinery. They lack cellular structure, don't respire, don't grow, and don't respond to their environment. They are considered non-living infectious agents.
hard.hint: Check each characteristic of living things against what viruses can and cannot do.

hard.q: Explain the difference between conduction, convection, and radiation as methods of heat transfer.
hard.a: Conduction: heat transferred through solids via particle vibration. Convection: heat transferred through fluids (liquids/gases) via currents (warm fluid rises). Radiation: heat transferred through electromagnetic waves, needs no medium.
hard.hint: Which can transfer heat through a vacuum? Which requires a fluid? Which needs particles touching?

hard.q: What is the difference between a theory and a law in science?
hard.a: A scientific law describes what happens (e.g. Newton's laws of motion); a theory explains why it happens (e.g. germ theory explains disease). Both are well-supported by evidence.
hard.hint: A law is a description; a theory is an explanation with underlying mechanisms.

hard.q: Explain how a concave mirror focuses light to form an image.
hard.a: Parallel rays of light reflect off the curved concave surface and converge at a focal point. Objects beyond the focal point produce real, inverted images; objects inside produce virtual, magnified images.
hard.hint: Think about how satellite dishes focus signals at one point.

hard.q: How do decomposers contribute to the carbon cycle?
hard.a: Decomposers break down dead organic matter, releasing COβ‚‚ (via respiration) back into the atmosphere and nutrients into the soil, making them available for plants again.
hard.hint: What would happen to all the carbon locked in dead organisms if decomposers didn't exist?

hard.q: Explain why mixing salt into water is a physical change and not a chemical change.
hard.a: No new substance is formed; the salt and water retain their chemical identities. The process is reversible β€” evaporation recovers the salt. The particles are dispersed but not chemically altered.
hard.hint: Can you get the original substances back? Is a new substance formed?

hard.q: What is the significance of the ozone layer and what threatens it?
hard.a: The ozone layer in the stratosphere absorbs harmful UV radiation from the Sun, protecting life on Earth. CFCs (chlorofluorocarbons) destroy ozone molecules, thinning the layer.
hard.hint: What would happen to life if more UV radiation reached Earth's surface?

hard.q: How does blood type inheritance work in a basic sense?
hard.a: Blood type (A, B, AB, O) is determined by alleles inherited from parents. Some alleles are dominant; O is recessive. Different combinations from parents produce different blood types in children.
hard.hint: Think about why two O-type parents can only have O-type children.

hard.q: Explain why space is called a vacuum and what this means for sound and light travel.
hard.a: A vacuum contains no matter (or very little). Sound needs particles to travel so it cannot travel through space. Light (electromagnetic radiation) does not need a medium and can travel through a vacuum.
hard.hint: Sound needs particles; light travels as waves that don't need a medium.

hard.q: What is meant by 'food security' and what threats does climate change pose to it?
hard.a: Food security: reliable access to sufficient, nutritious food. Climate change threatens food security through droughts, flooding, changing growing seasons, and extreme weather damaging crops.
hard.hint: Think about how changes in rainfall, temperature, and weather patterns affect agriculture.

hard.q: Describe the difference between a dominant and recessive allele.
hard.a: A dominant allele's trait is expressed even with one copy (Aa). A recessive allele's trait is only expressed with two copies (aa). Dominant alleles 'mask' recessive ones in heterozygous individuals.
hard.hint: In a pair of alleles, which one 'wins' and which one hides?

hard.q: What is the significance of Charles Darwin's voyage on HMS Beagle?
hard.a: Darwin observed vast diversity of species across continents and island populations (e.g. GalΓ΅pagos finches with different beak shapes). This evidence of adaptation helped him develop his theory of evolution by natural selection.
hard.hint: What did the different species Darwin observed have in common? How did they differ?

hard.q: Why is Earth's core important for life on the surface?
hard.a: The liquid outer core generates Earth's magnetic field (magnetosphere), which deflects harmful solar wind and cosmic radiation, protecting the atmosphere and life.
hard.hint: What protects Mars (which has no active core) from solar wind β€” and what happened to its atmosphere?

hard.q: What is the difference between aerobic and anaerobic respiration?
hard.a: Aerobic: Cβ‚†Hβ‚β‚‚Oβ‚† + Oβ‚‚ β†’ COβ‚‚ + Hβ‚‚O + energy (much energy released). Anaerobic: glucose β†’ lactic acid + small amount of energy (in muscles) or glucose β†’ ethanol + COβ‚‚ + small energy (in yeast).
hard.hint: Which needs oxygen? Which produces more energy?

hard.q: Explain why the tide is high twice a day.
hard.a: Earth's Moon creates a gravitational bulge of water on the side facing the Moon and another bulge on the opposite side due to centrifugal/tidal forces. As Earth rotates once every 24 hours, each location passes through both bulges.
hard.hint: There are two bulges on opposite sides of Earth. How many times does a point on Earth pass through a bulge in 24 hours?

hard.q: How does the distance from a light source affect its intensity?
hard.a: Light intensity decreases with the square of the distance (inverse square law). If you double the distance, the intensity falls to one quarter.
hard.hint: This is called the inverse square law. Think about light spreading out over a larger area.

hard.q: What was significant about the discovery of penicillin?
hard.a: Alexander Fleming discovered (1928) that mould (Penicillium) produced a substance that killed bacteria. This led to the development of antibiotics, revolutionising medicine and saving millions of lives.
hard.hint: What problem had previously made even minor infections potentially fatal?

hard.q: Explain how genetic variation arises in sexual reproduction.
hard.a: During meiosis, chromosomes are shuffled (crossing over, independent assortment) and each parent provides half the genetic material. The combination of two parents' genes creates unique offspring.
hard.hint: Two distinct mechanisms during meiosis increase variation before fertilisation even occurs.

hard.q: Why is biodiversity important for the resilience of an ecosystem?
hard.a: High biodiversity means more species fill each ecological role. If one species declines, others can fill its role. Low biodiversity means the ecosystem is vulnerable to collapse if a key species is lost.
hard.hint: Think about what happens to a food web if the only predator of a pest species disappears.

hard.q: What is DNA and what is its role in the body?
hard.a: DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) carries genetic instructions for the development, function, and reproduction of organisms. It is organised into genes, which code for proteins that carry out the body's functions.
hard.hint: DNA is like a set of blueprints β€” it contains all the instructions needed to build and run an organism.

hard.q: Describe the electromagnetic spectrum in order of wavelength.
hard.a: Radio β†’ microwave β†’ infrared β†’ visible light β†’ ultraviolet β†’ X-rays β†’ gamma rays (from longest wavelength/lowest frequency to shortest/highest).
hard.hint: An acronym like 'Raging Martians Invaded Venus Using X-ray Guns' can help you remember the order.

hard.q: Why does warm air rise?
hard.a: Warm air is less dense than cool air (particles move faster and occupy more space). Less dense air experiences greater buoyancy force than its weight, so it rises; cooler, denser air sinks to replace it.
hard.hint: Think about density: which is lighter per unit volume β€” warm or cold air?

hard.q: What is the difference between an infectious and non-infectious disease? Give one example of each.
hard.a: Infectious: caused by pathogens and can spread between people (e.g. flu, COVID-19). Non-infectious: cannot be transmitted between people (e.g. diabetes, heart disease, genetic conditions).
hard.hint: Can you 'catch' a non-infectious disease from someone else?

hard.q: How does a convex lens produce a magnified image (e.g. in a magnifying glass)?
hard.a: When an object is placed within the focal length of a convex lens, rays diverge after passing through. The brain extends these rays backwards to form a virtual, upright, magnified image on the same side as the object.
hard.hint: Why must you hold a magnifying glass close to an object for it to appear larger?

hard.q: Explain how the size of a shadow changes as an object moves closer to a light source.
hard.a: As the object moves closer to the light source, the shadow becomes larger (the object blocks more of the diverging light). Further away, the shadow shrinks.
hard.hint: Think about how a diverging light source (like a lamp) creates a wider beam.

hard.q: What is meant by 'sustainable development'?
hard.a: Development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs β€” balancing economic growth with environmental protection.
